articles.title: North Korea Confirms September 12 Missile Launch Was Joint Firepower Drill
articles.body:
North Korea’s state media confirmed Monday that a joint firepower drill by artillery and missile units across the Korean People’s Army took place on September 12, matching the timing of a ballistic missile launch that the South Korean military had detected the same day.
On September 12, South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said it detected multiple short-range ballistic missiles launched from the Wonsan area on North Korea’s east coast at around 5:20 a.m. KST Saturday. The missiles flew about 250 kilometers before landing in the ocean to the east of North Korea. The JCS added that its forces were closely monitoring North Korea’s activity under a firm South Korea-U.S. combined defense posture.
Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), one of the North’s state-controlled media, reported on September 14, two days later, that the launch stemmed from a joint firepower attack drill involving subunits from five artillery and missile joint units. The drill incorporated attack drones, a tactical cruise missile, a large-caliber thermal-pressure multiple rocket launcher, and a tactical ballistic missile, the KCNA said.
“It is one of the training tasks prioritized by the army to get familiar with the procedure for the operation of the integrated firepower control system, the systematic component of the strategic weapons combined management system, improve the specialty of the integrated automatic firepower control of various combat systems and increase the efficiency of destroying the targets with concentrated fire,” Director of the Artillery Bureau Yu Chang Son was quoted as saying in the KCNA report.
The launch came a day after South Korea, the United States, and Japan wrapped up Freedom Edge, a five-day trilateral exercise held from September 7 to September 11 to strengthen air, maritime, and cyber coordination against North Korean nuclear and missile threats. North Korea has previously cast both trilateral and South Korea-U.S. drills as provocations. The September 12 drill fits a pattern in which Pyongyang has answered major allied exercises with missile launches almost immediately after they conclude.
The missile test also came as U.S. President Donald Trump has pushed for a new summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, reviving the personal diplomacy that produced three meetings during Trump’s first term but no agreement on Pyongyang’s nuclear program. Trump has discussed meeting Kim during a possible trip to Asia as early as this fall. His aides have weighed a rendezvous around the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, in November, but no formal arrangements have begun.
However, Kim has kept the overture at arm’s length. He did not mention Trump’s outreach when he presided over a Workers’ Party political bureau meeting in late August even as he called for what state media described as “extraordinary responsibility” in carrying out state projects.
Pyongyang’s latest missile launch marked its first ballistic missile test since August 20, when the North fired a barrage of short-range ballistic missiles hours after Trump said he intended to meet Kim later this year. Neither major military exercises nor renewed diplomatic overtures have interrupted the North’s testing tempo this year.
In related developments on September 14, South Korea’s Unification Ministry said it plans to provide Kangdong County Hospital in Pyongyang with 166 types of medical equipment, according to a local media report. The support falls under a health and medical cooperation program aimed at modernizing the North’s rural hospitals, and Kangdong is considered the first completed example of Kim’s push for such facilities. Kim Dae-sik, a legislator with the main opposition People Power Party, who received the document, said the policy of aiding North Korea “while it pursues nuclear weapons” deserved reconsideration.
Separately, South Korea and the U.S. are set to hold their 29th Korea-U.S. Integrated Defense Dialogue in Busan from September 16 to September 18, with attention focused on Washington’s request for a possible South Korean deployment to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iran has blocked shipping since Israeli-U.S. strikes began in February. Seoul and Washington also plan to discuss the transfer of wartime operational control and shipbuilding cooperation.
Seoul said no decision has been made on the Hormuz issue. According to the recent poll surveyed by Hankuk Gallup on September 11, 55 percent of respondents said they do not support deploying troops to the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Ukrainian F-16s Shoot Down Jet Drones – But Is It Enough?
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine has been using US-made F-16 fighters to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones.
Speaking to a television channel during his recent visit to Canada, Zelensky said Ukraine has “sometimes” resorted to Western air-to-air missiles, such as the US-made AIM-9 and AIM-120, to shoot down newer, faster jet-powered drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We use the corresponding missiles on F-16s, shooting down jet drones,” Zelensky said, as reported by state media Ukrinform.
“It is expensive, but sometimes, when nothing can be done to shoot down a particular jet drone, human life is more important and more expensive, so sometimes F-16s were used against such drones,” he added.
Zelensky’s comments came as Canada announced a new $3 billion package for Kyiv, which includes an unspecified number of AIM-9s and AIM-120s.
Recent comments from Yuriy Ihnat, the air force’s spokesperson, suggest that Ukrainian F-16s have at times resorted to onboard 20mm cannons to down jet-powered drones, which he said poses major risks to the aircraft itself. Pilots would be closer to the drones based on their size at open-fire ranges compared to enemy fighters, bombers, or other crewed aircraft; this makes debris from the drones a follow-on hazard to the shooter’s aircraft.
Jet-powered drones, which blur the line between drones and missiles, have been increasingly used by Russia against Ukraine in recent attacks, posing challenges for Ukrainian air defenses as current interceptor drones struggle to catch up with their higher speeds.
Russian Drones Just Miss Former CIA Director David Petraeus: a View From a Train Near the Polish Border
While Ukraine has been developing jet-powered interceptor drones as a countermeasure, Zelensky’s remark suggests a potential gap in Ukrainian air defense, as the AIM-9s and AIM-120s are typically costlier than interceptor drones.
While the latest AIM-9X Sidewinder missile is estimated to cost over $450,000 per unit, Ukrainian Air Force F-16s almost always carry the AIM-9M which cost about $84,000 when originally purchased by the US Air Force (USAF). The AIM-120 is $386,000 per unit, according to the US Air Force – though TWZ reported that some variants can cost over $1 million per missile.
Ukraine began receiving the missiles as part of the armaments for its new NATO-standard aircraft donated by its allies, starting with the F-16 in mid-2024, though the total number received remains classified.
Ukraine’s demands for air-to-air missiles
The rise of jet-powered drones has exposed a gap in Ukraine’s layered air defense, with what was once reserved to counter cruise missiles now used to counter Russian drones.
Since 2022, Russia’s aerial threats against Ukrainian cities primarily consist of Iranian-designed, propeller-driven Shahed drones and their Russian variants, with the occasional cruise and ballistic missiles.
Those drones are often countered by machine-gun fire and electronic jamming or, more recently, by propeller-driven interceptor drones, with a 90% overall interception rate, whereas air defense missiles – both ground and air-launched – are reserved for cruise missiles, with the scarce and coveted Patriot systems reserved for the faster ballistic missiles.
But with more jet-powered drones flying over Ukraine, Kyiv has had to intercept them with the missile stockpiles reserved for cruise missiles – including the AIM-9s and AIM-120s, according to Zelensky.
Are the new pledges enough?
Ukraine has long struggled with the number of those missiles in its arsenal, with shortages reported in late 2025.
Kyiv’s allies have since tried to remedy the situation. On July 30, the Pentagon announced approval of a $3.5 billion contract to produce thousands of AIM-120s for countries worldwide, including Ukraine – while total production is estimated to reach thousands by 2031, it’s unclear how many were destined for Ukraine.
More recently, at the 36th Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting, Berlin said it would boost AIM-9 deliveries from Bundeswehr stocks – but again, the exact number is not disclosed.
But known deliveries – before Ukraine ran out in 2025 – suggest that numbers have been limited.
One publicized figure from Canada suggests it sent at least 12 AIM-120s, 43 AIM-9s, and 250 AIM-7s in 2023, excluding other components sent to Ukraine. Dutch monitoring site Oryx estimated 43 AIM-9s and 287 AIM-7s from Canada, with no AIM-120s mentioned.
At present, Russia is estimated to be launching 100-200 drones per day against Ukraine consistently, excluding cruise missiles, with the Air Force suggesting in late August that over half were jet-powered at times.
Assuming Russia launches only 50 jet-powered drones and cruise missiles at Ukraine per day, that would be around 1,500 targets for Ukraine to shoot down, AIM-120s or not.
The good news for Ukraine is that the industry is scaling up production of jet-powered interceptors, other air defense missiles are available, and Russia may be having trouble getting Chinese jet engines for the drones.
But the bad news is that it still needs to intercept over 1,000 jet-powered drones that fly like a missile each month, one way or another.

articles.title: Russia’s new jet drones are better at evading Ukrainian air defenses, but experts say Moscow’s drone program is ‘critically dependent’ on Chinese components
articles.body:
Russia’s new jet drones are better at evading Ukrainian air defenses, but experts say Moscow’s drone program is ‘critically dependent’ on Chinese components
Russia has made a “leap forward” in the mass production of long-range drones and cruise missiles that are far better at evading interception, The Wall Street Journal and the Financial Times report.
These weapons include jet-powered variants of the Geran drone and small Banderol cruise missiles. The original Gerans were copies of the slow Iranian Shahed drones, which Ukraine learned to shoot down effectively, according to the WSJ. Russian engineers, however, equipped the drones with turbojet engines, increasing their speed and survivability and making them harder for Ukrainian defenses to intercept.
The FT provides technical specifications for the drones. The first-generation Geran-1, powered by a piston internal combustion engine, could carry a warhead weighing up to 20 kilograms and reach a top speed of 185 kilometers per hour. The new jet-powered Geran-5 can fly at up to 600 kilometers per hour and carry a warhead weighing several dozen kilograms. The Geran-5 now resembles a missile more closely than it does the original Shahed.
According to the FT, Russia first used the Geran-5 in January 2026. In recent weeks, the newspaper says, the new Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones Russia has launched at Ukrainian cities have evaded air defenses far more effectively than their predecessors. Ukraine’s Air Force says Russia launched 2,800 jet-powered drones in August. Since August 27, the launches have been nearly continuous.
Ukrainian experts who examined the weapons’ wreckage believe components sourced from China in violation of international sanctions largely enabled the breakthrough in drone production. Analysts at DroneSec agree, saying Russia relies on Chinese parts, including jet engines, onboard computers, and other electronics. DroneSec CEO Mike Monnik says Russia is “critically dependent” on Chinese components for its drone program. Most of these Chinese-made parts are commercially available dual-use components.
Russia developed and deployed the new Geran variants in just a couple of years, upgrading earlier models, testing them in combat, and quickly beginning mass production, the WSJ reports. According to the FT’s sources, including some close to the Kremlin, Russia’s drone capabilities have grown so much that Tehran asked Moscow for the latest Gerans for its war against Israel and the United States.
Moscow has outpaced its adversaries, according to the WSJ. Ukraine developed one of the first jet-powered drones two years ago but lacks the resources and capacity to mass-produce them.
“In the West, we tend to underestimate Russia, but it can move very quickly from ideas and experiments to mass production. Western militaries should learn from Russia’s ability to complete that cycle,” said Kateryna Bondar, a senior fellow at the Wadhwani AI Center at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).
The FT says the new drones fly at speeds and altitudes that blur the line between drones and cruise missiles. “Soon we’ll probably see these drones having stealth capabilities, and that means it will become even more expensive to manufacture, procure and use them, but also more expensive to destroy them,” said military analyst Konrad Muzyka, head of the Polish consultancy Rochan Consulting.
The war in photos: Russian strikes on Kyiv

The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.

articles.title: Grossi’s toxic legacy: Greenlighting aggression, smearing Iran
articles.body:
Grossi’s toxic legacy: Greenlighting aggression, smearing Iran
In a brazen violation of diplomatic norms, Austria barred Iran’s nuclear chief from IAEA summit due to US pressure
TEHRAN — The head of the UN nuclear watchdog has once again seized the international stage to smear Iran and advance a hostile agenda dictated by the US, turning an ostensibly technical body into a political instrument of Western coercion.
Addressing the 70th regular session of the General Conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) in Vienna on Monday, Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi used his platform to deliver an alarmist, distorted narrative regarding Tehran’s nuclear activities, conveniently glossing over the blatant military aggression waged by the United States and Israel against Iranian territory.
Grossi sought to depict the disruption of technical cooperation as an arbitrary move by Tehran rather than the natural, security-mandated consequence of unprovoked foreign military attacks against sovereign, safeguarded facilities.
“The situation regarding the Agency’s oversight of Iran’s nuclear programme deteriorated in 2026. There were renewed attacks on that country at the end of February. We had to withdraw our inspectors and apart from an inspection of the Bushehr nuclear power plant in June, we have not conducted any in-field verification activities in Iran for more than six months,” Grossi said.
By framing the halt in inspections without holding the aggressors accountable for striking peaceful nuclear infrastructure, he brazenly inverted the roles of victim and perpetrator. “It is well over a year since the Agency lost continuity of knowledge in relation to the previously declared inventories of LEU and HEU enriched up to 60% U-235 at the declared nuclear facilities affected by the attacks of June 2025.”
Rather than condemning the catastrophic precedent of Washington and Tel Aviv bombing sites under full IAEA safeguards, Grossi predictably weaponized the aftermath of those very airstrikes to manufacture an artificial crisis and heighten international hysteria against Tehran.
Grossi noted, “The Agency’s lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern and needs to be addressed with the utmost urgency.”
In an obvious bid to amplify Western talking points and lend unwarranted international legitimacy to coercive measures against Iran’s peaceful civilian nuclear infrastructure, the director general went on to issue sweeping warnings about the erosion of the global non-proliferation framework.
He said, “I warned last year that the global nuclear non-proliferation regime was coming under strain from more than one angle. Discussions about whether to acquire nuclear weapons continue to surface even in countries in good standing with their obligations under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons.”
Grossi’s complicity exposed
Grossi’s inflammatory rhetoric in Vienna is not an isolated incident, but part of a systematic, long-standing pattern of subservience to Western geopolitical designs.
Crucially, just one day before the outbreak of the 12-day war in June 2025—in which Israel and the US launched aggressive military strikes against Iran—the IAEA Board of Governors adopted a confrontational, anti-Iran resolution. Grossi’s politically biased reporting and calculated timing served as the catalyst, directly laying the political and diplomatic groundwork for the US-Israeli war of aggression on Iran.
By systematically echoing Washington’s demands, refusing to condemn the bombing of safeguarded nuclear sites, and presenting routine technical matters as acute international threats, Grossi has effectively acted as an accomplice to US-Israeli crimes against the Iranian nation. Analysts widely view Grossi’s desperate drive to appease the White House and European powers as a calculated maneuver to secure Western backing for his personal political ambitions, specifically his campaign to succeed António Guterres as the next United Nations Secretary-General.
US dictates visa ban to silence Iran
Grossi’s diatribe coincided with an overt, orchestrated Western maneuver to silence Iran’s voice at the Vienna gathering. Mohammad Eslami, the Head of the Atomic Energy Organization of Iran (AEOI), was barred from attending the IAEA General Conference after the host country, Austria, capitulated to direct pressure from the Trump administration.
US officials made no effort to conceal their heavy-handed meddling in the affairs of an international body. US Energy Secretary Chris Wright told reporters in Vienna that Washington had actively opposed the participation of the Iranian delegation.
“He’s a sanctioned individual and we don’t want sanctioned individuals evading their sanctions. He asked for a waiver of the sanctions and it was denied,” Wright said.
Echoing this obstructionist stance, Preston Wells Griffith, the US ambassador to the UN in Vienna, confirmed that Austria’s exemption request was blocked after Washington lodged an objection with the committee.
“While we are focused on a diplomatic solution to the challenges posed by Iran’s nuclear program, we could not allow a UN-designated official to travel … without any meaningful cooperation on nuclear safeguards,” he said.
Eslami had been formally scheduled to address the global gathering to expose Western double standards and clarify Iran’s legal positions before Austria bowed to Washington’s diktat and denied him entry.
Iran condemns host-country violation
The brazen violation of diplomatic norms sparked immediate outrage in Tehran. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmael Baghaei said in his weekly press briefing on Monday that Austria’s move to deny a visa to Eslami for a trip to Vienna was “completely unjustified,” stressing that the Austrian government should have issued entry visas to the Iranian delegation.
He confirmed that Iran’s Foreign Ministry had summoned Austria’s chargé d’affaires to formally convey the Islamic Republic’s strong protest over the decision to the European country.
“They are seeking to prevent Iran’s voice from reaching the world. Austria’s claim that it took this action under US pressure does not absolve the host government of responsibility,” the Iranian spokesperson emphasized.
In Vienna, Reza Najafi, Iran’s ambassador and permanent representative to international organizations, mounted a fierce legal defense against the discriminatory move.
Najafi said preventing the head of the Iranian delegation from attending the conference violated the principle of sovereign equality enshrined in Article IV, Paragraph C of the IAEA Statute. He said the principle guarantees equal rights for all members and their enjoyment of the benefits of membership.
The envoy said the move also undermined Iran’s right to participate in the General Conference through a representative of its own choosing and weakened the privileges required for representatives to perform their duties under the IAEA Statute and the Agreement on the Privileges and Immunities of the IAEA.
Equal representation and participation are treaty-based membership rights that “cannot and must not be undermined,” he said.
Najafi further described the action as a violation of Austria’s obligations as host country under the IAEA Headquarters Agreement between Austria and the Agency.
He said the agreement requires Austria to take all necessary measures to facilitate the entry of representatives of member states into Austrian territory and issue their visas as promptly as possible. The obligation, he stressed, is binding and unconditional for representatives holding valid credentials.
Najafi warned that preventing the head of a delegation from attending the agency’s highest policy-making body undermined the conference itself, stressing that anything short of corrective action would set a dangerous precedent for all IAEA members.
The unlawful maneuver by Vienna and Washington drew sharp condemnation from other international delegations. The Russian ambassador to the UN in Vienna, Mikhail Ulyanov, said Austria had “grossly violated” its obligations as host nation of the IAEA.
Western nations had “unleashed a genuine campaign of visa-related abuses to settle scores with countries they deem to be undesirable,” he said.
Manufactured crises and failed coercion
The theatrical confrontation in Vienna unfolds as the Western bloc rapidly escalates its campaign of maximum pressure. Earlier this month, the UN atomic watchdog’s board adopted a resolution reporting Iran to the UN Security Council for the first time in 20 years because of its failure to cooperate, citing a long-running investigation into uranium traces detected by inspectors at undeclared sites. The hostile resolution was tabled by the UK, France, Germany, and the US.
This dangerous move followed the reckless decision last year by France, Britain, and Germany (the E3) to trigger the so-called snapback mechanism, an unlawful push designed to automatically reinstate expired United Nations sanctions against Iran over its peaceful nuclear program.
In response to the criminal aggression of June 2025, when the US struck Iran’s nuclear sites during the 12-day war, Iran hasn’t given IAEA inspectors access to the affected sites. Tehran maintains that an international agency cannot expect routine access while turning a blind eye to illegal foreign strikes on the very infrastructure it is supposed to safeguard.
The IAEA has also been unable to verify the status of a stockpile of highly-enriched uranium since the June bombing. According to the IAEA, Iran maintains a stockpile of 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium enriched up to 60% purity.
Despite relentless Western sanctions, sabotage, and Grossi’s overt collusion with imperialist powers, Tehran has reaffirmed that it will neither surrender its sovereign technological achievements nor bow to foreign dictates, underscoring that the Agency’s subservience to Western capitals has fatally compromised its standing as an impartial global watchdog.

articles.title: Russo-Ukrainian war, day 1664: Zelenskyy says Ukraine will only accept energy truce if West guarantees Moscow won’t break it after elections
articles.body:
Exclusive
Military
Ukraine keeps hitting the fuel that Russia's war runs on. Its latest target is the Slavyansk-EKO refinery, with an annual processing capacity of at least 3 million tonnes. The Ukrainian military struck it as part of a deep-strike operation, according to military intelligence.
Ukraine hit the radar that guards Sochi, the Russian resort city it struck ten days ago. Drones burned two fuel depots there ten days ago, and the Ukrainian military says the system meant to stop them is now the target.
He had survived Mariupol, Russian captivity and took over Ukraine's Azov grouping in Donetsk. Now Brigadier General Prokopenko warns Russia may mobilize up to 600,000 for its next offensive. Prokopenko, the Mariupol-defense commander now leading the Azov grouping in Donetsk, says the aim is to seize all of Donetsk and Luhansk.
Intelligence and technology
Modern war that the US is not ready for: For the price of one American cruise missile, Russia builds 20 "poor-man" drones and missiles. Russia is fielding cheap jet drones and missiles built with Chinese parts—slipping past defenses Ukraine and the West spent years building.
Iran armed Russia with Shaheds. Now it wants the jet-powered Geran-5 remake back to fight Israel and the US. Russia turned Iran's imported Shahed into a jet that flies at up to 600 km/h, with a new airframe closer to a cruise missile than to the propeller drone Tehran sent it.
Ukraine's FLYCAT strike drone is built to fly without satellite signals. Its bigger new sibling is designed to reach 200 km behind the front. Everything on the combat-proven FLYCAT but the engines is made in Ukraine, and Octava Defence says the new long-range version can stay airborne for more than two and a half hours.
Russia built five more halls for the drones it assembles using Chinese parts to hit Ukrainian cities. The nightly waves that reach Kyiv and the western border regions mostly begin on the assembly lines inside this zone.
International
"We expect specifics from our partners": Zelenskyy says Ukraine will accept energy truce with Russia only if West guarantees Moscow won't break it after its elections. Zelenskyy says any potential truce needs Western guarantees.
No NATO army has fought modern war: Ukrainian officers set their battlefield practice against NATO doctrine and exposed where its assumptions no longer fit. Ukrainian and NATO officers spent three weeks together in Poland.
Lithuania launches military exercises across 12 municipalities as Russia keeps probing NATO's eastern border. A larger multinational exercise is running at the same time on the Belarusian border, with about 2,500 troops from eight countries.
Humanitarian and social impact
Russian strikes will cost Ukraine's economy up to $10 billion this year, ministry says. Kyiv is answering with compensation and cheap credit, aimed at the companies losing warehouses fastest.
A fourth Ukrainian pharmaceutical warehouse has burned in a Russian strike since the start of the month. Russian forces damaged the newest one in Odesa, where the buildings belong to a wholesaler supplying drugstores across Ukraine.
Political and legal developments
Zelenskyy suspends prosecutor general who charged the bureau probing his own office. The agencies he accused are the ones whose independence Brussels treats as a condition of Ukraine's EU accession.
New developments
Belarus trains troops to fight saboteurs as Minsk puts its military on a war footing. Warnings that Russia could use Belarusian territory against Ukraine or a NATO state give the drills their edge.

articles.title: Kim Jong Un Calls Russia’s War ‘Sacred,’ Pledges Continued Support for Moscow
articles.body:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has pledged continued support for Russia and described Moscow’s war against Ukraine as “sacred,” as speculation grows that Pyongyang could send additional troops to bolster Russian forces.
In a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin, Kim reaffirmed North Korea’s commitment to expanding cooperation with Moscow and backing Russia’s war effort, AFP reported, citing North Korean state media.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Firmly convincing the victory of the Russian Federation in the present sacred war for defending the security interests of the country and international justice, I promise my invariable support to dear friend you and the fraternal Russian people,” Kim wrote, according to the Korean Central News Agency (KCNA).
North Korea has emerged as one of Russia’s closest military partners since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Pyongyang has supplied weapons and troops to support Russian forces, while analysts say North Korea has received economic assistance and access to Russian military technology in return.
South Korea’s intelligence service previously estimated that around 2,000 North Korean soldiers had been killed while fighting alongside Russian forces. A later assessment put the number of North Korean troops killed or wounded at roughly 6,000.
In his letter, Kim also pledged to broaden cooperation between the two countries, saying Pyongyang remained committed to deepening ties with Russia across multiple areas.
SBU Urges Residents of Occupied Ukrainian Territories Not to Participate in Russia’s September Elections
The message comes amid reports that North Korea could dispatch additional forces to Russia.
Kyiv has said that as many as 50,000 additional North Korean troops could eventually be deployed to Russia.
President Volodymyr Zelensky has cited the prospect of further North Korean involvement while urging South Korea to provide Ukraine with air defense systems capable of protecting its cities from Russian missile attacks.
Seoul has so far stopped short of supplying Ukraine with lethal weapons directly.

articles.title: Russia hits Ukraine train line used by foreign officials
articles.body:
The locomotive of a passenger train traveling from Kyiv to Warsaw was on Sunday morning hit by a Russian drone just kilometers from the Polish border, the Ukrainian minister of foreign affairs said, as Moscow’s airstrikes push closer to NATO territory.
The attack happened minutes after another train carrying European officials including former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt and former UK British prime minister Boris Johnson left the station on the way back from an annual conference in Kyiv. Former CIA director David Petraeus was at the station when the drone hit, the New York Times reported.
The strike marked the latest escalation by Russia in the war — in its fifth year — as acts of sabotage, arson and drone incursions proliferate across the continent.
Photo: Ukrzaliznytsia Press Office via AP
“This is Putin’s terror ‘knocking’ directly on the doors of the EU and NATO,” Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said in a post on social media, calling for Europe to increase sanctions against Russia.
Ukraine’s state railway operator confirmed a strike on a train in Volyn, about 2km from the Ukraine-Poland border in northwestern Ukraine.
Russian authorities have not yet commented.
Polish Minister of Foreign Affairs Radoslaw Sikorski said there was no violation of the border, but called the incident “escalation” by Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The drones involved in the incident were Geran-5 jet-powered drones, Polish authorities said.
Kremlin forces “struck a passenger train locomotive,” the railway company Ukrzaliznytsia said on Telegram.
“The monitoring group warned the train crew about the threat in advance, thanks to which no one was injured,” it said.
The train, which had 208 people aboard, would continue on to Poland after a delay at the border of about six hours, the Polish railways said.
Sunday’s strike was the second this weekend, Ukrzaliznytsia said.
Sybiha late on Saturday posted images of railway facilities struck in Lutsk in northwestern Ukraine and Fastiv, southwest of Kyiv.
“Unable to achieve its goals on the battlefield, Russia attempts to make the entire territory of Ukraine a battlefield and turns to systematic attacks against civilians, trains, and the infrastructure that keeps the country moving,” he said.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk, speaking after an emergency meeting with top civilian and military leaders, said he cannot exclude the potential of escalation by Russia to Poland’s territories in the next weeks or months, including attempts to disrupt or paralyze border crossings.
Poland would consider how to mobilize allies to be prepared for a common response if needed, he said.
Images on social media also showed a large fire at a gasoline filling station close to the border crossing between Yahodyn in Ukraine and Dorohusk in Poland.
Estonian Minister of Foreign Affairs Margus Tsahkna said on social media that members of his team had been “stuck at this very border crossing, unable to leave Ukraine because of the Russian drone threat.”

articles.title: Modern war that the US is not ready for: For the price of one American cruise missile, Russia builds 20 “poor-man” drones and missiles
articles.body:
Russia has fielded a new generation of cheap, jet-powered drones and cruise missiles faster than Ukraine or the US can build defenses against them, according to The Wall Street Journal. The weapons run on Chinese parts that slip past Western sanctions, and they are already getting through air defenses designed to stop slower drones. Analysts say the West underestimated how fast Moscow could move from an idea to a full assembly line.
Russia now leans on cheap, mass-produced drones to swamp Ukraine's air defenses with sheer numbers night after night, and its factories keep growing to keep the attacks coming. The bigger lesson reaches past this war: in a long fight, cheap weapons in large numbers can beat a small stock of expensive ones.
A cheap weapon that gets past Ukraine's defenses
Ukraine had learned to shoot down the Iran-designed Shahed drones Russia was launching. Then Moscow moved the goalposts. The newest model, the Geran-5, looks more like a missile than a drone—Mike Monnik, head of the drone-threat firm DroneSec, called it "essentially a poor-man's cruise missile," and it forced a rewrite of Ukraine's counter-drone playbook. The Geran-5 and the Banderol cruise missiles are each estimated to cost about $100,000. A US Tomahawk costs more than $2 million.
Russia built five more halls for the drones it assembles using Chinese parts to hit Ukrainian cities
Built fast, with China's help
Moscow needed only about two years to take each weapon from the drawing board to the battlefield, reworking earlier designs, testing them in combat, and pushing them into serial production. Ukrainian assessments, echoed by the drone-intelligence firm DroneSec, trace the leap to Chinese parts—the turbojet engines, the navigation computers, the radios—most of them off-the-shelf, dual-use gear anyone can buy. The weapons are aimed at Ukrainian cities and infrastructure—a Banderol struck a residential area of Kharkiv in July.
An expensive problem for the West
US forces and NATO have knocked down cheap drones with costly Patriot interceptors and fighter jets, often firing several interceptors at a single weapon. Western firms that built interceptors for slow drones are now scrambling to make faster, jet-powered ones. Kateryna Bondar of the Center for Strategic and International Studies said the West keeps underestimating how fast Russia turns experiments into production, and that Kyiv had years of warning yet was still caught off guard.
"I'm surprised everyone is surprised," she said.
At NATO's July summit in Ankara, members committed more than $40 billion to counter-drone defenses over the coming five years.

articles.title: Trump Signals Patriot Missile Production for Ukraine, With One Major Catch
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Trump Signals Patriot Missile Production for Ukraine, With One Major Catch
US President Donald Trump said Ukraine could receive a license to manufacture a less advanced version of missiles for the Patriot air defense system, suggesting Washington may allow production while withholding its most advanced interceptor technology.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to a White House video of Trump’s September 13 conversation with reporters aboard Air Force One, the US president was asked whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy could secure a license to produce Patriot missiles. Trump replied: “Less advanced version.”
Trump did not specify which interceptor could be covered by such an agreement or when a final decision could be made.
Two Patriot interceptors have been discussed publicly as possible candidates for licensed production—the PAC-3 Adapted Capability Effector and the PAC-2 GEM-T.
The PAC-3 Adapted Capability Effector, or PAC-3 ACE, is a new lower-cost interceptor introduced by Lockheed Martin in July 2026. It is designed to counter a wide range of air and missile threats while costing less than half as much as the more advanced PAC-3 MSE. The missile is designed to operate with the Patriot weapon system and Integrated Battle Command System.
The PAC-2 Guidance Enhanced Missile-Tactical, or GEM-T, is an earlier-generation Raytheon interceptor designed to engage airborne threats, including tactical ballistic missiles. Raytheon signed a $3.7 billion contract in April to supply GEM-T interceptors to Ukraine, with a new production facility in Schrobenhausen, Germany, expected to support the program.
Neither missile has been officially identified by the Trump administration as the version that Ukraine could be allowed to manufacture. The statement follows ongoing talks between Kyiv and Washington over localization of Patriot interceptor production.
On September 2, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio confirmed that the two countries were negotiating licensing arrangements, while noting that establishing production facilities for such complex weapons could take years and would not address Ukraine’s immediate shortage of interceptors.
Trump had previously taken a more cautious position. He said the United States had not yet agreed to allow Ukraine to manufacture Patriot interceptors and raised concerns over transferring advanced US military technology.
Ukraine has been seeking additional Patriot missiles as Russia continues large-scale missile attacks. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine received three times fewer missiles capable of defending against ballistic threats this year than in 2025, with partners citing military operations in the Middle East as one reason for reduced availability.
At the same time, Kyiv is working to secure longer-term supplies. Ukraine is contracting approximately 1,000 Patriot missiles with support from allies and European financing, although most are expected to arrive over several years rather than immediately.

articles.title: NATO pledges increased Ukraine support as Russia strikes near border
articles.body:
NATO pledges more Ukraine support after Russia strikes near Poland
NATO chief Rutte insists Western allies will not be intimidated by Russian attacks meant to ‘scare’ them off.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte has pledged additional support for Ukraine after Russian drone strikes hit close to the border with Poland.
Rutte insisted on Monday that the 32-nation military alliance will not be deterred from backing Kyiv in the Russia-Ukraine war, and that it will beef up its own defences along the eastern border with Russia.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Trump tells Zelenskyy to stop hitting Russian diesel supplies
- list 2 of 4Poland, Ukraine accuse Russia of ‘escalation’ after strikes near border
- list 3 of 4‘Attacks will be fully autonomous’: Russia, Ukraine race towards AI warfare
- list 4 of 4Why is Trump warning Zelenskyy not to hit Russian diesel refineries?
The NATO chief’s comments came as Poland pledged increased security along its border with Ukraine. On Sunday, Russian drones hit a train near the Ukraine-Poland border and a second strike hit close to another crossing point.
The strike that hit the train came minutes after a diplomatic delegation that included former British Prime Minister Boris Johnson and former Swedish Prime Minister Carl Bildt had passed through the station, according to Ukraine’s state rail operator.
“The strikes yesterday on trains in Ukraine close to NATO territory again show Putin’s desperation and also his desire to sow fear and terror,” Rutte said at NATO’s political headquarters in Brussels. “Russia is growing increasingly reckless as it continues its terrible war against Ukraine.”
Polish Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said on Monday that the Polish army had also recovered what was believed to be a Russian military drone from the Baltic Sea near the coastal village of Jaroslawiec.
Kaja Kallas, the European Union’s top diplomat, said the attacks close to the Polish border were “clearly meant to scare Western countries from supporting Ukraine,” and added: “We should show that we are there for Ukraine and we are not scared.”
Asked about the strike on the train, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian forces were operating “across the entire territory of Ukraine … and will continue to do so”.
Spillover fears
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Sunday that Moscow appears poised to intensify its campaign targeting Ukraine’s western borders.
“These coming weeks and months will be a time of very intensified actions on the Russian side, and unfortunately we cannot rule out that this escalation will also affect our territory,” Tusk said as he emerged from a security briefing in Warsaw.
Polish officials have said intelligence reports, including a CIA briefing last week, suggest that Russia is likely to attack border points and intensify sabotage actions inside European countries as part of its efforts to discourage states from supporting Ukraine.
Tusk said he would consult NATO allies on preparing a potential joint response.
Trump returns to the table
Meanwhile, United States President Donald Trump said that Ukraine and Russia have agreed not to hit each other’s energy infrastructure.
The US president has recently appeared ready to revive efforts to broker peace, albeit continuing to suggest he leans towards the Russian narrative on the war.
The cost of diesel fuel in particular has come into focus as inflation continues to dent Trump’s popularity ahead of the US midterm elections in November. Ukraine has found significant success in targeting Russia’s oil refining infrastructure in recent months.
“Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!” Trump wrote on social media.
Despite the US’s continued war on Iran, the US president has said he believes the hike in diesel fuel prices is caused by the war in Ukraine.
However, neither Russia nor Ukraine has confirmed the claim.
Russian forces hit two cargo vessels in the Black Sea on Monday, the Interfax news agency reported. One person was killed and another was injured during attacks on Russia’s Belgorod region, which borders Ukraine, local authorities said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy suggested on Monday that a de-escalating step concerning critical infrastructure could be “a first step towards peace”.
Ukraine is ready to halt strikes on Russia if its partners ensure that Moscow will refrain from hitting Ukrainian energy facilities, infrastructure and food supply routes, he said.
The Ukrainian leader has previously suggested that mutual strikes could be paused as a first step towards halting hostilities. However, the Kremlin has persistently insisted that Ukraine must hand over territory and demilitarise before halting it will end its attacks.

articles.title: SkyGuardian drones bought from US tested, source says
articles.body:
The first two of the four MQ-9B “SkyGuardian” drones Taiwan purchased from the US underwent their first flight tests at an air base in eastern Taiwan early yesterday, a source familiar with the matter said.
The unnamed source did not disclose further details about the test flights, saying that they were conducted at Hualien Air Base.
The tests were conducted after the military and the drone manufacturer completed the assembly of the two drones delivered to Taiwan earlier this year, the source added.
Photo: Yu Tai-lang, Taipei Times
On March 17, Deputy Minister of National Defense Hsu Szu-chien (徐斯儉) and Representative to the US Alexander Yui (俞大?) attended a handover ceremony in the US for two of the MQ-9Bs.
The US has agreed to deliver the four MQ-9Bs to Taiwan in two batches this year and next year.
The MQ-9Bs would provide Taiwan with “intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, target acquisition, and counter-land, counter-sea and anti-submarine strike capabilities,” according to the US Defense Security Cooperation Agency.
Su Tzu-yun (蘇紫雲), a research fellow at the government-funded Institute for National Defense and Security Research (INDSR), previously said that the role of the MQ-9Bs in Taiwan is to enhance battlefield reconnaissance and surveillance capabilities rather than serve as a primary offensive weapon.
INDSR researcher Hsieh Pei-shiue (謝沛學) wrote in 2020, when the US first approved the sale to Taiwan, that the drone is capable of linking to satellite communications networks shared among US allies.
That means Taiwan and the US could share battlefield intelligence instantly, providing opportunities for the two sides to cooperate during a conflict.
For example, if a cross-strait conflict breaks out, Washington could take advantage of anti-ship missile systems deployed along the First Island Chain to prevent Chinese People’s Liberation Army vessels from sailing into waters east of Taiwan to blockade the nation, Hsieh said.
MQ-9Bs are capable of long-term, long-range surveillance, meaning the drones could fly near Chinese vessels and provide critical intelligence for US forces to target them, Hsieh wrote at the time.
Another INDSR researcher, Kao Chih-jung (高志榮), yesterday cautioned that while the MQ-9B can detect and classify a large number of targets at once, it still requires final visual identification by human operators.
That limits the drone to conducting detailed, continuous surveillance on only two or three targets simultaneously, Kao said.
Consequently, the military should not rely solely on a handful of large drones, but should instead utilize the MQ-9B to conduct wide-area scans and designate high-value targets, he said.
That intelligence could then be distributed to small and medium-sized drones, shore-based radars and other combat units to build a more resilient “integrated reconnaissance and strike” network, he added.

articles.title: Russian spies ran a campaign against Kyiv on Anthropic’s Claude, and the AI chatbot’s maker caught them at it
articles.body:
A Russian state-linked espionage group ran much of its campaign against Ukraine on Claude, the AI assistant sold by US company Anthropic, which set out the case in a threat report published on 10 September, covering activity it disrupted between December 2025 and August 2026. Ukrainian government, military, and diplomatic staff recurred most often among the targets, with the drone supply chain second. Other Russian users of the same chatbot produced on-air tickers and voiceover scripts for state broadcasters, while Russian-speaking criminals went after the AI industry itself.
Ukrainian ministries and diplomats led the target list
Anthropic tracks the group as GTG-20006 and says its attribution matches public reporting that links it to Midnight Blizzard, a hacking group the US and UK governments attribute to Russia's SVR foreign intelligence service. A Russian-speaking operator using the handle JackPoterz ran campaigns against military intelligence targets in Ukrainian and European governments, plus diplomatic and defense bodies and individuals connected to US foreign policy.
More than 20 organizations appeared in the actor's planning and live operations, from ministries and embassies to think tanks and defense companies. Ukrainian government, military, and diplomatic staff came up most often, and the operators scanned email and remote-access systems across more than two dozen Ukrainian state organizations. Russia has worked these networks all war, treating Ukrainian media as a priority cyber target.
Ukraine’s media are top Russian cyber target: Hackers hit Ukrainian TV site with 200,000 requests in minute
Drone technology was the other target
The operators bulk-exported the mailboxes of at least two drone component manufacturers and went after a military drone maker. They also stole a complete proprietary software development kit for a drone vision system, the code and documentation engineers need to build on that hardware, then spent days pulling it apart. They recovered the product architecture, the parts list, the supplier dependencies, and details of a product the company had not announced. Military drone control and AI vision firmware drew their particular interest.
AI against AI over Ukraine: Russia’s Shahed now sees its target, and Ukraine’s interceptor sees Shahed
To reach people indirectly, the group also compromised at least three vendors running hotel guest WiFi and redirected guests to its own servers, pushing malware at their devices and hunting for Ukrainian officials and drone manufacturers. To reach people indirectly, the group also compromised at least three vendors running hotel guest WiFi and redirected guests to its own servers, pushing malware at their devices and hunting for Ukrainian officials and drone manufacturers. Microsoft documented the same method on 31 July, calling it CaptiveCrunch and tracing it to a Midnight Blizzard sub-cluster. Russian services have tracked the weapons pipeline before, tapping private cameras in Europe to watch arms shipments bound for Ukraine.
What the chatbot did for the operation
Trending Now
Claude fingerprinted mail systems, built the phishing infrastructure, ran commands inside victim networks, harvested credentials, and organized hundreds of gigabytes of stolen data, Anthropic found. Automated agents also checked whether the group's implants were being detected, rewrote flagged malware until it passed, and staged it for the next intrusion. The operators also seized WhatsApp accounts and targeted at least two former high-level Ukrainian officials that way, and stole cloud email from at least eight bodies, including a national prosecutor office and a military education institute.
Russian state media used the same chatbot
Four individual operators fed state outlets, among them a former Sputnik Moldova editor-in-chief. Anthropic says content generated with Claude reached Sputnik Moldova, RIA Novosti, Sputnik en Español, Sputnik Africa, and RT's English newsroom, including fabricated claims about Moldova's President Maia Sandu before the parliamentary election of 28 September 2025.
A Russian-speaking operator in Bangui also supplied daily material to Radio Lengo Songo, a station investigators say the Wagner Group founded and funded in 2017, coordinating with RT, Sputnik Afrique, and TASS.
Two crews went after the AI company itself
A Russian-speaking actor moved from hotel-booking and fintech intrusions to attacking AI firms, planting instructions in one vendor's testing system and hitting roughly 30 companies in four days while chasing an unreleased Claude model. The hunt for the model failed, though the actor did take production API keys from that testing system, and Anthropic says its own systems were never breached. A Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking group meanwhile sold fake discounted access to the assistant, routing customers to a different model and stealing their logins.

articles.title: Houthis strike Saudi targets anew as talks over Strait of Hormuz stall
articles.body:
Houthis strike Saudi targets anew as talks over Strait of Hormuz stall
RIYADH, Sept 15 - Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis launched a new wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia and were digging into positions on the western coast of Yemen along the Red Sea, Yemeni officials said, as urgent deliberations took place in Riyadh over how to respond to their lightning advance.
Meanwhile, Gulf Arab states postponed planned talks with Iran, raising concerns the Middle East conflict could spread further and threaten global oil supplies.
The Houthis on Monday said they fired dozens of missiles and drones at a military airbase in Khamis Mushait in southern Saudi Arabia, targeting aircraft hangars, radar systems, runways and ammunition depots in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen.
Saudi authorities issued emergency alerts there and in three other southern cities. Thirteen civilians were wounded in the Houthi attacks, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.
The Houthi advances in recent days, including the taking of Perim Island at the mouth of the Red Sea, have put further pressure on Saudi oil exports after an aerial attack on Thursday knocked Saudi Arabia's east-west pipeline offline. Riyadh blamed the pipeline attack on Iranian-backed militias in Iraq.
Saudi Arabia built the 1,200-kilometer (745-mile) pipeline across its territory from the Gulf to the Red Sea in the 1980s to bypass the Strait of Hormuz when it came under threat from the Iran-Iraq war at that time.
Traders said a prolonged shutdown of the Saudi pipeline could cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply while the strait is largely blockaded. Riyadh has not said when operations might resume.
Responding to the Houthi offensive, the Saudi and Yemeni air forces have stepped up aerial bombardment of Houthi targets, including around the historic Red Sea port of Mocha, but the Houthis have maintained effective control over almost the entire western coast of the country along the Red Sea, the officials with Yemen's internationally recognised government said.
“The Houthis are being put under heavy pressure. They in turn are putting more and more pressure on the Saudis, increasing their campaign of missile and drone attacks,” one of the Yemeni officials said.
Crude oil prices rose more than 4% on Monday before settling about 1% higher.
AMERICANS HESITANT TO STEP IN
The renewed Yemen conflict poses another challenge for U.S. President Donald Trump.
Three sources have told Reuters that Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention beyond intelligence support. Trump said over the weekend he had spoken with the Saudi crown prince and that the Houthis had also contacted Washington urging it to stay out of the conflict.
Saudi state media reported that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met U.S. regional commander Admiral Brad Cooper in Jeddah on Monday.
Saudi Arabia has led a coalition battling the Houthis since 2015, but the conflict had largely quietened under a ceasefire in recent years. Fighting reignited this month, with the Houthis pushing back forces aligned with the internationally recognised government.
HOPES FOR DIPLOMACY FADE
Oman had been due to host a meeting on Monday with Iran and Gulf states to discuss negotiations aimed at reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which before the war carried 20% of the world's oil exports. But Oman announced that the meeting had been postponed. Iran said the postponement was at the request of Saudi Arabia.
Trump on Monday repeated his frequent claim that Iran was eager to make a deal quickly, but Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, called the president's message a distraction, saying on X, "No talks until Iran's conditions are met."
Underscoring the volatility of shipping through the region, conflicting reports circulated about how and when an oil tanker was damaged.
Without giving a date, Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps said the Panamanian-flagged oil tanker El Gaia was hit by sea mines as it passed through a prohibited zone south of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Fars news agency reported on Monday.
But the U.S. military's Central Command immediately said the report was false and the tanker was "struck by an Iranian missile last month and rendered inoperable."
The United Nations' International Maritime Organization reported El Gaia was damaged on Saturday, but did not say how, and that two seafarers were missing.
Reuters could not immediately contact the ship's owners in Dubai to verify any of the accounts.
The world's most important oil shipping lane has been mostly shut down since the war began on February 28 as Iran has threatened vessels that transit the waterway without its authority.
"The IRGC Navy firmly declares that the Strait of Hormuz is closed and still under our smart control," the Revolutionary Guards said in the statement. REUTERS

articles.title: Finland shelters under French nuclear umbrella amid Russian, US uncertainty
articles.body:
Finland shelters under French nuclear umbrella amid Russian, US uncertainty
Finland becomes 10th European state to sign up to military cooperation and nuclear deterrence initiative.
Finland has agreed to join France’s Forward Deterrence Initiative, extending the coverage of the French nuclear deterrent to eleven European countries.
The announcement came as part of a new strategic partnership between Finland and France, formalised by the countries’ foreign ministers in Helsinki on Monday. Finland becomes the 10th European country to join the French initiative, which comes as Russia is viewed as a growing threat and increasing concern over the commitment of the United States to help protect the continent.
“Finland has decided to join forward deterrence,” according to their joint statement.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb wrote on social media that the initiative is “first and foremost about strengthening European security”.
A nuclear steering group will be set up in the coming months to begin implementing the cooperation, the two European Union states announced.
Stubb was careful to state that the initiative does not replace NATO’s nuclear deterrence, insisting that the move had been discussed extensively with the US and the military alliance.
However, Finland joins Britain, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Denmark and Norway in signing up for cooperation with France’s nuclear umbrella, as President Donald Trump’s shake-up of NATO has Europe – and especially those states closer to Russia in the east – reassessing their security arrangements.
Estonia is also in discussion with France with an eye on joining the enhanced nuclear deterrence, Prime Minister Kristen Michal told the AFP news agency.
“We are under NATO’s nuclear umbrella already. And France is also backing up our independence with the troops in Estonia. So if the cooperation can be deeper in the nuclear field, that probably will go so,” he said.
Under the initiative, the French president alone has the authority to decide when nuclear weapons are used, in contrast to NATO, which has a shared Nuclear Planning Group.
However, it offers joint exercises, the potential short-term deployment of nuclear-capable assets on allied territory and deeper consultation.
Finland does not intend to allow nuclear weapons to be stationed on its territory in peacetime, Stubb noted.
Finland is among a number of European countries that warn of the growing threat from Russia.
Finnish authorities seized a vessel in December suspected of intentionally severing undersea telecommunications cables amid fears of Russian sabotage in the Gulf of Finland.
The Fitburg was en route from the Russian port of St Petersburg to Israel at the time of the incident, according to Finnish officials.

articles.title: Israel eyes Yemen role as US holds back from Saudi-Houthi war
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel eyes Yemen role as US holds back from Saudi-Houthi war
Israel has signalled that it is prepared to play a greater military role against Yemen's Houthis, although Saudi Arabia is unlikely to embrace Israeli assistance despite Washington's reluctance to intervene directly.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has offered assistance to countries in the Arabian Peninsula as part of a wider campaign against the Houthis, according to Israeli media reports citing US sources.
The offer comes as Saudi Arabia seeks greater military support against the group while Washington has stopped short of direct intervention, instead offering intelligence-sharing and targeting assistance.
It follows major Houthi advances along Yemen's Red Sea coast, including the capture of Perim, or Mayyun, the strategically important island sitting in the Bab al-Mandab Strait between Yemen and Djibouti. Pro-Saudi Yemeni government forces on the Red Sea are said to have "collapsed" in the face of Houthi offensives.
Dr Andreas Krieg, a Middle East security expert at King's College London, told The New Arab that US reluctance did create an opening for Israel "in a narrow military sense", but warned against interpreting this as the beginning of a new Saudi-Israeli security alignment.
"Riyadh does not want to move from dependence on Washington to dependence on an Israeli security architecture," Krieg said.
"The Saudis increasingly regard Israel itself as one of the actors generating regional instability. They may see tactical convergence against Iran or the Houthis, but that is very different from trusting Israel with the defence of the Kingdom."
Israel has a direct interest in preventing the Houthis from consolidating their position around Bab al-Mandab.
The strait, just under 30 kilometres wide at its narrowest point, connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and Indian Ocean and is one of the world's most important shipping chokepoints.
For Israel, it is also the maritime gateway connecting the southern port of Eilat with the Indian Ocean.
Houthi attacks on commercial shipping following the outbreak of Israel's war on Gaza had already severely disrupted Red Sea traffic, while Israel has repeatedly struck Yemen in response to Houthi missile and drone attacks.
Krieg said Israel could potentially offer sophisticated intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance, electronic warfare, cyber and targeting capabilities, as well as its experience attacking Houthi missile, drone and command infrastructure.
But the fundamental Saudi problem, he said, was not a shortage of military firepower.
"The Saudi problem is therefore not primarily a lack of aircraft or bombs. It is political and strategic," Krieg said.
"Air strikes can destroy launchers, warehouses and command centres, but they cannot permanently remove the Houthis from Bab al-Mandab or govern territory in Yemen. Saudi Arabia discovered this painfully during its previous intervention."
Saudi Arabia led a military intervention against the Houthis beginning in 2015, but years of airstrikes and fighting failed to defeat the Houthis, who consolidated control over much of northern Yemen while developing increasingly sophisticated missile and drone capabilities.
Renewed Houthi advances now confront Riyadh with a difficult strategic problem as insecurity affects both of the principal maritime routes connecting Gulf energy exports with international markets.
Iran threatens shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, while Houthi control around Bab al-Mandab puts additional pressure on the Red Sea route. Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, designed to bypass Hormuz by carrying oil to the Red Sea coast, has also demonstrated its vulnerability after coming under drone attack.
Yet direct Israeli involvement could potentially worsen Saudi Arabia's predicament.
Krieg said overt Israeli assistance could bolster the Houthi claim that Riyadh was fighting as part of an Israeli-American coalition, while increasing the domestic and regional political costs for Saudi Arabia.
It could also make Saudi infrastructure appear an increasingly legitimate target to Iran and its regional allies.
Some indirect cooperation remains conceivable, particularly intelligence passed through American channels, Krieg said, while Saudi and Israeli forces could separately operate against the same threat.
But he cautioned that parallel operations "should not automatically be interpreted as an alliance or even close coordination".
Instead, Riyadh appears to be seeking a more diversified security architecture as doubts grow about Washington's willingness to bear the costs of defending its Gulf partners.
Krieg pointed to Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, alongside European maritime partners and greater Gulf and Arab-Islamic security cooperation, as more likely components of Saudi Arabia's attempt to reduce its dependence on Washington.
"The lesson Riyadh appears to be drawing is not that Israel should replace the United States," he said.
"The lesson is that Saudi Arabia needs a much more diversified security system in which it has greater agency."
Israel's willingness to intervene against the Houthis therefore exposes a convergence of Israeli and Saudi interests, particularly around Red Sea security, without necessarily bringing the two countries strategically closer.
"Replacing American dependency with Israeli dependency would not represent strategic autonomy," Krieg said.
"From the Saudi perspective, it would simply exchange one vulnerability for another, and potentially for a much more politically dangerous one."

articles.title: Anthropic Disrupted Russian Attempt to Develop Autonomous Drone Swarms
articles.body:
As concerns grow around the direction that unfettered Artificial Intelligence development may be taking, a report by the AI safety and research company Anthropic underlines the need for oversight of the use and development of AI technology if the doomsday scenario is to be avoided.
Who used the Claude coding agent to develop killer drones?
In its quarterly report “Detecting and Countering Misuse of AI,” published earlier this month, the company identified a group of Russia-linked developers, with the designation GTG-27005, that was using its used Claude coding agent to create software for autonomous kamikaze drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Anthropic believes that, although the system was being developed for military use, the group’s members were likely independent, university-based specialists. It had not identified any specific links with the Russian Armed Forces as the group used a number of virtual servers to avoid geographic restrictions. It said the group showed qualities consistent with the Russian hacking group “Midnight Blizzard,” which had used generative AI tools to prepare cyberattacks. The move to the development of autonomous combat systems was a new departure for the group.
What were the developers hoping to achieve?
The Anthropic report said the operation, was known as “DroneDoc” and “Seraphim.” The group registered its accounts in late 2025 but began in earnest in mid-May 2026. It used the Claude Coding agent to write and review software code and to store the resulting components directly in their project files.
China, India, Turkey Remain Top Buyers of Russian Fossil Fuels
The code was integrated with drone simulation software and computing resource training models rented from commercial suppliers. The resulting system was designed to select targets, including people, and issue attack commands without further operator intervention.
The ultimate aim seems to be to operate attack drones as a swarm and to make decisions autonomously. The use of Claude would allow the development of shared memory for the swarm in a fault-tolerant coordination system – a distributed network architecture that maintains synchronization, and task allocation even when individual drones or components fail and communications were lost or individual components failed.
The team was also developing an onboard compact language model that would determine the drone’s next action after swarm members engage a target: attack another target, continue surveillance, or return to base.
Trained using real combat footage from Ukraine
The developers used combat footage from the fighting in Ukraine gained through social media to train a computer vision system, in which Ukrainian personnel and equipment was designated as hostile, while Russian military systems were added to a list of targets that could not be attacked.
Demonstration simulations were carried out in Ukraine’s Donetsk region Ukrainian frontline cities and transportation corridors.
Anthropic battles the illicit use of AI in the war in Ukraine
In total, the company identified and subsequently blocked nine accounts linked to the project. Along with a regional university Anthropic also found connections with the Russian Academy of Sciences.
The report also describes the growing use of AI to organize cyberattacks against Ukrainian government officials and military targets. One Russia-linked group used AI in phishing campaigns, malware distribution, WhatsApp account takeovers, and attacks conducted through compromised hotel Wi-Fi networks.
The slogan of the US National Rifle Association (NRA): “Guns don’t kill people, people kill people,” could just as easily apply to AI, based on this latest incident. It underlines that calls for vigilance over the development of AI are not overstated but it is the user rather than the technology that needs to be controlled.

articles.title: Air Force Stacks Inert Sentinel ICBM Ahead of First Test in 2027
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force has erected an inert version of its LGM-35A Sentinel intercontinental ballistic missile at Vandenberg Space Force Base, Calif., the service announced Sept. 14.
Officials also confirmed at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference that they still expect to finish restructuring the long-troubled Sentinel program by the end of the year and conduct a first test launch in 2027.
The announcement did not specify when the vertical stacking was completed but said that it showed “the maturity of the missile’s design and verified that all critical subsystems are on track.”
An accompanying image shows the missile with “US AIR FORCE” running vertically down its side, along with the Air Force roundel and the emblems of Air Force Global Strike Command and the Air Force Nuclear Weapons Center.
In its own announcement, contractor Northrop Grumman said the stacking was a four-month test process that involved transporting missile components “on specially designed vehicles from across the U.S.” to Vandenberg, where technicians “rigorously tested mechanical operations including transportation, mobile crane use, and safe vertical integration while validating all interface connections on the test pad.”
The successful stacking “proved the viability of all missile stages, propulsion elements, shroud, and subcomponents to be assembled into a single configuration on the test pad,” both Northrop and the Air Force said in their releases.
The service has tested the different stages of the Sentinel’s solid rocket motor multiple times in recent years, as well as the new reentry vehicle that will sit atop them. But it has yet to put them all together for a single test of the entire system.
The Air Force also said that its 719th Test Squadron used the stacking event to complete its first “flight test design review” of the Sentinel to ensure it meets requirements for “performance, safety, and mission assurance ahead of flight testing.”
This February, officials announced they were targeting 2027 for the first test launch. Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink confirmed in his keynote address at Air, Space & Cyber that the 2027 timeframe still holds.
Holding steady represents a win for the program; in 2024, officials were hoping for a first launch in early 2026. But massive cost and schedule overruns forced the program to restructure and slowed progress, leading the Government Accountability Office in 2025 to project a first launch in March 2028.
Gen. Dale R. White, director of critical major weapons systems, is overseeing Sentinel as the program tries to rebuild momentum from those overruns, which triggered a congressional notification and a Pentagon review under the Nunn-McCurdy Act.
As part of that process, Pentagon leaders rescinded Sentinel’s Milestone B decision, which authorizes officials to work on engineering and manufacturing development. Program leaders were instructed to restructure to manage the cost growth and schedule slip.
White told reporters during a roundtable at the Air, Space & Cyber conference that the restructuring process is nearing completion.
“We’re still on track for Milestone B. … That is going very well,” White said. “That was one of the areas I had concern early on about how you kind of navigate those waters and make sure you get that recertification right.”
Sentinel first received a Milestone B certification in 2020, but officials found over time that some of their baseline assumptions were no longer accurate.
The ground facilities in particular were the source of most of the problems rather than the missile itself. Those led to some “hard conversations” during the restructuring, White acknowledged, but senior leaders have now “pretty much locked down the majority of the design” for the infrastructure.
As part of that process, officials agreed Sentinel will no longer use the same silos as the Minuteman III, which are already around 60 years old. In March, the Air Force and Northrop broke ground on a new prototype silo in Promontory, Utah.
Broadly speaking, White said, the Air Force now has a better handle on the program as it progresses toward Milestone B once more.
“In terms of the cost piece, we’re learning as we go along because of just the sheer amount of data that we have now,” he said. “It’s so much more mature than when we did this [six] years ago, and so it’s been really fantastic, because we’ve integrated both the Air Force Cost Analysis Agency and [the office of Cost Assessment and Program Evaluation] with us, and we’re going through this together.”
White declined to say what the restructured program may cost. The previous baseline from 2020 was $77.7 billion; officials said in 2024 it would be closer to $141 billion. White has said he is treating the latter as a cap on the program’s cost.
“I don’t think we’re anywhere near a number right now,” White said Sept. 14. “I’m very comfortable with what I have seen, though, and I think that we’re certainly within the realm of what we have talked about all along. So I don’t think you’ll see any surprises from a cost perspective.”

articles.title: Lithuania launches military exercises across 12 municipalities as Russia keeps probing NATO’s eastern border
articles.body:
Lithuanian troops began military exercises across 12 municipalities in the southern half of the country on 14 September, training to respond to different types of military threats, LRT reported. The exercises will run through 18 September.
NATO's eastern flank has faced growing security pressure from Russia's war against Ukraine. Lithuania borders Russia's Kaliningrad Oblast to the southwest and Belarus to the east, while its territory forms part of the land route connecting the Baltic states with Poland and the rest of NATO.
The exercises involve multiple types of drones, boats, weapons, and wheeled military and civilian transport vehicles, with troops moving on foot and by vehicle during the day and at night. No imitation ammunition or pyrotechnics will be used, the army said.
Recent airspace incidents
Vilnius International Airport was closed on 13 September for 38 minutes after radar detected what was initially feared to be a drone. An Italian air force detachment based at Šiauliai as part of NATO's Baltic Air Defense mission scrambled a fighter jet, which identified the contact as a flock of birds.
Vilmantas Vitkauskas, head of Lithuania's National Crisis Management Center, told LRT radio that a large concentration of birds moving in one direction can register on radar as a drone-like object.
Separately, Poland said on 14 September that its military had found a suspected Russian military drone near its Baltic Sea coast. Polish Defense Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz said a preliminary inspection indicated it was a Russian military drone.
Operational Command spokesman Jacek Goryszewski told TVN24 it was most probably a Russian Gerbera, a cheap long-range drone built from plywood and foam that is often used as a decoy but can carry explosives, and said it had drifted to shore under military observation, with no violation of Polish airspace recorded since late July.
Multinational drills near Belarus
Another multinational exercise, Strong Griffin 2026, is also underway in Lithuania's Švenčionys district near the Belarusian border. Running from 2 to 20 September, it involves about 2,500 troops and 500 pieces of equipment from Lithuania, the United States, Poland, the Netherlands, France, and Portugal, plus partner countries Ukraine and Moldova, according to LRT. Drone work is integrated across it, from reconnaissance to long-range strikes and countering enemy drones.
European intelligence services expect the danger to grow rather than fade. Dutch military intelligence assesses that Russia could mount a regional conflict against NATO within a year of the fighting in Ukraine ending, and reports that preparations for sabotage across Europe have been rising again since mid-2025.
