articles.title: Trump declares Russia-Ukraine deal to halt strikes on energy targets as Zelenskyy voices doubt
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has said that Ukraine and Russia have agreed not to target each other's energy facilities, even as Kiev doubts Moscow’s willingness to abide by it.
"Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian energy targets. Russia has agreed to do likewise!" Trump said on his Truth Social network on Monday.
"The world's diesel price rise is mostly caused by the Russia-Ukraine War, not Iran."
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine is ready to halt strikes on Russia if its partners ensure that Moscow will refrain from hitting Ukrainian energy facilities, infrastructure and food supply routes.
Posting his comments after Trump’s comments, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was not convinced that Russia was willing to abide by any agreement.
"The war must be brought to an end. And a de-escalatory step regarding critical infrastructure could be the first step toward peace. We expect specifics from our partners," Zelenskyy said on the Telegram app.
There was no immediate reaction from Moscow.
Trump's comments come as oil prices continue to soar in the seventh month of the Iran war, raising American fuel costs and inflation just weeks before the US midterm elections.
The US leader has insisted that the Iran war will finish immediately after the midterms and gas prices will drop.
Trump had lashed out at Zelenskyy during a trip to Ireland on Sunday, saying he had to do "one thing" and "stop knocking out diesel fuel" refineries in Russia due to growing shortages.
"Let him go after targets, but not diesel fuel, because he's causing a shortage of diesel," Trump said, again insisting the Russia-Ukraine war, not the US-Israel war on Iran, was to blame.
Trump added he had spoken to Ukraine's leader about the country's stepped-up attacks on such sites over recent months.
"There are plenty of other targets. Don't hit diesel fuel because that's hurting. That's hurting the world. We don't want him to hit diesel fuel. He's hitting diesel refineries."
Ukraine has hit numerous Russian oil refineries far from its border with Russia, while Moscow has also intensified its long-range attacks in recent months, leading to a jump in civilian deaths.
Kiev has been firing record numbers of drones at Russia, while Moscow has been launching all-time high missile attacks.
Trump said last week he had a "great conversation" with Russian President Vladimir Putin, insisting that Putin wanted to make a deal to end the war.
Putin "is wanting to make a deal, and if Zelenskyy is wanting to make a deal, that'd be very nice," Trump told reporters on Wednesday.
Zelenskyy said last week he would be willing to meet Putin at the G20 summit at Trump's own Doral resort in Miami in December, but the Kremlin immediately ruled it out.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says Ukraine ready to de-escalate if US secures real readiness from Russia to end war
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said that Ukraine was ready to de-escalate the war with Russia if its rival did the same, after US President Donald Trump announced that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that "we see that the Russians are feeling pressure because of our precise responses against Russia's war economy".
He noted that "so far no one has seen any genuine desire from Russia to move toward ending the war".
"But if our American partners succeed in securing a real readiness from Russia to stop this war of destroying lives, and to do so sincerely and for the long term, Ukraine will make its own de-escalatory steps."
With international oil prices climbing again, US President Trump had at the weekend criticised Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries, saying they were contributing to a shortage of diesel fuel.
In one of social media posts, the US leader announced on Monday that "Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do likewise!"
Russia made no immediate comment. But in his daily address, Zelensky highlighted "a strong proposal from the United States regarding a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure".
He added: "If this can become the first de-escalatory step -- stopping Russian strikes on our critical infrastructure, and ours in response -- then Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation."
Rail strikes get worse
Trump has insisted that the Russia-Ukraine war was driving up fuel costs for Americans who vote in crucial midterm elections in November.
A previous push by Trump for a ceasefire has been sidelined by the US-Israeli war with Iran, now in its seventh month. US envoys went to Moscow and Kiev earlier this month without announcing a breakthrough.
While Ukraine has hit refineries deep inside Russia, Zelenskyy has stepped up calls for allies to provide more anti-missile defences as Russia intensifies its attacks.
Russian strikes on Ukraine's rail network are worsening each week, the CEO of the state Ukrainian Railways operator told AFP news agency on Monday, after a strike hit a train frequently used by diplomats near the Polish border at the weekend.
"It's growing exponentially. Each month, each week is generally worse than the previous one," said Oleksandr Pertsovsky.
NATO-member Poland said on Sunday that Russia hit a train about two kilometres from the Polish-Ukraine border, just days after Kiev officials said road crossing checkpoints on the border with Moldova had been targeted.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said on Sunday that Warsaw had obtained information that Moscow might be planning attacks on border crossings.

articles.title: Iran rejects foreign interference, and warns against US unilateralism
articles.body:
Iran rejects foreign interference, and warns against US unilateralism
TEHRAN- Iran has rejected allegations of involvement in Yemen’s decision-making and a recent attack on Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline, while reiterating that regional security arrangements should be shaped by the countries of the region rather than outside powers.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei, speaking at his weekly press conference in Tehran on Monday, said Yemenis independently determine their country’s policies and stressed that Iran has no role in decisions taken by Yemen’s Ansarullah movement. He also called for equal maritime security for all countries, arguing that those who attack regional states cannot simultaneously claim to be guardians of maritime security.
Yemenis make their own decisions
Baqaei said developments in Yemen should be viewed against the backdrop of years of attacks and an “unjust siege” imposed on the country. He maintained that Ansarullah is an independent actor that makes decisions according to its own interests.
He also pointed to repeated US and Israeli attacks on Yemen and said the Yemeni people’s position on the Palestinian issue demonstrated their independent outlook and concern for the wider Muslim community.
At the same time, the Iranian spokesman warned that some actors were seeking to exploit divisions among Muslim countries to deepen regional disputes. He argued that maritime security and freedom of navigation must be guaranteed for all states rather than selectively invoked by outside powers.
Baqaei separately categorically rejected US allegations that Iran was involved in a recent attack launched from Iraqi territory against Saudi Arabia’s East-West oil pipeline. He described the allegations as unfounded and said Washington was seeking to aggravate divisions among regional countries at a time of heightened tensions.
He again stressed that Iran has no role in decisions taken by Ansarullah, adding that Yemen’s recent developments should be understood in the context of years of conflict, blockade and repeated US and Israeli strikes.
Tehran and Muscat finalize understanding on maritime routes
The Iranian spokesman also disclosed that Iran and Oman have finalized an understanding concerning maritime routes in the Strait of Hormuz, while consultations continue over how the arrangement will be formally announced.
Baqaei said a planned meeting of regional foreign ministers in Oman was canceled at Saudi Arabia’s request. The meeting had been intended to provide an opportunity for Iran and Oman to present their understanding of maritime routes and discuss the rights and sovereignty of coastal states.
He emphasized that the Iran-Oman initiative was designed to create an opportunity for regional countries to discuss the establishment of a secure regional environment without intervention by outside actors. He rejected suggestions that Tehran’s approach was driven by short-term fluctuations in oil prices, stressing that foreign-policy and national-security decisions cannot be reduced to a single economic factor.
According to Baqaei, the agreement between the two coastal states has now been finalized. Tehran and Muscat will consult on the next steps, including how the understanding should be announced or registered.
He also criticized US claims concerning maritime security, referring to a recent attack on an Iranian vessel near Hengam Island that killed Iranian national Jamshid Rajabi and wounded several others, including two Pakistani nationals working aboard the vessel. Baqaei argued that such incidents contradicted Washington’s stated concerns about maritime safety.
Iran's nuclear policy remains unchanged
Baqaei also rejected speculation that Iran has altered its nuclear doctrine or is considering withdrawal from the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT).
He said Iran’s nuclear policy remains clear and argued that discussion of nuclear deterrence is a natural consequence of repeated attacks and acts of sabotage against Iranian nuclear facilities.
He questioned why countries should be surprised by such discussions when the NPT’s objectives of preventing proliferation and advancing disarmament have not been fully achieved.
The spokesman said Iran’s nuclear facilities had been subjected to dozens of acts of sabotage despite operating under International Atomic Energy Agency supervision, while Tehran had continued to meet its safeguards obligations. Against this backdrop, he said discussions by Iranian lawmakers and other officials about deterrence should not be considered unusual.
Baqaei also linked the issue to security in the Strait of Hormuz, saying that matters concerning Iran and Oman primarily concern the two coastal states. He argued that insecurity in the strategic waterway is a consequence of US actions in the region.
US must end sanctions and intervention
Addressing Iran-US relations, Baqaei said Washington must end 'illegal and interventionist measures' against the Islamic Republic.
He said Iran and the United States had reached an understanding on June 17 at the highest level but Washington violated the agreement 21 days later and resumed or intensified 'unlawful and aggressive actions,' including a naval blockade and economic warfare.
According to Baqaei, the steps required from Washington are straightforward: halt its interventionist measures, compensate for 'crimes committed against Iran,' and end sanctions and economic warfare. He warned that if the United States continued its actions, Iran would maintain the measures it considers necessary in response.
Ties with Turkey and China
Baqaei said Iran’s relationship with Turkey extends well beyond Ankara’s role in facilitating communications between Tehran and Washington. He described the two neighboring countries as partners with broad common interests and longstanding ties.
He said Iranian and Turkish foreign ministers remain in regular contact and pointed to shared concerns over the Israeli regime’s expansionism and its activities across the region. Regarding reports of restrictions on bilateral trade, Baqaei said the issue was under discussion and warned against 'media campaigns' intended to magnify the effects of US sanctions.
The spokesman also welcomed China’s position on regional security, describing Beijing’s role as constructive and its latest remarks at the BRICS summit as valuable. He said Iran welcomed Chinese efforts to promote regional stability but stressed that Tehran’s dispute with Washington was not primarily a question of mediation.
“The problem is not the lack of mediators,” Baqaei said in substance, arguing that the central issue was 'Washington’s lack of genuine willingness and good faith to pursue diplomacy.'
BRICS and SCO platforms against unilateralism
Baqaei said members of the BRICS grouping and the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) were using multilateral platforms to oppose 'US unilateralism' and to develop practical responses to its consequences.
He rejected the idea that Iran could be isolated, arguing that countries were increasingly using international and regional institutions to voice opposition to unilateral measures and to seek alternatives to policies imposed by dominant powers.
According to Baqaei, the US attack on Iran and its partnership with a “genocidal regime” had undermined Washington’s credibility and contributed to growing international concern over the erosion of norms underpinning global peace and security. He added that even some traditional US allies in Canada and Europe had begun recognizing the need to contain 'Washington’s belligerent unilateralism.'
Civilian casualties in Lamerd
At the beginning of his press conference, Baqaei spoke about his recent visit to Lamerd in southern Iran, which he said was targeted at the beginning of the US-Israeli military aggression against Iran on February 28.
He said the destruction and human toll he witnessed were considerably more severe than what had been conveyed through media reports. According to Baqaei, four missiles weighing about 500 kilograms each and carrying thousands of pellets were detonated over the city, including near a stadium, residential areas, a blood-transfusion center and an educational facility.
He said 21 people, including an Afghan national, were killed and described the attacks as a war crime.

articles.title: Wilsbach Shares Airmen’s Stories of Epic Fury, Says 10 Got Battlefield Promotions for DUDE 44 Rescue
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Ten Airmen received battlefield promotions for their roles in the daring rescue of DUDE 44, the crew of an F-15E Strike Eagle that was shot down over Iran this spring, Air Force Chief of Staff Ken. S. Wilsbach announced Sept. 14.
Wilsbach revealed the promotions—a rarity in the Air Force—and more details about Airmen’s actions during Operation Epic Fury in a keynote address at AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Over the course of Epic Fury, which lasted from Feb. 28 until a shaky ceasefire in early April, the U.S. struck more than 13,000 military targets. In what was the biggest air campaign in a generation, around 500 combat aircraft executed around 250 sorties per day—10,000 sorties in 38 days, Wilsbach said.
American air bases in the Middle East went under “Alarm Red” conditions to take shelter, meaning there was an imminent threat of danger, 1,200 times. Wilsbach also said there were 48 airfield repairs and 420 “long lonely sweeps” to ensure that explosive ordnance was not left on the runway.
“That walk is exactly what the name suggests: one EOD technician, leaving a place of relative safety and approaching a suspected bomb or unexploded munition to render it safe for everyone else,” the chief said.
DUDE 44
Amid all these high-risk operations, the rescue of DUDE 44 in early April stood out as an example of the lengths the U.S. military was willing to go to save its service members.
In a recent interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, Lt. Gen. Derek C. France, who was commander of Air Forces Central and the Combined Forces Air Component Commander for U.S. Central Command at the time of the mission and helped oversee the effort, said the rescue was one of his proudest moments in command.
“Watching 44 Bravo [the F-15E weapon systems officer] and getting the word that he was going to make it home and out of Iran with all the forces that were involved in that, knowing on Easter morning this guy was going to go see his family and call his wife for the first time in 48 hours was a high point, an emotional point for me having gone through that whole ordeal for the past 40-plus hours, and then recognized that we had got a win and got this guy back to safety,” France said.
For his part, Wilsbach singled out a particular battle manager—call sign “Peaches”—who coordinated the extraordinary search-and-rescue operation over 50 hours. To rescue the two-man crew, she and her team integrated the operations of 176 aircraft, including fighters, bombers, tankers, intelligence platforms, and special operations forces.
“Think about the complexity of that problem,” Wilsbach said. “Aircraft operating at different speeds, altitudes, fuel states, with different sensors, weapons, and responsibilities, while an adversary was actively trying to stop them.”
And that team was just part of the effort. Maintenance teams, Wilsbach said, generated additional fighters while tanker crews extended the force’s range and dwell time, and intelligence Airmen tracked threats.
“Every one of those Airmen was doing something different, yet all were contributing to the same mission,” Wilsbach said. That led to the 10 battlefield promotions, a rare occurrence when enlisted personnel are promoted for extraordinary performance of duties while serving in combat or under combat conditions.
“I had the distinct honor of promoting six of those heroes, ranging from staff sergeant to chief master sergeant, during a recent trip,’ Wilsbach said.
The dramatic rescue of the DUDE 44 crew began after an Iranian heat-seeking surface-to-air missile slammed into the two-seater fighter aircraft. Both crew members ejected. The pilot was rescued on the first day by a force that included A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft, HC-130 Combat King IIs, HH-60W July Green II rescue helicopters, drones, and special warfare Airmen. That rescue operation was executed under close-range gunfire.
But the WSO, dubbed DUDE 44 Bravo, was not rescued for another day. He was injured in the fall, hitting the ground at a speed of 70 to 100 miles per hour after he struggled to unfurl a damaged parachute, according to an interview he gave to the CBS News program “60 Minutes.”
After landing five miles away from the pilot, DUDE 44 Bravo was suffering from a broken back, a broken arm, a broken shoulder, a sprained ankle, and cuts to his head and face. To elude capture, he scaled a 7,000-foot-tall ridgeline.
Airmen in Epic Fury
Wilsbach cited the work of Airmen across Epic Fury to emphasize his main directives for the service: be “ready to fight, built to endure, and integrated to win.”
The rescue of DUDE 44 was a prime example of integration, the chief said.
To illustrate readiness to fight, Wilsbach told the story of an unnamed base under attack from Iranian missiles.
“As missiles were inbound, Airmen sprinted toward bunkers,” Wilsbach said. “A missile struck nearby in a hangar, and the aircraft inside burst into flames. The bunker withstood the blast, but the force of the impact damaged the door so badly it wouldn’t open, trapping the Airmen inside.”
A security forces NCO used a pry bar to force the door partially open and spoke with the Airmen inside. But then the ejection seat on the burning aircraft ignited, “sending glass and metal fragments through the air,” Wilsbach said. At last, the Airmen were able to get the door open and run for cover. Finally, the door gave way, and the Airmen ran for cover.
Wilsbach also shared the story of an F-15E crew chief, Garrett, who stayed with the jets on the flight line until the last F-15E taxied and took off while others were running for cover. “ When somebody later asked him why, his answer was simple: they needed those airplanes in the air,” Wilsbach said.
Hundreds of miles away, two Senior Airmen, Shanea and Nolan, tracked a swarm of enemy drones headed toward their base and, Wilbach said, achieved more than 10 surface-to-air kills.
Shanea and Nolan’s actions in particular show the need for the Air Force to advance point defense and make it a “core function of air and space power,” Wilsbach said; the Air Force can no longer be assured that it is safe from drone and missile threats, including at airfields in the United States.
“Don’t you think we ought to have them at every base?” Wilsbach said of a new field of Airmen specializing in point defense. “If every base is going to be threatened, we have to have somebody who knows how to defend it.
“If we had a more robust base defense, you know, perhaps those bases wouldn’t have been as damaged as they were,” Wilsbach added. “Look at Israel; they have a significantly layered, very robust defense of their country, and they didn’t take that many hits, very few, in fact. And that shows you what a good defensive system can do, which can help you to operate not quite with impunity, but almost, and you can just keep generating airpower, and your defensive systems take care of the incoming.”
To hammer home his point about endurance, Wilsbach told the store of a a B-1 pilot, with the call sign Rocket, who coped with a harrowing refueling at night, in heavy clouds, and with jet fuel spraying across his cockpit windscreen.
The B-1 crew described the experience as “refueling by Braille,” Wilsbach said.
“A bomber pilot who couldn’t see depended on the tanker crew to guide them,” Wilsbach added, noting that the B-1 went on to complete a 34-hour mission.
Another example, the chief said, was an MQ-9 pilot, call sign Suit, who launched his drone while its airfield was under attack. The drone struck a target, then returned to base to conduct a damage assessment of the runway. That mission was one of many the MQ-9 conducted during Epic Fury, Wilsbach noted, with a remotely piloted aircraft striking more than 800 targets. It also played a key role in dynamic targeting and locations where the U.S. did not want to operate crewed aircraft. “Many more targets were hit because the MQ-9 found them and then passed them off to another platform,” Wilsbach said. “There’s a lot more than the 800 that they hit, and we were doing this in areas that were highly defended. And though we did decimate the Iranian Air Force and the Iranian Navy, and then we significantly attrited other capabilities that they have, it wasn’t easy. Iran’s not a pushover.”

articles.title: ‘Our Victory or Defeat’: Ukrainian Top Commander Reveals What Could Force Russia to Reconsider the War
articles.body:
Ukraine’s success or failure in the coming months will largely depend on whether it can defend its skies against Russian ballistic missiles and faster jet-powered attack drones, Brig. Gen. Andriy Biletsky said at the annual Yalta European Strategy (YES) conference in Kyiv.
“Our victory or defeat will depend on whether we can protect Ukrainian skies this winter,” said Biletsky, commander of Ukraine’s 3rd Army Corps.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He said Ukraine must counter two principal threats: ballistic missiles and jet-powered attack drones, including Shahed- and Banderol-type weapons.
If Ukraine withstands Russia’s winter air campaign and prevents further battlefield advances, Moscow could face a fundamental decision over whether to continue the war, Biletsky said.
“If we pass this test with dignity and effectiveness, I think March or April will confront Russia with an existential question: Why and how should it continue the war if it has not achieved any of its strategic objectives?” he said.
That moment could create an opportunity for negotiations and a lasting peace largely on Ukraine’s terms, Biletsky added.
The commander said Russia is pursuing two main strategic objectives: completing its occupation of Ukraine’s Donetsk and Luhansk regions and weakening the country’s ability to resist through attacks on civilians, energy facilities, industry, and the economy.
Europe Prepares for War as Germany Sends Up to 1,000 New Troops
According to Biletsky, Russia’s political leadership has demanded that its forces seize the entirety of the two eastern regions by the beginning of 2027, while Russian military commanders have set a deadline of mid-April.
“Russia’s political leadership is demanding that they finish it within the absolutely unrealistic timeframe of the beginning of 2027,” the commander said.
Russia has repeatedly set new deadlines for capturing all of the Donetsk region, a central war objective that its forces have failed to achieve despite years of costly offensives.
Ukraine is preparing for intensified fighting around Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, two key cities in its remaining defensive belt in Donetsk. Biletsky and Denys Prokopenko, commander of the National Guard’s 1st Azov Corps, are among the commanders overseeing the region’s defense.
Biletsky said the situation on the front remains difficult but is not the worst Ukraine has faced during the war.
“It is not easy. It is difficult. But the front is not going through its hardest period compared with previous years,” he said.
Ukraine has “every chance” of holding advantageous defensive positions, preserving its belt of fortified cities, and improving its position in parts of the Donetsk front, he said.
“I think that in the near future, within a month, we will demonstrate these improvements to the entire world, and they will be undeniable,” Biletsky said. He did not provide operational details.
The 22nd YES Annual Meeting was held in Kyiv on Sept. 11-12 under the theme “Peace Through Strength NOW!” It brought together about 700 politicians, diplomats, military personnel, veterans, business leaders, activists, and experts from 28 countries.

articles.title: Zelensky reveals details of Canada's assistance in defending Ukrainian skies
articles.body:
Zelensky reveals details of Canada's assistance in defending Ukrainian skies
President Volodymyr Zelensky announced this in an interview with the “Yedyni Novyny” telethon during his visit to Canada, according to Ukrinform.
“The issue of air defense is our top priority. The Prime Minister (of Canada, Mark Carney—ed.) announced the purchase of missiles for the Patriot PAC-3 systems—anti-ballistic missiles—worth 350 million. This is an air defense package. In addition, we discussed the AIM-9 and AIM-120 missiles with him. These are the missiles we also use for air defense in the NASAMS systems, which protect many different facilities, including energy infrastructure,” Zelensky said.
He noted that these missiles are also used on F-16 fighter jets.
The president emphasized that the air defense package from Canada will include “both funds and individual missiles.” “And there are also some agreements that require him (Mark Carney—ed.) to engage in direct dialogue with other leaders who, for various reasons, cannot sell anything directly to Ukraine,” the head of state added.
As reported by Ukrinform, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney stated during a joint press conference with Volodymyr Zelensky in Calgary that Canada and Ukraine had finalized an agreement on the procurement of critically important air interceptors through the JUMPSTART mechanism. This equipment package, valued at 350 million Canadian dollars, will help protect Ukraine’s citizens, infrastructure, and airspace.
