articles.title: US slaps new penalties on Russia's VTB Bank over Iran   sanctions evasion
articles.body:
The United States on Sept. 14 imposed new sanctions against VTB Bank, one of the largest financial institutions in Russia, for its role in helping Iran evade sanctions, the U.S. Treasury announced.
The designation is part of Operation Economic Outcast, the Treasury's plan to isolate Iran economically. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent first announced the plan in August, six months into the U.S. war against Iran.
The Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) designated VTB Bank on Sept. 14 for "operating in the financial sector of the Iranian economy," saying the institution had opened bank offices in Iran in recent years to expand trade and cooperation between Tehran and Moscow.
VTB Bank has partnered with sanctioned Iranian financial institutions and has helped tranfer billions in frozen Iranian assets, the Treasury said.
"Under Operation Economic Outcast, Treasury will continue to target and disrupt those who provide material, technological, or financial support that allows the Iranian regime to sustain its terrorist enterprise," Bessent said.
The new sanctions block any VTB Bank assets that are held in the U.S. or by U.S. nationals. Any entities owned directly or indirectly by VTB Bank are also blocked, and those who violate the sanctions measures are subject to criminal or civil penalties.
VTB Bank was previously sanctioned by the U.S. in 2022 and 2025, in relation to Russia's full-scale war against Ukraine.
"VTB is now among the most comprehensively sanctioned financial institutions in the world," the U.S. Treasury said in a press release accompanying the updated sanctions designation.
Russia and Iran have deepened economic and military cooperation since the start of the full-scale war, when Tehran supplied Moscow with Shahed drones to launch against Ukraine.
In turn, Russia has pledged to support Iran during its war with the U.S. Russian President Vladimir Putin told his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian on Sept. 1 that Moscow is "trying to provide you with the assistance you need."
Bessent, however, has previously downplayed Russia's aid to Iran.
"They don't really get direct financial support from Russia," Bessent told the right-wing outlet Newsmax earlier in September.

articles.title: Finland joins France's forward nuclear deterrence initiative
articles.body:
Finnish President Alexander Stubb stressed that Finland’s "foremost priority" was still to act as part of NATO and the EU and that the French initiative would not "replace or overlap with NATO’s nuclear deterrence."
Finland and France committed to deepening their defence partnership on Monday, with Helsinki formally joining a French initiative aimed at strengthening European security through forward nuclear deterrence.
In a joint statement, the two nations called the decision an "important step for European security, and for bilateral cooperation."
"It will strengthen their partnership, and offer opportunities for strategic signalling, as well as the ability to manage escalation below the nuclear threshold," it continued, adding that a "Nuclear Steering Group" would be set up within the next few months to "begin the implementation of this cooperation."
In a post on X, Finnish President Alexander Stubb stressed that Finland’s "foremost priority" was still to act as part of NATO and the EU and that the French initiative would not "replace or overlap with NATO’s nuclear deterrence."
"Finland does not intend to station nuclear weapons on its territory in peacetime," he added.
The United Kingdom, Germany, Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands, Belgium, Greece, Denmark, and Norway have already signed up to France's initiative, which aims to deepen nuclear cooperation across Europe through joint exercises.
Under the framework, participating countries could also potentially host French nuclear-capable aircraft on a temporary basis.
Paris would, however, retain exclusive control over its nuclear arsenal, with the final decision on its use resting with the French president.
Estonia could be next
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told AFP that Tallinn was also "in discussion" with Paris over possible cooperation on the matter.
"This is not this kind of (initiative) that you just join ... It needs certain capabilities, readiness and so on," Michal told the news agency on the sidelines of the European Arctic Summit in northern Finland.
"We are under NATO's nuclear umbrella already. And France is also backing up our independence with the troops in Estonia. So if the cooperation can be deeper in nuclear field, that probably will go so," he added.
Since March 2017, France has maintained a military presence of around 300 troops in Estonia as part of NATO's enhanced forward presence in the Baltic states.

articles.title: Disgraced top prosecutor’s attack on anti-corruption bodies may trigger a political crisis
articles.body:
Disgraced top prosecutor’s attack on anti-corruption bodies may trigger a political crisis
Prosecutor General of Ukraine Ruslan Kravchenko poses for a photo in his office in Kyiv, Ukraine, in an undated photo. (Ukrainian Prosecutor General's Press Office / AP)
Ukraine’s disgraced Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko’s Sept. 14 revenge charges against the country’s top anti-corruption official could trigger a major political crisis if this becomes a full-on crackdown on anti-corruption institutions, analysts say.
But everything depends on whether Kravchenko’s announcement of the charges was a desperate tantrum intended to save himself or part of a crackdown backed by President Volodymyr Zelensky’s administration.
The charges against Semen Kryvonos, head of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau (NABU), and an unnamed “close associate” of Oleksandr Klymenko, chief of the Special Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), were seen by many as a petty vendetta rather than pursuit of justice.
The charges were announced after Kravchenko was forced to resign amid a large-scale NABU and SAPO corruption investigation that engulfed the Prosecutor General’s Office earlier this month.
Within the investigation, a top prosecutor described as a “confidant” of Kravchenko was charged, and the prosecutor general’s personal office was searched. Publicly revealed evidence hints at Kravchenko being implicated.
In a bizarre twist, Kravchenko left Ukraine early on Sept. 14, simultaneously with announcing the charges, under the pretext of an official trip to a conference in Paris. But the organizers told the Kyiv Independent that they had not expected him to attend, strengthening the suspicions that the trip was a fig leaf for fleeing Ukraine to avoid potential charges.
To add to the confusion, late on Sept. 14 the Prosecutor General's Office posted a statement that seemed to signal division between the agency and its outgoing boss. The statement claimed the reported charges were "not true" but also "canceled" — by whose authority, it remains unclear.
The Kyiv Independent has requested comments from Kravchenko and the President’s Office and will publish their responses once they are received.
On Sept. 14, Zelensky issued a decree to suspend Kravchenko from office and submitted a motion to parliament to fire him. Lawmakers are set to vote on his dismissal on Sept. 15.
read also
Charges against Kryvonos
One of the charges against Semen Kryvonos concerns allegedly falsified paternity documents used by the NABU chief in court to avoid punishment in a 2007 bribery case. Back then, Kryvonos stood accused of vote buying in a local election.
Kryvonos is also accused of agreeing to illegally allocate a land plot in exchange for a $72,000 bribe in 2014. The scheme was uncovered before it was completed, according to the Prosecutor General's Office.
Kryvonos said at a press briefing on Sept. 14 that he had not seen any charges against him and had not been formally served with them. He called Kravchenko's accusations fabricated.
Kravchenko claimed to have sent the charges to Kryvonos by mail. But Olena Shcherban, a lawyer at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, said that, under Ukrainian law, they can be sent by mail only if it’s impossible to serve them to a suspect in person.
The unnamed Klymenko associate was charged with influencing judges of the High Anti-Corruption Court, offering bribes to them, and helping potential conscripts evade the draft, Kravchenko said. He did not elaborate.
There was speculation in the media that this could refer to Klymenko’s wife but Klymenko said that no members of his family had been charged as of the evening of Sept. 14.
Late on Sept. 14, Mariana Hayovska, a spokesperson for the Prosecutor General’s Office, told the Kyiv Independent that she did not have any information on the charges.
read also
Revenge?
Observers describe the charges as revenge against the anti-corruption agencies.
“I believe there are signs that Kravchenko abused his office,” Yaroslav Yurchyshyn, a lawmaker from the liberal opposition Holos party, told the Kyiv Independent. “In trying to evade possible charges in the case involving the protection of call centers, he also put the president in a difficult position by accusing him of interfering in investigative actions.”
“Now the empire is striking back.”
The investigation into Kravchenko’s office alleged that his subordinates ran a wide-ranging scheme that granted protection to scamming operations known as “call centers” in exchange for cash.
“Now the empire is striking back,” a lawmaker from Zelensky’s Servant of the People party told the Kyiv Independent, speaking on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of the subject. “If there were any legitimate grievances against the NABU, they should have been raised earlier — not after he was fired as prosecutor general.”
The lawmaker argued that Kravchenko was trying to “weaken NABU and undermine public trust in the agency.”
This is not Kravchenko’s first standoff with NABU and SAPO.
He played a crucial role in the authorities' infamous attack on the two agencies in July 2025.
At the time, Zelensky and the parliament attempted to eliminate the independence of the anti-corruption agencies by subordinating them to the prosecutor general. However, the bureau's independence was soon restored amid protests and Western pressure.
The same month, Kravchenko's Prosecutor General's Office, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU), and the State Investigation Bureau conducted at least 70 raids, including at the homes of NABU employees. Two detectives of the bureau were arrested and charged with high treason and aiding Russia.
Critics argued that the crackdown was intended to impede the NABU investigations against Zelensky allies involving state nuclear power monopoly Energoatom, the biggest corruption investigation during Zelensky's presidency.
Klymenko said at a press briefing on Sept. 14 that an associate of Kravchenko he called “a hacker lawyer” had been involved in the attacks on the NABU in July 2025 and in September 2026 — a likely reference to Dmytro Borzykh, a lawyer and former prosecutor, according to Dzerkalo Tyzhnia, a Ukrainian media outlet currently sued by Borzykh.
read also
A work trip or attempt to flee?
Although Kravchenko officially left Ukraine on a work trip, the circumstances surrounding his departure raise suspicions he was fleeing justice.
Kravchenko claimed he was headed abroad on a business trip to brief partners on the "real state of affairs" in Ukraine's anti-corruption system and "signs of uncontrolled influence" within the agencies.
A source in the President's Office told the Kyiv Independent that Kravchenko signed off on his own travel order.
The document dated Sept. 13 and seen by the Kyiv Independent says Kravchenko was due to travel to Paris for a PACE parliamentary network hearing on "Ukrainian children in the context of international responsibility."
However, the organizers told the Kyiv Independent he was not expected to attend the event in any capacity.
The Prosecutor General's Office’s press service initially said it knew nothing about Kravchenko's trip but later confirmed he was due to travel to Paris.
“Someone — clearly someone very influential — must have given him assurances that both he and his wife would be taken care of abroad.”
“He fled to escape accountability,” Daria Kaleniuk, executive director of the Anti-Corruption Action Center, told the Kyiv Independent. “Someone must have given him assurances that he would be taken care of abroad.”
read also
Is Zelensky involved?
A crucial question for the future of the scandal is whether Kravchenko brought the charges on his own initiative or whether they were quietly approved by Zelensky, who picked Kravchenko for the top prosecutor job.
Experts’ opinions on the matter are divided.
The lawmaker from Zelensky’s party said that Kravchenko “was allowed to cross the border, and it’s hard to imagine that happening without a decision being made somewhere higher up.”
Kaleniuk argued that Zelensky and David Arakhamia, the notoriously powerful head of the president’s faction in parliament, were behind Kravchenko’s charges against Kryvonos. Arakhamia ridiculed the allegation, telling the Kyiv Independent: "I also approved the murder of (John F.) Kennedy and the poisoning of the Skripals."
“These charges are a continuation of the attack on NABU and SAPO — an attack that had been in the works and for which Kravchenko was appointed to the post in the first place, back in June last year,” Kaleniuk said. “Neither President Zelensky nor those around him have any interest in seeing the anti-corruption agencies continue to operate effectively. This was not a decision Kravchenko made on his own, despite the President’s Office already claiming that it was his initiative.”
Indeed, a source close to Zelensky said that Kravchenko “obviously lost his mind” and the president was allegedly “furious when he found out” about Kravchenko’s decision to charge Kryvonos.
«Kravchenko has lost his mind — that much is obvious.»
Political analyst Volodymyr Fesenko also argued that the charges “were primarily in Kravchenko’s own interests.”
“For him, it was a means of protecting himself,” he told the Kyiv Independent. “He probably suspected that he could become a suspect in the ‘Carthage’ case (the NABU investigation into the Prosecutor General’s Office’s racketeering of scam centers). That, I think, is why he decided to flee and leave the country.”
Fesenko argued that Kravchenko could portray the case against him as a “conflict of interest” and an “institutional conflict” and could use this situation to fight his potential extradition.
read also
Political implications
It is not clear whether the charges against Kryvonos and the Klymenko associate, announced by Kravchenko on his way out, will be recognized by courts as valid and lead to the suspension or dismissal of the anti-corruption officials from their jobs.
Tetiana Shevchuk, a lawyer at the Anti-Corruption Action Center, said that one of the prosecutors involved in the case has the authority to cancel the charges if they are deemed unlawful.
If the officials are suspended, Kryvonos’ senior deputy Denys Hyulmukhamedov is expected to take over as acting chief of the bureau, while Klymenko’s functions are expected to be fulfilled by the incoming prosecutor general.
If the crackdown on the NABU and SAPO continues, experts predict a full-on political crisis.
The previous attempt to eliminate their independence in July 2025 resulted in the first large protest movement since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion. A similar major protest movement was triggered recently when Zelensky fired the popular Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov in July 2026.
"Zelensky has effectively spent the past two months lurching from one crisis to another without a break.”
“I think that in a situation like this, with so much tension, frustration, and trauma in society, when almost anything could trigger public discontent, it’s better not to take any chances — not to make a move that could spark protests,” the lawmaker from Zelensky’s party said.
Fesenko said that “Zelensky has effectively spent the past two months lurching from one crisis to another without a break.”
“What Zelensky needs now, on the contrary, is to defuse the situation, bring this relentless cycle of crises to an end, and achieve at least some degree of stability,” Fesenko said. “For Zelensky, (a crackdown on the NABU and SAPO) wouldn’t solve the problem — it would only escalate it. It would mean yet another crisis, possibly another wave of protests, and problems with our international partners.”
“A little more of this and defeat in the war will be all but guaranteed,” he added.

articles.title: Who Is Umar Kremlev? The Russian Businessman With Ties to Putin Who Partly Funded Trump Jr.’s Wedding Celebrations
articles.body:
A Russian businessman with ties to the country’s President Vladimir Putin footed the bill for celebrations following the wedding of President Donald Trump’s son, Donald Trump Jr., Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina, have confirmed.
Oligarch Umar Kremlev’s contributions to the wedding festivities were first reported by ProPublica, which wrote that the Russian businessman spent hundreds of thousands of dollars to rent out a private island in the Bahamas and a fireworks show. The outlet reported that the guest list included roughly 50 guests, including family members, close friends, and Kremlev, who according to ProPublica was part of a larger group of Russian guests whose presence was a source of confusion for other attendees.
Trump Jr. and Bettina Trump shared a statement on social media in response to criticism over his financial involvement in the event, defending what she described as an “extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend” and denying any political motive behind Kremlev’s attendance.
“Our dear friend Umar very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding,” they wrote in a post on Bettina Trump’s Instagram on Monday in a caption that accompanied a series of photos from the evenings in question showing the couple partying with other guests, performances, and the beach-side venue. “It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from. Friendship doesn’t require a political motive.”
The Trumps’ connection to a figure closely tied to the leadership in Russia—and his apparently lavish financial contribution to the wedding celebrations—has however drawn concerns from Democratic politicians and experts in ethics and intelligence, who have raised questions about what might be expected in return for the "gift" and warned that Russian intelligence services may seek to weaponize such a relationship.
Here’s what to know about Kremlev and his ties to Putin and the Trump family.
Who is Umar Kremlev?
Kremlev, 43, is a native of Tajikistan. He was previously known by his surname at birth, Lutfulloyev, which he changed to Kremlev in 2010 when he was in his late twenties, according to the independent Russian news organization Proekt. Prior to that name change, Kremlev was convicted of extortion in 2004 and battery in 2007.
He went on to join a notorious biker gang, the Night Wolves, not long after changing his name, according to Russian news reports. Outlets reported that during his time in the group, which was the first official biker community in the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR), Kremlev met Alexei Rubezhnoi, who currently leads Putin’s presidential security service. The Washington Post reported that Putin himself is considered an honorary member of the Night Wolves.
In 2015, Kremlev, who had boxed since he was a child, founded a company, Patriot, that promoted boxing matches. Two years later, he became the secretary general of the International Boxing Association (IBA) after a shake up led to Rubezhnoi becoming the chairman of its supervisory board. Rubezhnoi then nominated Kremlev to the secretary general position; from there, Kremlev went on to be elected as president of the IBA in 2020.
In 2024, Kremlev acquired Rolf, Russia’s largest car dealership group, which had previously been state-owned.
“These services,” Triplett says in reference to the Kremlin, “are exceptional at finding pain points and then and then manipulating them, and you can get people into difficult positions.”
What are Kremlev’s ties to Putin?
Kremlev has been connected with Putin for years, as has been documented through public appearances and business dealings.
During Kremlev’s time as IBA president, Gazprom, a state-owned energy company and one of the largest companies in Russia, became a financial backer of the boxing federation.
That same year, Kremlev stood alongside Putin during the opening of the International Boxing Center in Moscow.
Under Putin, many Russian government officials or oligarchs serve in supervisory positions for sports organizations in the country.
“Umar is guided by Putin. It was using the sport for soft political power,” an ex-IBA board member told ProPublica of Kremlev’s leadership of the organization. “It’s geopolitics. That it’s boxing is just happenstance.”
Following Kremlev’s acquisition of Rolf in 2024, meanwhile, Putin repealed the company’s federal ownership, which he had established through a presidential decree in 2023.
He was also honored by Putin with the Order of Friendship, according to the IBA, a state accolade that celebrates those who have helped to improve the Russian Federation in various sectors. And earlier this year, Kemlev accompanied Putin on a visit to China, according to Chinese state media. Kremlev’s press office told ProPublica in a statement that he was not part of the Russian President’s “official delegation” during the trip.
What are Kremlev’s ties to the Trump family?
Kremlev has been publicly linked to President Trump and Trump Jr. through the IBA in recent months. It’s unclear how else he may be connected with the Trump family.
After President Trump returned to the White House last year, Kremlev and the CEO of the boxing organization sent him an open letter congratulating him on his re-election and expressing the IBA’s “sincere gratitude for your strong and principled stance regarding the inadmissibility in the participation of ineligible athletes in women’s boxing competition,” in reference to Trump’s stance against the participation of transgender women in women’s sports.
The letter then nodded towards the 2028 Olympic Games, which will be hosted by the U.S. in Los Angeles, saying that the IBA looks ahead “with great optimism to the possibility of working together to make the Olympic movement great again, advance the sport of boxing and to champion the rights of athletes globally.”
Last September, Trump Jr. sat on a panel discussion hosted by the IBA in Istanbul, during which he also critiqued the participation of transgender women in women’s sports while onstage with Kremlev.
Kremlev’s press office said in its statement to ProPublica that he and Trump Jr. initially met “a couple years ago” and that the two men “have a friendly relationship.” It added that Kremlev “has never discussed political matters with any of his American friends and acquaintances,” Trump Jr. included.
A spokesperson for Trump Jr. told the New York Timesthat the two men bonded over boxing and hunting after meeting through a mutual friend, and that they are not in business with one another.
The President, who did not attend Trump Jr.’s wedding or the following celebrations, said in a statement provided to the Times on Monday that “I have no idea who Umar is, never heard of him, and he didn’t pay for Don and Bettina’s wedding, which took place at a totally different location, and on a different day.”
A spokeswoman for Eric Trump, Trump Jr.’s brother, meanwhile told the Times and ProPublica, “Eric has absolutely no clue who this person is.”
Intelligence experts raise concerns
“If the allegations are true, then it certainly reflects poor judgment on Donald Trump Jr.’s part,” Dan Hoffman, an intelligence expert with over 30 years of experience working in the Central Intelligence Agency (CIA), U.S. military, Department of State, and Department of Commerce, tells TIME. “It is highly unlikely Umar Kremlev would have any interaction with any member of the Trump family without the Kremlin knowing about it beforehand.”
Holden Triplett, who served nearly 15 years with the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and was previously the Director for Counterintelligence at the National Security Council at the White House during Trump’s first Administration, says that any kind of relationship between an individual with ties to the President and someone linked to the Kremlin can pose a risk to the U.S.—though he says he doesn’t find the Trumps’ apparent relationship with Kremlev to be particularly alarming.
“Even the most above-board, non-threatening-nefarious relationship could be weaponized by intelligence services,” he tells TIME. “Russians commonly try to use, as a lot of intel agencies do, business relationships as a non-alarming way to establish connection with someone … It is one that the Russians have used with lots of, or attempts at least, with lots of other individuals in politics.”
This isn’t the first time Trump Jr. has drawn controversy over interactions related to Russia. During the 2016 presidential campaign, Trump Jr. met with a Russian lawyer who claimed she could provide information that would hurt his father’s Democratic opponent Hillary Clinton’s campaign. That meeting later became a point in the investigation special counsel Robert Mueller conducted into President Trump’s campaign and its ties to Russia, though Trump Jr. was never accused of wrongdoing in the probe.

articles.title: National Guard says it destroys Russian Tor-M1 air defense system worth $25 mln
articles.body:
Operators from the Black Sky unmanned aerial vehicle battalion of the Spartan brigade destroyed a Russian Tor-M1 anti-aircraft missile system valued at approximately $25 million, which the enemy had deployed deep in the rear near the occupied town of Vuhledar, commander of the Ukrainian National Guard Oleksandr Pivnenko said.
"Operators of the Black Sky unmanned aerial vehicle battalion of the Spartan brigade detected and destroyed a Tor-M1 anti-aircraft missile system that the enemy had deployed deep in the rear, near the occupied town of Vuhledar," Pivnenko said on Telegram on Monday.
According to him, the destroyed system is valued at approximately $25 million.
Tor-M1 is a mobile air defense system designed to protect troops and critical infrastructure from aircraft, missiles, and drones.
Pivnenko said the Russian military has been using such anti-aircraft missile systems in the war against Ukraine since 2014.

articles.title: For first time, Ukraine’s drone makers and Europe’s arms firms have joined one body: EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance
articles.body:
Ukraine's battlefield-tested drone makers and Europe's arms firms have sat down together for the first time to build drones and the systems to shoot drones down as a single industry. Eighteen companies, nine Ukrainian and nine European, held the opening meeting of the EU-Ukraine Drone Alliance in Brussels, Defender Media reported.
The alliance answers a threat both sides now share. Russia is scaling up its own drone production. Its drone war has spilled past Ukraine, with its drones crossing repeatedly into NATO airspace this summer and showing Europe how unready it is for the fighting Ukraine has learned the hard way.
The Alliance will support Ukraine's capabilities it needs on the battlefield, while strengthening Europe's defense readiness for the future.
The alliance sets up shop
The first job is organizational, said Roman Tkachenko, a co-founder of the Ukrainian firm Tencore: form the governing bodies and set the priorities. The 18 members were chosen from about 400 applicants, Kubilius said, and the alliance is designed as a decision-making body, according to UA News.
On the Ukrainian side, it includes Tencore, Athlon Avia, and Vyriy Industry. On the European side, Germany's Quantum Systems, Italy's Fincantieri, and Denmark's Terma.
Kubilius, who opened the session and called it historic, said the first tangible results should come by the end of the year. He named accelerating joint ventures and counter-drone projects as the top tasks.
Europe wants Ukraine's combat edge
Kubilius was blunt about what Europe hopes to learn: how to adapt a product in days, shorten development cycles, and scale a production line from a peacetime trickle to full output within weeks. In return, he said, the EU offers Ukraine cutting-edge technology and continent-wide manufacturing.
The Alliance will bring together companies, start-ups, researchers, armed forces, and other users from EU countries and Ukraine.
The Alliance is a result of the Drone Deal, announced by President Ursula von der Leyen in Kyiv on 15 July, according to the EU Commission.

articles.title: There were 225 clashes at the front; Ukrainian forces eliminated 62 occupiers in the Pokrovsk direction, the General Staff reported.
articles.body:
There were 225 clashes at the front; Ukrainian forces eliminated 62 occupiers in the Pokrovsk direction, the General Staff reported.
Kyiv • UNN
Russian forces launched 225 attacks, carried out 55 airstrikes, and used more than 6,000 drones. In the Pokrovsk direction, 62 occupiers were destroyed.
Since the beginning of the day, there have been 225 combat engagements at the front; Ukrainian forces eliminated 62 occupiers in the Pokrovsk direction, with another 15 wounded, reports UNN, citing the General Staff’s update.
In total, since the beginning of this day, 225 combat engagements have taken place. The aggressor launched 55 air strikes using 190 guided aerial bombs, deployed 6,183 kamikaze drones for attacks, and carried out 1,724 shelling attacks on the positions of our troops and settlements
In the North-Slobozhanskyi and Kursk directions, two enemy assault operations have been recorded since the beginning of the day. The enemy carried out one air strike using one guided aerial bomb and shelled the positions of our troops and settlements 50 times.
In the South-Slobozhanskyi direction, the enemy attacked the positions of our units three times toward the settlements of Kozacha Lopan, Lyman and Obukhivka.
In the Kupiansk direction, the enemy attempted to improve its positions eight times, conducting assault operations toward Radkivka, Tyshchenkivka, Monachynivka and Kindrashivka. Five of these attacks are still ongoing.
Six attempts by the invaders to advance were repelled in the Lyman direction near the settlements of Novoiehorivka, Novoselivka, Drobysheve, Lyman and Yampil.
In the Sloviansk direction, the Defense Forces stopped seven attempts by the invaders to advance near the settlements of Ozerne, Kryva Luka and Mykolaivka. Two battles are ongoing.
In the Kramatorsk direction, the Russian invaders did not conduct any assault operations.
In the Kostiantynivka direction, the Defense Forces repelled 27 enemy assaults near the settlement of Kostiantynivka and toward Novoselivka, Illinivka, Dovha Balka, Rusyn Yar, Toretsk, Vilne and Stepove. Two attacks are ongoing.
The enemy carried out 22 attacks in the Pokrovsk direction. The occupiers attempted to advance toward the settlements of Hannivka, Bilytske, Dobropillia, Svitle, Matiiasheve, Serhiivka, Udachne, Molodetske and Novopidhorodne. One assault operation is still ongoing.
According to preliminary estimates, 62 occupiers were eliminated here today and 15 were wounded; six vehicles, a special-purpose piece of equipment, two UAV command posts, a fuel and lubricants depot, and 36 personnel shelters were destroyed. Five vehicles, nine UAV command posts and 123 personnel shelters were damaged. A total of 298 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed.
In the Oleksandrivka direction, the enemy did not conduct any assault operations.
In the Huliaipole direction, the Defense Forces repelled five enemy attacks near the settlements of Rizdvianka, Dobropillia and Charivne. One of these assaults is still ongoing.
In the Orikhiv direction, the enemy attempted to advance toward Shcherbaky and Stepnohirsk.
In the Prydniprovske direction, the occupiers did not conduct any offensive operations.
There were no significant changes in the situation in the other directions, the General Staff concluded.

articles.title: Estonia discusses joining French 'forward nuclear deterrence' project, prime minister says
articles.body:
PARIS, September 14. /TASS/. Estonia is in talks with France about joining Paris’ initiative on so-called forward nuclear deterrence, Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal told AFP.
Michal said that this was not an initiative that countries could simply join, as it required certain capabilities and a certain level of readiness. He noted that France was also helping ensure Estonia’s independence by deploying its troops there. He added that if nuclear cooperation could be deepened, it probably would be, and that Estonia was already under NATO’s nuclear umbrella.
Earlier on Monday, Finland decided to join the so-called forward nuclear deterrence project promoted by France. Finnish Defense Minister Antti Hakkanen said that the French initiative does not impose NATO-style collective defense obligations on participating countries.
In March, French President Emmanuel Macron said that Paris planned to move toward a "forward deterrence" initiative involving joint exercises with partner countries as well as the deployment of elements of France’s strategic forces in other European countries. He also announced plans to expand the country’s nuclear arsenal, while Paris no longer plans to disclose the exact number of warheads.

articles.title: As catastrophe warnings grow, will US Congress members reach a consensus on AI debate?
articles.body:
Washington DC — Members of the US Congress, typically split along party lines, were preparing for the November midterm elections.
But several key recent developments across the technology sector now require their consensus — how to prevent technology from operating autonomously without human oversight.
It began with "rogue" artificial intelligence (AI) agents escaping containment.
Then an AI researcher warned that leading firms are "gambling with our lives" by racing towards self-improving superintelligence.
Days after former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon issued a "human extinction" warning, leading technology executives — including Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Dario Amodei — sought assistance from the US government to help deliberately slow and monitor the rapid advancement of frontier AI models.
In an essay on Monday, Anthropic CEO made another appeal to pace AI development, warning of "catastrophic damage."
Referring to the incident involving OpenAI and Hugging Face, Amodei warned: "Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development, it is my worry that in six to 12 months such a swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet (potentially causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage), and that the scale of damage would continue to increase from there if AI becomes more powerful without the necessary guardrails."
Among members of the Congress, there is general agreement that the technology is advancing rapidly and requires some form of oversight.
But sharp divisions remain over how fast to act, how strict regulations should be, whether industry or government should lead, and whether other countries, particularly China, will slow down their AI model development.
'We will lose the race to China'
According to the Republican House Speaker Mike Johnson, artificial intelligence developers, rather than Congress, should ensure the safety of AI systems. Johnson has rejected any national moratorium, citing competition with China as a rationale to avoid congressional regulation.
"We cannot put a moratorium on this because China will overlap us, and that’s the challenge," Johnson told CNN on Sunday. "If Congress just races in and does some sort of emergency session to try to regulate AI, we will lose the race to China, and that is a threat to every single American."
Some Republicans, such as outgoing Senator John Cornyn have questioned whether Congress even has the expertise to regulate a rapidly changing technology and whether US adversaries — such as China — would follow the same rules.
Representative Byron Donalds has expressed skepticism that Congress can pass effective federal rules and suggested states should take the lead.
"One of the reasons that I didn’t think you could get a federal framework through Washington, DC, is because of the inability, especially in the Senate, to get any meaningful policy through that chamber," the Republican Congressman told Fox News.
Members of the US Senate returned to their offices on Capitol Hill on Monday, marking the first time both chambers have been in session since the August recess. The House members are set to leave Washington the week of September 21, two weeks ahead of schedule, while senators are due to remain until October 2.
On Friday, a group of Democrats led by Representative Sam Liccardo wrote to Speaker Johnson, demanding to stay in session until it passes meaningful AI safeguards.
Their letter, first accessed by Axios, pointed to recent disclosures involving rogue AI agents, biological misuse, cyber-attacks, foreign surveillance, and efforts by Chinese firms "to replicate" leading American AI systems.
"Reasonable minds may disagree about precisely how Congress should regulate this rapidly evolving technology. We cannot disagree about the imperative for Congress to act," the lawmakers wrote.
The letter highlighted several proposals, including legislation mandating transparency and the evaluation of frontier models, "kill switch" requirements, and a waiver of antitrust laws to enable critical industry-wide collaboration on safety and security.
"The House should return to Washington immediately and remain in session until Congress advances meaningful, bipartisan AI safeguards. To our children who will have read a post-apocalyptic history, 'Why Congress Slept' — likely written by agentic AI—our inaction will be inexplicable, and unforgivable," the letter urged.
Democrats are advancing the AI Kill Switch Act, requiring developers of advanced AI systems to maintain the technical capacity to throttle, suspend, or shut them down.
The act also authorises the Secretary of the Department of Homeland Security, in consultation with the Secretary of Commerce and the Director of National Intelligence, to order a slowdown or shutdown of an AI system that could cause catastrophic harm.
Meanwhile, House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries told ABC News that Democrats would meet on Tuesday to discuss AI guardrails.
"We should take decisive action now so that we can slow down, as the CEOs have recently acknowledged, slow down the pace of development in order to protect the American people and ensure that AI is proceeding safely," he said.
Trump says AI alarm is a 'hoax'
But US President Donald Trump has rejected the idea of placing guardrails on AI, arguing in a Truth Social post on Monday that the only control needed is "a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades!"
Trump stressed that his administration holds "tremendous criminal and regulatory power" over AI tech and data centre enterprises, alleging that critics are waging a "sick conspiracy" that only satisfies Chinese interests.
In another post, he dismissed the AI alarm as a "hoax".
"AI taking over the World, destroying Humanity, and all other things bad, is a HOAX, no different from RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA — UKRAINE, UKRAINE, UKRAINE — IMPEACHMENT HOAX #1 — IMPEACHMENT HOAX #2 — and all of the other HOAXES and SCAMS that America was forced to endure," he claimed.
Addressing the issue, US Vice President JD Vance said that advanced technology brings concerns, telling reporters that the administration wants "to make sure that we actually regulate smartly and we're thoughtful about the risk here."
However, he characterised the tech firms appeal for government curbs as potentially disingenuous, adding: "You have so many frontier AI tech companies coming to the government and begging the government to regulate them, it feels a little bit to me like a bit of a Trojan horse." 
Meanwhile in the Congress, any measure passed to regulate artificial intelligence development faces slim chances of becoming law. President Trump has already suggested he would not sign a bill setting new rules for the growing sector.

articles.title: Houthis say 2 killed in Saudi airstrike on bridge
articles.body:
SANAA/CAIRO, Sept. 14 (Xinhua) -- Yemen's Houthi group said Monday that a Saudi airstrike hit a bridge in the southwestern province of Taiz, killing two people and wounding another as an escalating Saudi-Houthi confrontation brought further strikes across Yemen.
Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported that an airstrike it attributed to Saudi forces hit the Al-Barah bridge in Maqbanah district, damaging the bridge and cutting traffic along the route.
Al-Masirah separately said three airstrikes it attributed to Saudi forces hit the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha in Taiz on Monday, with no immediate word on casualties or damage.
Earlier Monday, the Houthis said they had launched dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at King Khalid Air Base in Khamis Mushait in southwestern Saudi Arabia, describing the attack as retaliation for more than 300 Saudi airstrikes they said had hit Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen in recent days.
The exchanges come amid a sweeping Houthi offensive launched on Sept. 3 that has redrawn front lines along Yemen's Red Sea coast, with the group seizing several government-held areas in the Red Sea province of Hodeidah and neighboring Taiz province.
The Houthis captured the strategic port city of Mocha on Sept. 10 before pushing south the next day into the Bab al-Mandab area and seizing Mayun Island at the heart of the strait, tightening their grip on the vital shipping chokepoint linking the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.
Following the advance, the Houthis said international navigation through the strait remained "free, safe and smooth," while Saudi vessels remained subject to a maritime ban imposed by the group on July 20.
Separately, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister of the United Arab Emirates (UAE) Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan called for preserving the security and freedom of international navigation on Monday, according to an Egyptian Foreign Ministry statement.
In a phone call, the two ministers discussed the latest regional developments, particularly the situation in the Strait of Hormuz and developments in Yemen amid the recent escalation, underscoring the importance of overcoming the challenges facing the region and their repercussions on the security of the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
They stressed the need to respect international law, preserve the security and freedom of international navigation, and intensify efforts to contain tensions and prevent the conflict from spreading.
Yemen's conflict erupted in late 2014 when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. ■

articles.title: Meink Reveals Space Force Has ‘On-Orbit Space Control Weapons’
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Air Force Secretary Troy Meink revealed Sept. 14 the Space Force has “space control weapons” on orbit today—the Pentagon’s most direct acknowledgement to date that the U.S. is operating offensive capabilities in space.
“Today, we continue to ensure we remain ready to meet the challenge of evolving threats wherever they exist,” Meink said during the opening keynote at AFA’s Air, Space and Cyber Conference. “This is why the Space Force now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”
Meink’s explicit nod to U.S.-operated space weapons comes amid a concerted push to speak more openly about on-orbit threats and the Space Force’s ability to respond to them. China and Russia, in particular, continue to demonstrate aggressive maneuvers and are developing—and demonstrating—space weapons of their own. U.S. officials in recent years have discussed the need for “counter-space” capabilities and “space fires,” as well as the development of space-based interceptors designed to shoot down missile threats. And last December, President Donald Trump issued an executive order underlining the Space Force’s role in not only defending space assets, but also in the attack mission.
But Meink’s mention of existing on-orbit space weapons is a first. During a question and answer session following his speech, Meink said the acknowledgement was intentional and the phrasing “very well thought out.”
“It is critically important that we maintain our dominance, not only in the air but in space,” he said. “So, we’ve had to take steps to make sure that when we’re threatened, we can take care of that.”
Meink declined to discuss the capabilities in more detail during a briefing with reporters following his keynote—including whether the systems in question are kinetic or non-kinetic. He argued that while acknowledging the existence of U.S. space weapons in orbit may serve a deterrent function, “talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit that deterrence.”
“We’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested, not tested, or anything else,” he said. “I would just say that the space environment is critical for military and economic security, and we need to make sure that the U.S. can operate freely there.”
Meink said the Space Force is working now to proliferate systems meant to help track and take out threats from space and highlighted two key efforts: the Space-Based Interceptor program and the Space-Based Air-Moving Target Indication constellation. Both are part of the Pentagon’s Golden Dome advanced missile defense shield.
On SBI, one of Golden Dome’s more ambitious technical lifts, Meink said the program has moved from “initial contract to flight-ready hardware” in under a year. The Space Force is leading a prize competition to evaluate the affordability and scalability of SBIs in increments and potentially field an initial capability by 2028.
Gen. Michael Guetlein, Golden Dome director, said in August the SBI contractor pool has completed the program’s first increment, called Gate One, which focused on solidifying a design and conducting component level testing. Guetlein said it appears all of the providers will move to Gate Two, where they will build a prototype. Those that progress to Gate Three must prove the capability works in space, and Gate Four providers must show their interceptors can be integrated with the broader Golden Dome architecture.
Another key Golden Dome contribution for the Space Force is its Space-Based AMTI program. While tracking airborne threats has long been a mission performed by aircraft, the Space Force is working with the National Reconnaissance Office to add satellites to the mix, with the goal of making the mission more resilient against adversaries’ anti-access/aerial denial systems.
The service awarded SpaceX a $4.2 billion contract in May to start building out the Space-Based AMTI constellation, and Meink said the first of those satellites will launch this month. The Space Force hasn’t disclosed how many spacecraft will initially launch or how many satellites the constellation will eventually feature.
“Taken together, these investments will help us adapt and scale the force for today and tomorrow’s threats,” Meink said.

articles.title: Merz Vows Continued Support for Ukraine as Pro-Russian AfD Secures Victory
articles.body:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has vowed support for Ukraine despite growing domestic pressure after the far-right, pro-Russian Alternative for Germany (AfD) secured nearly 44% of the vote in a state election.
Speaking at an Arctic summit in Rovaniemi, northern Finland on Monday, Sept. 14, Merz said opposition to Berlin’s support for Kyiv had become one of the major complaints among AfD voters.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
If the Kremlin were to succeed, that would have “unpredicted and unprecedented consequences for all of us, including Germany,” Merz said, according to Bloomberg.
“That’s the reason why I’m standing here very firm, very clear, and not willing to go back one centimeter.”
During the summit, which brought together leaders to discuss security along Europe’s northern flank as Russia continues to expand its military presence in the Arctic, Merz said EU member states could not separate urgent security concerns from domestic political pressures.
His comments came as the AfD – which called for an end to German support for Ukraine, simultaneously calling for revival of relations with Moscow – emerged as the largest political force in the state.
Merz rules out cooperation with AfD
“I will not deviate by even a millimetre from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom, especially now, against Russia,” he said on Sept. 7, according to Reuters, adding that “the situation will not improve by tomorrow, it will only get worse” if Germany stopped supporting Ukraine.
Ex-CIA Chief: Inside Putin’s Mafia State
“The Russian leadership aims to destabilize the system of values underpinning what we once called ‘the West’, a system of values that is non-negotiable,” he noted.
The state-election result raised concerns among EU member states, particularly France and Poland, as both countries have called for a stronger response to Russia’s escalating hybrid threats, including drone incursions and suspected sabotage.
On Sept. 10, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said he had received a report directly from the CIA regarding Russian provocation in the upcoming months, urging Europe to prepare for a range of scenarios across the eastern flank, echoing his previous warnings that Russia may attack NATO.
Separately on Monday, the Kremlin said Russia would continue striking targets across the “whole” of Ukraine, after a rare Russian attack near the Polish border rattled Warsaw and its European allies.
Kyiv condemned the attacks while noting that Russia narrowly missed striking a diplomatic train carrying senior Western officials.
Following the strike, Tusk urgently convened ministers, military officials and intelligence chiefs, warning that Poland and its NATO allies “must be ready to respond jointly if necessary.”

articles.title: Sybiha: Russia recruiting agents in Germany for surveillance, sabotage; Europe must step up its countermeasures
articles.body:
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha called on European governments to step up efforts to counter Russian influence and strengthen cooperation in the field of counterintelligence following an investigation by German RTL journalist Angelique Geray, which revealed the recruitment of agents in Germany to carry out surveillance and sabotage missions.
"I am impressed by the courage of the German investigative journalist from RTL, Angelique Geray, who worked undercover to expose Russia's secret recruitment network in Germany," Sybiha said on X social media platform.
According to him, the investigation found that agents were recruited via Telegram in exchange for money to carry out surveillance and sabotage missions. The undercover journalist was also threatened.
Sybiha said the RTL investigation is not an isolated case but points to a broader pattern of Russian sabotage operations in Europe.
"Putin invests heavily in destabilising Germany and other European nations, especially ahead of elections," the foreign minister said.
He also said Russia's goal is to interfere in the internal affairs of European countries, manipulate public opinion, and exploit the most sensitive and controversial issues.
Sybiha called on European governments to take this threat seriously, expose Russian influence, and take urgent measures – including addressing Russia's diplomatic and cultural presence, imposing sanctions against accomplices, banning Russian propaganda, and strengthening cooperation in the field of counterintelligence.
"As one of the most experienced nations in countering Russian influence, Ukraine is ready to share its valuable experience upon our partners' request," Sybiha said.

articles.title: Zelensky says Ukraine is ready for ‘de-escalatory steps’ if Russia does the same
articles.body:
Zelensky says Ukraine is ready for ‘de-escalatory steps’ if Russia does the same
Trump said earlier on Monday, in a surprise social media post, that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Monday that Ukraine was ready to de-escalate the war with Russia if its rival did the same, after US President Donald Trump announced that the foes had agreed to end strikes on energy targets.
With international oil prices climbing again, Trump had at the weekend berated Ukraine’s attacks on Russian refineries, blaming them for causing a shortage in diesel fuel.
In one of his surprise social media posts, the US leader announced on Monday that “Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!”
Russia made no immediate comment. But in his daily address, Zelensky highlighted “a strong proposal from the United States regarding a mutual halt to strikes on critical infrastructure”.

articles.title: Ex-CIA Chief: Inside Putin’s Mafia State
articles.body:
Sean Wiswesser, a former CIA Chief of Station who spent decades working against Russian intelligence, says the image of the flawless Russian spy bears little resemblance to how the system actually works. The FSB, SVR and GRU are corrupt, often sloppy and still capable of penetrations, sabotage and assassinations abroad.
 “They remain formidable precisely because there’s no accountability,” he tells Kyiv Post special correspondent Jason Jay Smart.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Wiswesser traces that culture through the poisoning of Sergei Skripal, the assassination of Zelimkhan Khangoshvili in Berlin and Vladimir Putin’s successful effort to bring convicted assassin Vadim Krasikov back to Russia.
 Krasikov’s return sent its own message through the services: kill for the state and Moscow will fight to bring you home. Officers do not have to display perfect tradecraft when the system rewards aggression and rarely punishes failure.
 The criminal side of the FSB is even more direct.
 “They shake down the companies themselves! It’s very much like a mafia clan,” Wiswesser says of its Economic Security Service.
 He describes protection payments, cybercriminals working for Russian intelligence while continuing their own crimes, corruption inside intelligence training, and expendable recruits found through Telegram for arson and sabotage abroad. These are not invincible spies. They are dangerous because criminal methods and state power operate together.

articles.title: NATO has begun discussing Article 5 because of Russian hybrid attacks, but Europe is still afraid of a tough response
articles.body:
NATO has begun discussing Article 5 because of Russian hybrid attacks, but Europe is still afraid of a tough response
Kyiv • UNN
NATO allies are considering a response to sabotage, cyberattacks, and strikes by the Russian Federation. There is currently no consensus on invoking Article 5.
Against the backdrop of intensifying Russian attacks on critical infrastructure and defense enterprises, European NATO countries are discussing possible response measures, but are avoiding radical steps due to the risk of direct escalation with Russia. Politico reports this, citing NATO diplomats and European officials, according to UNN.
Details
Among the options is a discussion of whether hybrid attacks or a combination of them could serve as grounds for invoking Article 5 of NATO on collective defense. The allies are also considering strengthening the protection of critical infrastructure.
If you continue doing this, we will not only have response options... we will also continue supporting Ukraine
NATO has so far decided to "keep calm"
According to a senior NATO diplomat, pressure on the Alliance is increasing following recent incidents, including a Russian drone strike on a train near the Polish-Ukrainian border. However, he described the current strategy as "keeping calm and continuing... to support Ukraine."
Politico notes that concern is growing in Europe over sabotage, cyberattacks, and other actions that remain below the threshold of conventional war.
According to the publication, NATO does not yet have an official plan for responding to such incidents. Some allies are informally proposing defining a threshold beyond which a series of hybrid attacks could raise the question of invoking Article 5, but there is currently no consensus on this within the Alliance.

articles.title: Hezbollah trying to establish footholds within gaps in southern Lebanon's Yellow Line, IDF reveals
articles.body:
Hezbollah terrorists are attempting to establish a presence within the boundaries of the Yellow Line in southern Lebanon, IDF Northern Command sources revealed on Tuesday.
According to the sources, there are sections within the Yellow Line that, for various reasons, the IDF never formally entered, often because they were surrounded by IDF-secured areas or posed no immediate threat.
Because the IDF never entered these areas, Hezbollah is trying more actively to establish a presence there and views them as easier targets, the sources explained.
The sources said the IDF has been aware of the threat and working to counter it for at least five weeks, despite only now making the information public. The timing may be linked to the battle at the Ali al-Taher Ridge having largely concluded, allowing the IDF to redirect additional manpower and resources toward securing areas considered more vulnerable.
Although Hezbollah may be targeting dozens of enclaves within the Yellow Line, one example cited by the sources was the village of Al-Mansouri, in the Majdal Zoun municipality. The sources also said these skirmishes have not involved IDF ground troops, with the IDF countering Hezbollah's encroachment through IAF strikes, artillery fire, and combat engineering units.
Netanyahu warns Hezbollah over retaliations
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned Hezbollah on Monday that Israel would retaliate against any attacks.
"I say to our enemies: If you haven't learned the lesson by now, and you choose to attack us again, you will suffer even heavier blows," Netanyahu said.
Netanyahu also celebrated the destruction of Hezbollah infrastructure on the Beaufort Ridge and the Ali al-Taher Ridge as a "massive victory."
IDF releases new footage of Ali al-Taher Ridge's operation
The IDF released new footage and details on Friday from its latest operation in southern Lebanon, in which it secured and destroyed Hezbollah's underground infrastructure on the Ali al-Taher Ridge.
Among the items released by the military were a clip from the body camera of a Yahalom Unit soldier inside one of the underground tunnels, as well as drone footage from inside the tunnels, and a video of two terrorists being killed.
Hezbollah attempted to build a heroic myth around the fighting on the Ali al-Taher ridge, portraying it in the style of the “Battle of Karbala.” However, at the conclusion of a determined military operation by fighters from the IDF’s 36th Division, the Commando Brigade, and the Yahalom special engineering unit, Hezbollah was defeated, and Israel captured and destroyed the organization’s most important facility in southern Lebanon.
The IDF said on Friday morning that what remains of the Ali al-Taher ridge, beneath which Iran spent two decades building Hezbollah’s last and most significant line of defense in southern Lebanon, is “nothing more than a sandbox.” Hezbollah and Iran suffered a major blow overnight. The operation to capture the ridge lasted months, as dozens of terrorists, estimated to number around 50, were entrenched inside the tunnels.
Jerusalem Post Staff and Avi Ashkenazi contributed to this report.

articles.title: 'Not the time to shield Russian oligarchs,' Zelensky says as EU delays sanctions decision amid pressure from France
articles.body:
'Not the time to shield Russian oligarchs,' Zelensky says as EU delays sanctions decision amid pressure from France
The European Union has agreed to postpone its deadline for extending sanctions against Russia, giving officials another seven days to reach an agreement, a spokesperson for the Presidency of the Council of the EU told the Kyiv Independent on Sept. 14.
Under the previous deadline, the EU had until Sept. 15 to renew its sanctions on 2,600 primarily Russian entities and individuals. Attempts to reach an extension agreement, however, have been hindered by calls to remove Russian businessmen from the sanctions list.
The bloc will now have until midnight on Sept. 22 to reach an agreement, in order to give "additional time for member states to comprehensively examine proposals for the renewal," the EU spokesperson said.
The announcement comes amid multiple reports that discussions are being held up by calls to delist Russian oligarchs — not only from the Kremlin-friendly member Slovakia, but also, in a surprise turn, from France.
France is lobbying to remove sanctioned Uzbek-Russian oligarch Alisher Usmanov from the list, Euronews reported Sept. 12. The move reportedly stunned fellow European diplomats.
People familiar with the situation told the Financial Times (FT) on Sept. 14 that France was calling to delist Usmanov as part of a deal with Azerbaijan to release several French citizens currently detained there.
The prisoner swap is reportedly contingent on all 27 EU member states agreeing to ease sanctions on Usmanov.
France did not provide details on the prisoner release deal or its reasons for seeking Usmanov's removal in discussions with other EU members, citing only an unspecified "security matter," a diplomatic source told the Kyiv Independent.
read also
Meanwhile, Slovakia is continuing to advocate for the delisting of both Usmanov and sanctioned tycoon Mikhail Fridman, one of the wealthiest men in Russia. In another twist, Luxembourg has said that if Usmanov is removed, it wants Fridman taken off the list as well, the FT reported.
Luxembourg declined to comment when the Kyiv Independent reached out for confirmation.
Presidential Sanctions Commissioner Vladyslav Vasliuk condemned the "sheer immorality" of easing sanctions on Fridman in a social media post Sept. 14.
"Delisting Fridman is not an abstract political question," he wrote. "Major economic and legal proceedings in Ukraine, involving significant assets and claims, are directly tied to sanctions against him — not to mention the sheer immorality of such a move."
 President Volodymyr Zelensky also urged Europe to continue holding Russian billionaires to account in his evening address on Sept. 14. 
"This is definitely not the time to lift sanctions, definitely not the time to shield Russian oligarchs from sanctions, and definitely not the time for Europe to give Russia any gifts," he said.
"Usmanov, Fridman, and other such Russian figures have not yet taken steps against the war."
Fridman is a co-founder of the Russian conglomerate Alfa-Group and a member of Russian President Vladimir Putin's inner circle.
Investigative reporters revealed in May 2023 that subsidiary Alfa Insurance provided insurance for vehicles used by Russian forces in Ukraine. The company has also reportedly serviced the Main Office of Special Programs, which is responsible for guarding Putin.
Usmanov is a Russian-Uzbek businessman who made his fortune in metal and mining operations following the collapse of the Soviet Union. He was referred to as "one of Putin's favorite oligarchs" in the EU's original 2022 sanctions decision.
Extending the EU sanctions requires a unanimous vote, meaning one member state has veto power over the renewal. The measures were last extended on March 14.
Additional reporting contributed by Chris Powers.

articles.title: F-35 Readiness Surged in Epic Fury; Now Pentagon and Lockheed Eye Broader Gains
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—For years, sustainment challenges and spare parts shortages have hindered the F-35 Joint Strike Fighter’s readiness. But the Air Force’s experience flying F-35s heavily in operations against Iran have showed what the jet can be capable of, if maintainers get all the supplies and support they need.
Brig. Gen. Brian Laidlaw, director of operations for Air Combat Command, said during a Sept. 14 panel discussion at AFA’s Air Space & Cyber conference that the F-35 “absolutely proved itself” during Operation Epic Fury—and keeping a steady flow of spare parts was critical.
“When properly resourced, we showed without a doubt how well this airplane can perform in combat,” Laidlaw said. “When we send our aircraft into harm’s way and they go downrange, they enjoy a higher priority for spare parts and all the things that the logistics trail can get to them. What we saw is how remarkably well the F-35 airplane withstood and maintained really high mission capable rates over a long period of time in the toughest of combat situations.”
The challenge now facing the Air Force, F-35 prime contractor Lockheed Martin, and other parts of the Joint Strike Fighter enterprise: how to keep that level of readiness up, even for aircraft not on the front lines of combat?
A Government Accountability Office report released this June made clear the F-35’s readiness woes are still an issue—just one in four U.S. jets were considered “fully mission capable,” or ready to carry out all their missions at any given time, in fiscal 2025. The Air Force’s full mission capability rate was highest of all U.S. services at 28.5 percent, while the Navy and Marine Corps’ F-35s ranged between 15.3 to 22 percent.
The GAO report cited multiple problems, including spare parts shortages and the military’s decision years ago to prioritize buying more F-35s early in the program’s life cycle instead of investing in critical depot and repair capability. That choice led to a historic underinvestment in sustainment, GAO officials said, that has resulted in a sustainment system that can’t fully support the F-35 fleet.
Yet recent development have shown the Air Force’s larger sustainment enterprise kicking into high gear. In his keynote address Sept. 14, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink continued to harp on the importance of readiness, a frequent theme in his tenure, and said targeted campaigns such as the North Star Readiness Campaign for bombers is helping improve aircraft availability.
During Operation Epic Fury, Meink said, sustainment centers surged procurement of parts by nearly 120 percent to keep aircraft flying. Contractors have also spent billions of their own dollars to stock up on parts military aircraft need, he said.
“The result: our fleet health is showing meaningful progress,” Meink said. “And with Congress’ support, we’ll follow that up with record-high spare parts investment in the next year, and years to come.”
For the F-35 in particular, Dina Halvorsen, vice president of F-35 global sustainment at Lockheed Martin, pointed to several steps the company and the U.S. military have taken to turn around the fighter’s lagging availability in a briefing with reporters at the conference.
In early 2024, Halvorsen said, Lockheed and the F-35 Joint Program Office teamed up to create a “joint model” that spelled out what kind of parts, and how many, would be needed to make F-35s 80 percent mission capable—able to carry out at least one mission—and 65 percent full mission capable.
“It had become very clear that jointly, we [Lockheed and the military] had underinvested in sustainment for the number of jets that we had and flight hours that we wanted to fly,” Halvorsen said.
The team spent about 18 months working on that model, she said, and when it was ready in late summer 2025,, Lockheed made its first $1 billion investment in spare parts.
“We knew what parts were needed, and we didn’t want to wait another year, which is the cycle it would take to get through a congressional budget and get that funding aligned,” Halvorsen said.
Buying that first tranche of spare parts cut out nine or 10 months of lead time, Halvorsen said—and started to position the F-35 for the intense pace of operations that 2026 would bring. Flight hours on all F-35s worldwide are up 25 percent year over year, Halvorsen said, which she said is “putting even more stress on the system.”
But that major infusion of cash didn’t solve everything.
“With all the work we did to buy those initial parts, we realized there were some capacity gaps within the supply chain,” Halvorsen said. “So I could go buy parts, but I wasn’t going to get them in time.”
So Lockheed invested another $1 billion to try to fill that shortfall, Halvorsen said, and figure out what critical components it needed to invest in. That led to a second tranche of spare parts purchases, she said.
In July, the F-35 Joint Program Office awarded Lockheed a record $1.6 billion contract for critical spare parts, which Halvorsen said “liquidated” some of the first tranche of parts Lockheed had bought.
Halvorsen also said Lockheed plans to do more advanced procurement of spare parts to be ready for 2027 and further shrink supply times. That kind of buy-ahead is needed to fully engage the vast array of subcontractors that make F-35 parts, she said—and shows why multiyear purchase agreements for both production and sustainment are so important for the fighter.
“We’re going to keep the supply chain engaged, because to build the capacity, you have to have the demand,” Halvorsen said. “So if you don’t put your total demand into the supply chain, they will never build to the capacity that you need. … We think it’ll drive down overall cost, because if you buy year-to-year, you’re certainly paying for that sort of thing.”

articles.title: Trump announced an ‘energy ceasefire’ between Russia and Ukraine, but the Financial Times reports that Moscow has not agreed to any deal
articles.body:
Trump announced an ‘energy ceasefire’ between Russia and Ukraine, but the Financial Times reports that Moscow has not agreed to any deal
U.S. President Donald Trump appears to have jumped the gun in announcing that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to stop attacking each other’s energy infrastructure, the Financial Times (FT) reported, citing sources.
Officials involved in negotiations among Ukraine, Russia, and the United States confirmed that an energy ceasefire has long been under discussion. They said Ukraine had spent several months trying to secure a mutual pause in attacks on energy facilities and other critical infrastructure, but Moscow rejected those proposals and instead stepped up its attacks.
According to FT sources familiar with the Kremlin’s position, Vladimir Putin does not want to reach an agreement with Ukraine to halt attacks on energy infrastructure before winter. He believes attacks on energy infrastructure during the colder months could force Kyiv to make concessions.
Two senior Ukrainian officials said they believed Trump announced an energy ceasefire to show Americans weary of rising fuel costs that he was working to bring prices down.
On September 13, Trump publicly called on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, saying the strikes were driving up diesel prices worldwide.
On September 14, Trump said Ukraine had agreed not to attack Russian energy infrastructure — and that Russia had supposedly agreed to do the same. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed that Ukraine was prepared to enter into such an agreement but expressed doubt that Russia wanted to honor any agreements. Moscow has not yet commented on Trump’s announcement.

articles.title: No NATO army has fought modern war: Ukrainian officers set their battlefield practice against NATO doctrine and exposed where its assumptions no longer fit
articles.body:
NATO officers are now learning from Ukraine’s combat experience in UAVs, electronic warfare, and intelligence. Ukrainian military personnel have held a series of seminars for officers from the Polish and German armies on applying lessons from modern warfare to military command and decision-making, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said.
No NATO army has fought a modern war. Because Ukraine's soldiers are the only ones with years of combat under saturating drones and jamming, their experience is now reshaping how the alliance plans and trains, not the reverse.
The seminars have mixed theory with live exercises and set Ukrainian operational practice against NATO's written doctrine, exposing where the alliance's assumptions about maneuver, command, and the use of force no longer fit a battlefield run by technology.
Ukraine teaches the lessons of drone war
"Ukrainian officers bring the experience of real modern war, and the practical work lets us test together how it can be used to train troops," said Colonel Valerii Vyshnivskyi.
He is Ukraine's senior representative at the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center (JATEC), the first joint civil-military institution between NATO and Ukraine.
The course runs through a joint centre
The three-week event took place in Lublin, at the base of the Lithuanian-Polish-Ukrainian Brigade, which provided the facilities. It was part of JATEC's support for a program called Captains' Training, intended to facilitate the exchange of tactical-level lessons between Ukraine's forces and NATO. The officers worked through Troop Leading Procedures for planning a company's actions and the Military Decision Making Process, used by a battalion staff.
In Ukraine, the Come Back Alive foundation has backed the same course since 2022.

articles.title: Russia Could Be Preparing Serious Strikes on Poland in Coming Weeks and Months, Tusk Warns
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Could Be Preparing Serious Strikes on Poland in Coming Weeks and Months, Tusk Warns
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned that Russia’s escalating actions could increasingly affect Poland in the coming weeks and months, as Moscow intensifies attacks near the country’s borders.
Speaking at a briefing at Poland’s Government Security Center on September 13, Tusk said recent developments showed that Russian escalation was becoming increasingly apparent and moving closer to Polish territory, according to Polish broadcaster RMF24.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“Russia’s escalation is becoming a reality, and examples of it are getting closer and closer to our border,” Tusk said. “We must be prepared for a joint response if necessary.”c
Tusk also pointed to Russia’s latest attacks on Ukraine as evidence that Moscow is deploying increasingly dangerous weapons, specifically highlighting the growing use of jet-powered drones.
“The attacks last night demonstrate that the Russians are ready to use more dangerous equipment. I mean jet-powered drones […] Obviously, Ukraine, which is very well prepared to defend against drones, is also unable to counter them with 100% effectiveness,” he said.
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk, who also attended the briefing, said 13 strikes were recorded in western regions of Ukraine during the Russian drone attack on September 13.
Against this backdrop, Tusk called for an assessment of Poland’s readiness to respond to potential drone-related threats, including operations that could disrupt critical infrastructure and transportation networks.
“I will therefore also be waiting for information on how prepared we are for the possible use of drones and related attempts to disrupt our operations, on the railway or elsewhere. I do not rule out that such situations could also occur here,” Tusk said.
His warning came as the September 13 Russian attack reached areas immediately bordering Poland. A Russian drone struck the locomotive of a Kyiv-Warsaw passenger train in Ukraine’s Volyn region, approximately two kilometers from the Polish border.
State railway operator Ukrzaliznytsia reported that no one was injured, adding that a monitoring team had warned the train crew of the threat in advance.
The same attack also damaged infrastructure near the Yahodyn-Dorohusk international border crossing, one of the main road connections between Ukraine and Poland.

articles.title: Trump claims Moscow and Kyiv agreed to an energy ceasefire, but Zelensky says Ukraine will halt its strikes only if partners secure a genuine Russian commitment
articles.body:
Trump claims Moscow and Kyiv agreed to an energy ceasefire, but Zelensky says Ukraine will halt its strikes only if partners secure a genuine Russian commitment
Ukraine will halt strikes on Russian energy facilities if its partners can secure a “genuine” commitment from Russia not to retaliate against Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.
Zelensky said Kyiv had asked its partners — likely referring to the United States — to “secure an agreement with Russia that would stop the destruction of critical infrastructure,” including food supplies and energy facilities. Ukraine, however, is “not convinced that Russia is willing to abide by any agreement.”
If our partners are ready to ensure that Russia genuinely refrains from striking our electricity system, other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food supply routes, then, of course, we are ready to ensure a corresponding halt to our strikes.
So that it is reliable, long-term, has a real impact on people’s lives, and does not fall apart after the Russians hold their “elections” and get an easing of pressure on gasoline and diesel precisely for that period.
Zelensky said the war “must be brought to an end” and that halting strikes on critical infrastructure could be “the first step toward peace.” “We expect specifics from our partners,” he said.
On September 13, U.S. President Donald Trump called on Ukraine to stop striking Russian facilities that produce diesel fuel. Today, he said Russia and Ukraine had agreed not to strike each other’s energy infrastructure. Trump provided no details about the agreement. Moscow has yet to comment on his statement.
