articles.title: Destroying Ukraine has ‘totemic’ role for Russia, British expert says
articles.body:
Destroying Ukraine has ‘totemic’ role for Russia, British expert says
British expert Jade McGlynn, Head of the Ukraine and Russia Program with the Centre for Statecraft and National Security at King’s College London, said this in an interview with Ukrinform.
“Their entire ideology revolves around claiming that the Ukrainians are just Russians who've been brainwashed or being used by the West as their proxy element,” the expert said.
In this regard, she believes the only thing that will change the calculus in the Kremlin would be if Moscow “has to choose between the stability at home and continuing to prosecute the war.”
“Destroying Ukraine has taken on this totemic role within the Kremlin's vision of Russia and its role in the world so the only thing that would force a reconsideration or recalculation would be if there begins to be a lot of trouble at home. I think the focus should be on the home front, the deep strikes on various elements, exerting much more pressure on the economy,” McGlynn said.
She believes the Russian people will not necessarily rise up against the regime, but such social tensions “always find a way, sometimes in quite unexpected ways.”
According to the researcher, many Russians are still “very happy to go along with the war, provided it doesn't affect them.”
“So, I think it's reasonable to show, including through petrol prices, the millions that make this war possible, whether because they work in the propaganda studios or in military production factories, or simply paying taxes, that there are consequences and that you can no longer ignore the war. It can no longer remain just some special military operation somewhere far away that you don't need to know about,” the expert said.
Therefore, she believes, any measures that increase this pressure would be helpful.
At the same time, she stressed that the West needs to do more to support Ukraine, particularly as winter approaches, including by providing more interceptor missiles.
“We’ve seen some very positive moves from European countries in the last few days in terms of procuring them. But it’s also about ensuring that Ukrainians have generators in order to have access to heat over this winter, because if this is going to end up being a race to exhaustion, then we need to be doing a lot more to ensure that it's not Ukraine that’s exhausted first,” the expert stressed.
As reported, on Sunday, U.S. President Donald Trump called on Ukraine to stop striking Russian oil refineries amid a sharp rise in diesel fuel prices worldwide.
Earlier, U.S. Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he believed Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries had affected diesel fuel prices in the United States.

articles.title: Russia experimenting with FPV drones deployed from Shaheds, Ukraine says
articles.body:
Russia experimenting with FPV drones deployed from Shaheds, Ukraine says
As reported by Ukrinform, Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, said this during a television broadcast.
“The enemy has already experimentally used FPV drones on the same Shaheds. In principle, there is already video that has been posted on social media. I would not say that this is currently being used on a large scale, or how useful it will be for the enemy,” Ihnat said.
He noted that Russia is constantly improving its Shaheds and Gerberas and upgrading their communications, navigation, and electronic warfare systems.
“Essentially, we need to keep up with the times in order to neutralize these new threats, including the enemy’s use of FPV drones that can be carried on the same Shaheds,” Ihnat said.
It was reported that information had circulated on social media claiming that Russian forces had begun using Shaheds as carriers for FPV drones, delivering them deep into Ukrainian territory. In particular, reports referred to the use of this tactic in the Kyiv region.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 4, Serhii Beskrestnov (Flash), an unofficial adviser to the President, said that no evidence had been found over three days that FPV drones were being deployed from jet-powered Shaheds during Russian attacks on Kyiv.

articles.title: Air Force Leaders Eye Point Defense Acquisition Czar, Say It’s No Longer a ‘Side Hustle’
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—Air Force officials are exploring the idea of creating a new acquisition office to oversee the point defense mission, in the service’s latest move to intensify its focus on defending airbases from drone and missile attacks, Air Force Secretary Troy E. Meink said Sept. 14, during AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference.
Since late 2023, the Air Force has been racing to get ahead of rapidly growing drone threat after unidentified drones hovered unchecked over Langley Air Force Base, Va., catching base commanders off guard. Since then, the service has been on a steady march to bolster airbase defense against drones and other new missile threats with everything from new doctrine on the “Point Defense of Air Bases” to plans for creating a point defense career field to ensure personnel are trained and equipped to defend bases from aerial attack.
Meink and Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach both devoted significant portions of their keynote addresses at the conference to point defense—reflecting the growing focus and urgency from senior leadership to tackle the issue.
“We can no longer treat point defense as a side hustle,” Wilsbach declared. “We must make it a core function of air and space power.”
On the personnel side, the new point defense career field will be operational in two years, Wilsbach said. Already, the Air Force has selected its first two career field managers—Wilsbach recognized one of them during his keynote.
On the acquisition side, the Air Force is now considering standing up a new portfolio acquisition executive, or PAE, to focus on “the kit side” of point defense “to further increase security for our Airmen and Guardians,” Meink said.
“How do you make sure that they have the kit they need to do the job?” Meink said, adding that the explosion of counter-drone innovations from industry “is a rapidly changing environment.”
PAEs are a new construct, introduced during recent Pentagon acquisition reforms to replace program executive offices. The idea is to combine several programs within a single mission area and give PAEs authority to move funds between programs and adjust requirements based on evolving needs. The Department of the Air Force currently has 26 PAEs—17 in the Air Force, nine in the Space Force.
“We are delegating almost every authority we legally have to our PAEs for most programs,” Meink said. “That now includes milestone decision authority, a big first on our acquisition community.”
Meink cautioned that the creation of a point defense PAE is “not going to be tomorrow.” But he sounded confident that it is a matter of when, not if, the new organization is created: “We’re already walking down the road, and eventually we’ll evolve into PAE for it.”
The need, he added, is clear.
“There definitely has to be continually increasing focus on making sure we can defend our Airmen and Guardians wherever they are in the world,” Meink said.
Wilsbach teased one acquisition program that may one day fall under the future point defense PAE, saying the Air Force will create a “point defense weapon system,” an umbrella effort that will bring together kinetic and nonkinetic counter-drone capabilities. He offered no further details about the new program.

articles.title: Zelenskyy called on Europe not to give gifts to the Russian Federation and to extend sanctions against oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
articles.body:
Zelenskyy called on Europe not to give gifts to the Russian Federation and to extend sanctions against oligarchs Usmanov and Fridman
Kyiv • UNN
Zelenskyy said that sanctions against Russia must not be eased, and called for restricting its finances and ballistic missile production. The war requires this.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy stressed that sanctions against the Russian Federation matter and called on everyone not to give gifts to Moscow and to introduce even stronger restrictions, UNN reports.
We all understand: sanctions against Russia really matter. This is definitely not the time to lift sanctions, definitely not the time to save Russian oligarchs from sanctions, and definitely not the time for Europe to give gifts to Russia. Usmanov, Fridman and other such Russian figures have not yet taken steps against the war. This is not the time for Europe to forget what is happening
According to him, new sanctions are needed and, "to be honest, stronger ones – such that Russia cannot adapt to them, including anti-ballistic sanctions – against all Russian ballistic-missile production, sanctions that restrict Russian finances." That is, measures that limit the war.
Lindsey Graham’s sanctions bill is still a bill, unfortunately, and not a law. It is important that it become law. I thank everyone in the world who supports this approach, who knows that strength works
We remind you
On Monday, EU countries were unable to extend one of the bloc’s sanctions regimes against Russia, five EU diplomats told Politico. Three of them said that EU ambassadors would reconvene later on Monday for further discussions.

articles.title: Disarray at Pentagon under Hegseth hindering key missions — media
articles.body:
NEW YORK, September 15. /TASS/. Disarray at the Pentagon under US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is preventing senior commanders from focusing on key priorities, The New York Times reported.
According to the newspaper, Hegseth’s tenure has seen an unprecedented purge of senior officers in the Pentagon’s modern history, as well as restrictions on where officers may study and what arguments they may advance in academic papers. An atmosphere of suspicion fueled by leaks from the department has also led to the widespread use of polygraph tests in an effort to identify sources disclosing internal information to the media.
The war with Iran has compounded the Pentagon’s problems, undermining sailors’ morale and depleting its supply of interceptor missiles. Numerous current and former Pentagon officials described Hegseth’s turbulent tenure as a persistent distraction that has diverted senior commanders from these priorities and fueled distrust among the department’s top leadership.
The newspaper also noted that Hegseth had dismissed or blocked the promotions of around 80 generals and admirals with decades of experience, leaving numerous senior Pentagon positions vacant for extended periods.

articles.title: Russian oligarch close to Putin paid for part of Donald Trump Jr’s lavish wedding
articles.body:
Donald Trump Jr and his wife, Bettina, confirmed on Monday that a Russian oligarch close to Vladimir Putin partially paid for the couple’s wedding celebrations in May, following a ProPublica report revealing Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the events.
Trump Jr, the US president’s eldest child, married the Palm Beach socialite in a lavish three-day celebration across two exclusive private islands in May.
Citing records and interviews with three anonymous sources familiar with the event, ProPublica reported that Kremlev, a member of the Russian president’s circle, footed the bill to rent one of the islands where a reception was held and where guests slept, along with other large expenses, including a huge firework show.
In a statement signed by the couple and shared on Bettina Trump’s Instagram after ProPublica’s report was published, they confirmed Kremlev’s contributions to the celebrations and characterized them as “an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful”.
A top Democrat demanded answers on the Trumps’ ties to Kremlev.
“Why did a Russian oligarch close to Putin fund Trump Jr.’s wedding in the Bahamas?” posted Robert Garcia, the ranking member and lead Democrat on the House oversight committee, on social media. “Umar Kremlev spent hundreds of thousands of dollars on the President’s son. What did he get in return? We need answers.”
Kremlev has a longstanding relationship with Putin. He is the head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), a sporting body that has been backed by the state-owned Russian energy company Gazprom. According to ProPublica, the wedding payments came from an IBA-affiliated entity in Dubai that the boxing association uses for financial transactions.
In the days before the wedding party, he reportedly went to China as part of a delegation accompanying Putin, and the month prior the Russian president had bestowed him with a state honor, the Order of Friendship. The Ukrainian government has imposed sanctions on Kremlev, citing his closeness to Putin and Russian security services.
Alexander Lagutin, a businessperson who has held senior roles at a Russian defense contractor and a state-backed energy company, had been with Kremlev on the China trip. Kremlev’s right hand at the IBA, Elena Sobol, attended the wedding, too.
While the event was extravagant, the guest list was intimate, with only about 50 people attending, most of whom were immediate family, close friends and business partners of the couple. Then there was Kremlev, who reportedly didn’t attend the ceremony itself, which was limited to just 18 guests, but was present with a large contingent of Russians at the party, much to the confusion of the other guests. The group reportedly sometimes stood off by themselves speaking Russian, according to ProPublica.
The affair has raised questions about the implications of a member of Putin’s circle financially supporting and gaining such intimate access to the US president’s family. In recent years Trump Jr has emerged as a leading campaign surrogate for Trump and has even been touted as a potential political heir.
Donald Sherman, the president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington (Crew), said it is in the public interest for Congress to strongly consider requiring financial disclosure statements of a president’s adult children, in addition to the president themselves.
The crux of the issue is the nature of the friendship, and whether the giving of gifts is genuine or designed to influence, Sherman said. “We know that private companies and foreign governments have been seeking to gain Don Jr’s favor in order to serve their own financial interests. And so, it’s important that there is a measure of transparency when folks tied to the Russian government are lavishing the president’s rich adult son with expensive gifts.”
He added: “Most of us learn as children that ‘there’s no such thing as a free lunch’. It’s one thing if, in the nature of this friendship, there’s a mutual exchange of lavish gifts. It’s another if someone’s daddy becomes president and then all of a sudden this new friend starts giving gifts – that context very much matters.”
In similar vein, retired FBI official Frank Montoya Jr told ProPublica: “If I’m paying for your wedding, at some point, you’re going to owe me something. This should be unthinkable for the son of the president.”
It remains unclear why Kremlev helped pay for the wedding and why he was there, when he appears to have only met Trump Jr – the executive vice-president of the Trump Organization, who has a personal net worth somewhere in the ballpark of $300m – quite recently.
Donald Trump famously didn’t attend the wedding. “He’d like me to go, but it’s going to be just a small, little private affair,” the US president told reporters a few days before the nuptials. “I said, you know, this is not good timing for me. I have a thing called Iran and other things.”
In response to detailed questions from ProPublica, a spokesperson for Trump Jr did not deny that Kremlev had helped fund the wedding. “Umar is a personal friend of Don,” the spokesperson said, adding Kremlev is “not someone he has a business relationship with” and that the men met through a mutual friend in the hunting world.
In their joint Instagram statement, Trump Jr and Bettina Trump thanked “our dear friend Umar” who “very generously hosted two incredible nights of celebrations for us AFTER our wedding”.
They said they “got married privately” on 22 May “surrounded ONLY by our family”, and said the Russian businessman had simply given them a gift.
“Friendship doesn’t require a political motive. Generosity doesn’t automatically come with an agenda. And sometimes a wedding gift is simply a wedding gift,” they said.

articles.title: Trump’s son, Donald Jr, confirms Russian businessman paid for his post-wedding festivities
articles.body:
Trump’s son, Donald Jr, confirms Russian businessman paid for his post-wedding festivities
WASHINGTON - A Russian businessman with ties to the Kremlin paid for celebrations after the wedding of US President Donald Trump’s eldest son and his new bride, the couple confirmed on Sept 14.
Donald Trump Jr and Bettina Trump said in a jointly signed post on Bettina’s Instagram account that their “dear friend” Umar Kremlev “very generously hosted two incredible nights” of festivities in the Bahamas in May.
The confirmation came after the ProPublica investigative website reported that Kremlev footed the bill for hundreds of thousands of dollars for the parties.
“It was an extraordinarily generous wedding gift from a friend, and something for which we were and remain incredibly grateful,” said the post by Bettina and Don Jr.
President Trump did not attend the wedding or the festivities, saying he had to stay in Washington during talks on the Iran war.
Kremlev is head of the International Boxing Association (IBA), with which the International Olympic Committee severed links after repeated warnings over financial governance and ethical concerns.
Putin ties
Russian President Vladimir Putin presented Kremlev with the “Order of Friendship” award in April 2026, according to an IBA press release, which featured a photo of Putin and Kremlev shaking hands.
“During the ceremony, the Russian President praised the IBA’s resilience in supporting athletes despite political pressures,” the IBA statement said.
The IBA website also featured photos of Donald Trump Jr on stage with Kremlev at an event in Istanbul in September 2025.
Bettina Trump’s Instagram post was accompanied by 20 photos including one of the newlywed couple on a beach, and others of President Trump’s other children Eric Trump, Ivanka Trump and Tiffany Trump.
“It’s unfortunate that something so personal and happy can be recast as something political or sinister simply because of who someone is or where they come from,” the post added.
ProPublica posted a group photo from the wedding that it said showed the top of Kremlev’s head.
According to Russian investigative media outlet Proekt, Kremlev is a Tajik native who worked as a mid-level boxing promoter and cultivated links with the Federal Protective Service (FSO), whose role is to protect high level officials in Russia.
Kremlev is also a member of the pro-Kremlin Night Wolves biker club, it reported.
Members of the Night Wolves rode down en masse to Ukraine’s Crimea peninsula just after it was annexed by Russia in March 2014 and members have also fought side by side with pro-Russian separatists in eastern Ukraine. AFP

articles.title: Ukrainian Drone Crew Hits Four Russian Grad Rocket Launchers in One Mission, One 45 Km Away
articles.body:
- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukrainian Drone Crew Hits Four Russian Grad Rocket Launchers in One Mission, One 45 Km Away
A Ukrainian drone crew destroyed two Russian BM-21 Grad multiple rocket launchers and damaged two more during a single deployment, with one of the strikes carried out after a 45-kilometer drone flight.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to Ukraine’s 42nd Separate Mechanized Brigade on September 14, the operation was conducted by a crew from the Perun Unmanned Systems Battalion. The crew commander, who uses the call sign “Zhulyk,” said the four Grad systems were the first targets of this type struck by the battalion.
“During this operation, our crew destroyed two Grads and hit two more. These were the first Grads in our battalion. We set every record we could: both for time spent on position and for range. We flew 45 kilometers and struck the target,” Zhulyk said.
The brigade did not disclose the exact location of the strikes or specify what type of drone was used.
The crew remained at its position for 60 days, conducting operations during both daytime and nighttime. Its personnel included an FPV pilot, an explosives specialist, a navigator, and other members responsible for supporting long-range drone missions.
Zhulyk said the crew operated continuously because each member had a separate role and there was no replacement team available.
“We have a 24/7 workload. We work at night, we work during the day. There is no rotation where one person flies while someone else sleeps—there is nothing like that. Everyone has their own job,” he said.
According to the brigade, reaching and leaving the position presented an additional challenge because Russian forces were also conducting aerial reconnaissance in search of Ukrainian drone teams. The crew reached the position in roughly half a day, while leaving it after the two-month deployment took nearly two days and required stops along the route.
The BM-21 Grad is a truck-mounted 122mm multiple launch rocket system originally developed by the Soviet Union and remains widely used by Russian forces for battlefield fire support.
Earlier, on September 11, Ukrainian forces destroyed a rare North Korean Type-75 multiple-launch rocket system deployed by Russia, according to Ukraine’s 40th Separate Artillery Brigade. The launcher, which carries 12 rocket tubes, was located and then struck directly by a Ukrainian drone.

articles.title: Zelenskyy appointed Humeniuk commander of the Medical Forces
articles.body:
Zelenskyy appointed Humeniuk commander of the Medical Forces
Kyiv • UNN
Kostiantyn Humeniuk replaced Anatolii Kazmirchuk as commander of the Medical Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. Previously, he was the chief surgeon of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy appointed the Ukrainian Armed Forces’ chief surgeon, Kostiantyn Humeniuk, as Commander of the Medical Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, replacing Anatoliy Kazmirchuk. This is stated in the relevant decrees by Zelenskyy, reports UNN.
Details
By Decree No. 909/2026, Zelenskyy dismissed Anatoliy Kazmirchuk from the position of Commander of the Medical Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, and by Decree No. 910/2026 appointed Kostiantyn Humeniuk to the position.
Deputy Head of the Office of the President Pavlo Palisa said that "the President made this decision jointly with the Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine."
"Humeniuk has well-deserved authority among the military and the trust of the volunteer community. There is a lot of work and challenging tasks ahead. The top priority in this position is preserving the life and health of the Ukrainian soldier," Palisa wrote.
What is known about Humeniuk
Kostiantyn Humeniuk is the chief surgeon of the Armed Forces of Ukraine under the Medical Forces Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, a colonel of the medical service, and a Candidate of Medical Sciences.
Since 2001, he served at the Military Medical Clinical Center of the Air Force and the Military Medical Clinical Center of the Central Region. He advanced from the position of a resident in the emergency surgery department to head of the clinic of endoscopic surgery and endoscopic diagnostics.
In May 2014, he was in the ATO zone, where he served as the senior officer of a forward medical and nursing brigade as part of the 95th Airmobile Brigade; in 2015, he was the leading surgeon of the 59th Military Mobile Hospital near Luhansk. In 2017, he was the chief surgeon of the ATO; in 2018–2019, the chief surgeon of the Joint Forces Operation. Since 2019, he has been the chief surgeon of the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
In May 2022, at a military mobile hospital in one of the frontline cities near Bakhmut, he performed Ukraine’s first modern laparoscopic kidney-removal operation for a gunshot wound involving destruction of the organ.
In November 2023, Zelenskyy appointed a new Commander of the Medical Forces of the Armed Forces of Ukraine. In particular, Anatoliy Kazmirchuk, head of the National Military Medical Clinical Center "Main Military Clinical Hospital" in Kyiv, took the position instead of Tetiana Ostashchenko.
In August, MP Mariana Bezuhla stated that Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Mykhailo Drapatyi had removed Kazmirchuk, whom she called "Syrskyi’s man"—referring to the former Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, who was dismissed from the position in July.
Bezuhla also called Kazmirchuk the "author of orders concerning ‘all fit’ personnel."
To remind you
The Ministry of Defense of Ukraine introduced a unified electronic outpatient log in the Medical Information System of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (MIS of the Armed Forces of Ukraine), which will replace 11 paper medical logs.

articles.title: The Kremlin welcomes Trump’s call for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries but won’t promise reciprocal restraint
articles.body:
The Kremlin welcomes Trump’s call for Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries but won’t promise reciprocal restraint
The Kremlin declined to say whether it would stop striking Ukraine’s economic infrastructure if Kyiv halted its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
At a September 14 briefing, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov was asked about Donald Trump’s call for the Ukrainian Armed Forces to stop striking Russian facilities that produce diesel fuel.
“Of course, we welcome any call for the Kyiv regime to stop striking civilian economic infrastructure,” he said.
Asked whether Russia was prepared to halt its strikes on Ukraine’s economic infrastructure in response, Peskov declined to answer.
The U.S. president said a day earlier that strikes on Russian oil refineries were causing diesel shortages and driving up prices. “This isn’t done by the Middle East; this is done by what’s happening with Russia and Ukraine,” he said.

articles.title: Canada Seeks 'Unique Alliance' With E.U. Amid U.S. Trade War. Here's What It Could Look Like
articles.body:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada is seeking a “unique alliance” with the European Union as he aims to strengthen international ties amid a deepening trade war with the U.S.
“What we are looking, and will begin discussions for, [is] a unique alliance with the European Union,” Carney told reporters at the Toronto International Film Festival on Sunday. “We share the same values, we have the same priorities, and we have very complementary strengths.”
Canada’s European pivot has been months in the making, following growing tensions between Carney’s government and the Trump Administration. Canada’s retaliatory tariffs came into effect last week, matching the economic pressure imposed by the U.S. after negotiations collapsed last month. Carney has encouraged Canadians to take back economic power at the kitchen table, and many have embraced a boycott of U.S. products. Trump has also repeatedly threatened Canada’s sovereignty, speaking openly of his desire to annex the country and make it the “51st state.”
The U.S. accounted for 72.5% of Canadian merchandise exports in 2025, according to the country's annual trade report, making it Canada’s largest trading partner. But Carney is keen to build an international support network that isn’t reliant on the U.S.
At the E.U.-Canada summit in June 2025, Canada established a new Security and Defense Partnership with the bloc. “Our partnership is grounded in the core values we share: democracy, human rights, the rule of law, and open, rules-based markets," read a joint statement marking the occasion.
In January, Carney notably met with China’s President Xi Jinping to forge what he referred to as a “new strategic partnership” to end Canada's economic reliance on the American market. Carney agreed to cut his country’s 100% tariff on Chinese electric cars in return for lower tariffs on Canadian farm products, including canola seeds, a major Canadian export.
Continuing with these efforts, Carney on Monday brought together executives and senior leaders from global investment firms to encourage them to invest in the country at the Canada Investment Summit in Toronto.
He’s heading for a three-day trip to Europe on Tuesday, where he’ll meet with various European leaders including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham. He’s also set to address the European Parliament in Strasbourg, France, on Thursday, in what could symbolize the mark of a new era between Canada and Europe.
Here’s a look at the alliance options on the table between Canada and the bloc, and what that could mean for U.S.-Canada relations.
Is Canada trying to join the E.U.?
Canada is not looking to join the E.U. as a member, Carney clarified amid questions over what a firmer relationship between his country and the 27-member bloc might look like.
“We’re not looking to become a member,” Carney said, emphasizing he’s instead keen to form an alliance. “We’re stronger together, and this is at a time where the world’s more dangerous and divided, and friends need to stick together in these times.”
Article 49 of the Treaty on European Union explicitly states that any “European State” can apply for membership, making Canada ineligible.
However, a report in the Wall Street Journal, quoting officials from both sides, said Carney is keen for Canada to become an “associate member” of the E.U.
When approached for comment, the European Commission directed TIME to remarks made during a Monday press briefing in Brussels.
“Canada is a strategically important partner for the European Union, and indeed a close friend,” the European Commission’s deputy chief spokesperson Olof Gill told reporters. “We deeply value this co-operation. You will recall that at our E.U.-Canada summit last year, we set a very high level of ambition for cooperation across the board, this year our ambition is even higher.”
When asked directly what discussions had taken place between Canadian and European officials, or what this “unique alliance” could look like, Gill declined to answer.
TIME has reached out to the Canadian Prime Minister’s office for comment.
Frank Schimmelfennig, a professor of European politics at ETH Zurich, predicts that Canada may wish to pursue deeper cooperation through additional trade agreements, or take inspiration from countries that have close relationships with the bloc without being E.U. members.
“Canada is already one of the most integrated non-European countries. It has the densest network of institutional relationships with the E.U.,” he tells TIME, referencing the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), a major free-trade deal between the E.U. and Canada, signed in 2016, and Horizon Europe, an initiative on collaborative research launched by the European Union in 2021 and joined by Canada in 2024.
“Canada could have more of the same, which means additional sectoral agreements for sectors that haven't been covered yet,” he says. “That would basically be a lateral extension of the current relationship. Anything more, would mean access to the internal market which would require an arrangement like the EEA.”
The European Economic Area (EEA) includes countries such as Iceland and Norway, which are not members of the E.U., and provides for the free movement of goods, services, and people within the E.U.’s member states, while enabling cooperation across multiple industries.
“The EEA countries have access to the E.U. internal market in return for adopting the relevant E.U. regulations and directives, so that would be a much denser legal integration than what Canada has now,” says Schimmelfennig.
Burgeoning E.U. relationship comes amid deepening U.S.-Canada trade rift
At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Carney declared a "rupture" in the international rules-based order. He said "great powers" were using tariffs and financial systems as instruments of coercion. He did not directly name Trump or the U.S.
The speech came at a moment of acute transatlantic tension over Trump’s push to annex the semi-autonomous Danish territory of Greenland and his short-lived threats to tariff European allies until Denmark relented.
Patrick Leblond, an associate professor at the University of Ottawa, says Carney’s movements now are in response to the world “seeing a United States that is becoming more protectionist, nationalist, and willing to use its leverage points to gain concessions, including on very close allies like Canada and Europeans.”
“For Canada, [the consensus is] we need to do more with partners who share our values based on liberal democracy, open markets, rule of law, international agreements, and the first port of call for Carney is the European Union,” Leblond tells TIME.
These trade efforts, he continues, may allow Carney to “build momentum, and hopefully bring other countries” into a broader coalition of what the Canadian leader has often called “middle powers."
In July, Carney, in a joint op-ed with Finland’s President Alexander Stubb, urged the “middle powers of the world” to “unite.”
Championing middle power countries that possess significant economic power and diplomatic influence, but lack market or military power, the leaders implored: “In a rapidly changing world, we have the grit and the sisu to chart the path ahead—and we know that so have many others whom we invite to join us on this quest.”
Leblod explains that “ultimately trust has been eroded” with the U.S. and Canada must re-think its place in the wider global economy in the long-term.
“The first time we thought Trump was a blimp, but he's not, and we're looking at what's happening in terms of democracy and political polarization, and a lot of Canadians think we can't rely on the U.S.,” he says.
According to a poll by Nanos Research, conducted between Aug. 30 and Sept. 2, 74% of Canadians disagreed that “the U.S. is a trustworthy ally of Canada.” An earlier poll by Angus Reid Institute, conducted between July 10-14, found that 42% of respondents said they think the Canadian government should approach the U.S. as an enemy/potential threat.
The E.U. has also clashed with Trump over tariffs, his Greenland annexation threats, and the wider split between the U.S. President and several European leaders.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in February warned of “a deep rift” between Europe and the United States, arguing that the latter “will not be powerful enough to go it alone.” But relations have since soured further amid the fallout of the Iran war, particularly between Merz and Trump.
Meanwhile, Canada has also embraced Europe in the cultural space. It was announced earlier this year that Canada will join the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027, becoming the first new participant since Australia in 2015.
Carney to address European Parliament
Carney’s highly-anticipated speech at the European Parliament in Strasbourg this week stems from an invitation extended by European Parliament president Roberta Metsola.
Leblond predicts Carney will use the speech “to reiterate a lot of the things he mentioned at Davos,” but with a strong, intentional focus on the E.U.
“I would expect that he will use that address to call on the E.U. to work with Canada to push this idea of co-operation beyond the North Atlantic and include partners and allies in the Indo-Pacific,” he says.
The Canadian leader is also expected to be a guest at the State of the European Union debate, where European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen is due to deliver a speech outlining the Commission's work and plans for the future.
Von der Leyen called E.U.–Canada ties “one of the closest partnerships in the world” when she celebrated 50 years of E.U. diplomatic presence in Canada in May. She declared the two sides were “closer than ever” as they confronted wars, an energy crisis and “new fractures in old alliances.”
Schimmelfennig says Canada inching closer to the E.U. is a strong display of “how both partners are affected by the deteriorating transatlantic relationship” with the U.S. “They feel that they need to move together because the world is getting more dangerous, and more difficult for both [parties],” he says.

articles.title: Zelenskyy: Ukraine ready to refrain from hitting Russia critical infrastructure if partners ensure cessation of Russia strikes on Ukraine
articles.body:
Ukraine has offered partner countries to ensure an agreement with Russia that will halt the destruction of critical infrastructure, President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said.
"If partners are ready to ensure Russia's real willingness not to hit our electricity, our other energy facilities, critical infrastructure, and food transit, then we are, of course, ready to ensure the corresponding absence of our strikes. For this to be reliable, long-term, and have a real effect on people's lives, rather than collapsing after Russians hold their 'elections' and receive a temporary easing of tension regarding gasoline and diesel precisely for that period," Zelenskyy said on Telegram on Monday.
He stressed that "Ukraine is not sure that Russia has the desire to comply with any agreement."
"Food, energy, and other elements of basic life guarantees must be protected, and Russian strikes are primarily directed against this. Every day, targets include Ukrainian energy facilities, port infrastructure, logistics, and even food and pharmaceutical warehouses," the president indicated.
At the same time, the head of the Ukrainian state noted that "the war must be ended, and a de-escalation step regarding critical infrastructure can be the first step toward peace."
"We expect specifics from partners," Zelenskyy summarized.
Earlier on Monday, US President Donald Trump announced a mutual agreement between Ukraine and Russia to refrain from strikes on energy sector facilities, and also linked the rise in global diesel fuel prices primarily to the war between the two countries. "Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!" he wrote on his social network Truth Social.
He also stated that the rise in global diesel fuel prices is driven primarily by the war between Russia and Ukraine, rather than Iran.

articles.title: New special envoy for Britons detained overseas warns of limits of role
articles.body:
The special envoy for British citizens detained overseas has spoken about the difficulties he faces in his new role, as families express concern over the position’s mandate in complex consular cases.
In his first public engagement, Alistair Burt, the former Conservative Middle East minister, spoke candidly about the difficulties and limitations of the new appointment, made following years of mounting criticism of how the Foreign Office handled the cases of British citizens detained overseas.
“I don’t make policy. I’m not a minister. I don’t have that authority. It will ultimately be the foreign secretary and the prime minister who will need to make the changes in policy or changes in approach if required,” Burt told an audience in Westminster, following his appointment on Monday evening.
“The best thing I can do is not disguise from you the difficulties of the role,” added the former minister.
Burt, who plans to meet the new foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, later this week, was tipped for the post more than a year ago. Burt was candid about the complexities of detention cases and of his role to “kick the tyres” of the policies involved.
Burt, whose new role is appointed by the Foreign Office but not paid for by it, said he has already started to meet families of those with complex cases, and said there was “much to be gained” from stronger international condemnation.
There is a strong view that the US special presidential envoy for hostages has secured more success and clout inside the diplomatic system, and used more innovative techniques to negotiate the release of Americans.
Burt said he plans to meet his US and Canadian counterparts in the coming weeks, and is open to discussing broader cooperation with European leaders.
The Foreign Office describes the purpose of the role as being to advance the government’s commitment to British nationals in the “most difficult and complex detention cases overseas” at the direction of the foreign secretary. The role is intended to advocate within and represent government, and engage with families.
Speaking alongside Burt at Monday’s parliamentary event was Nazanin Zaghari-Ratcliffe, a dual national who was arbitrarily detained in Iran for six years before being released in 2022.
A documentary was played showing the ordeal her family went through to secure her release, as well as that of Anoosheh Ashoori, for whom a historic £400m debt was paid to Iran.
“I recognised the payment of the debt and I let my foreign secretary know repeatedly,” said Burt of Nazanin’s case, adding, “I got that one right.” That wasn’t the case, he admitted, for Matthew Hedges, a British academic sitting beside him, who was accused of spying for the UK government in the United Arab Emirates and was arrested and tortured.
“Other cases I didn’t handle as well as I would have liked,” said Burt. “I’m very grateful that Matthew has seen me since to talk about his experiences.”
While welcoming the appointment, Zaghari-Ratcliffe also expressed a fear of quiet diplomacy turning into an “excuse” for government inaction.
Lawyers and campaigners at the event also expressed concerns over the limited mandate of the special envoy role, and called for the position to be independent of the Foreign Office and for the UK to be bolder in its diplomacy.
In attendance was also Laila Soueif, who went on hunger strike in pursuit of freedom for her son, British-Egyptian activist Alaa Abd el-Fattah, who was released from an Egyptian jail in 2025 after serving six years, as well as Naomi Connell, a friend of Lindsay Foreman and Craig Foreman, who has campaigned for the couple’s release from Iran’s Evin prison.
Also present was Heather Cornelius, whose husband, Ryan, has been arbitrarily imprisoned in Dubai for more than 18 years. The family discussed their case with Burt when he was a minister in 2018, said Heather, expressing scepticism over whether the envoy role, which runs for 18 months, will do anything other than liaise with and reassure families.
“He’s not going in there saying: ‘Yes, I know I can make a difference, I know I can help these people.’ He’s not saying that. He’s just saying: ‘Well, it’s very difficult,’” said Cornelius, who delivered a letter to Andy Burnham earlier on Monday, asking for the prime minister to help secure her husband’s release.
“They’re relying on other countries being involved, and of course that’s good, but Britain can do something, and they can do more,” she added.

articles.title: EU Extends Russia Sanctions for 7 Days Amid Dispute Over Delistings
articles.body:
EU member states have extended sanctions tied to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine for another seven days, following Friday’s failure to reach an agreement amid calls to delist Russian-Uzbek oligarch Alisher Usmanov and Mikhail Fridman, co-founder of Russia’s Alfa Bank.
The EU’s Committee of Permanent Representatives (Coreper) approved the temporary extension at a meeting on Monday, Sept. 14, just one day before the sanctions were set to expire on Tuesday, Sept. 15.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Coreper agreed to extend the regime for 7 days – until midnight Tuesday, Sept. 22,” a spokesperson for the Irish presidency told Ukrinform. “Currently, legal procedures are being completed to enter into force on this decision.”
“The consultations will continue, and in the near future this issue will be submitted for consideration again,” the spokesperson noted.
Dispute over delistings
The latest decision gives EU ambassadors additional time to assess proposals for renewing the restrictions, and it comes after a second failure by the EU ambassadors to agree on renewing the Western sanctions.
On Friday, France joined Slovakia in seeking the removal of Umanov from the sanctions list, according to four EU diplomats cited by Euronews.
“Slovakia still wants Usmanov and Fridman delisted, but the issue is now further complicated as France also wants Usmanov off the blacklist,” Rikard Jozwiak, Radio Liberty’s editor, said separately in a statement on X.
Anthropic Disrupted Russian Attempt to Develop Autonomous Drone Swarms
While Usmanov built his wealth through investments in technology, metals and mining, Fridman – an Israeli-Russian businessman born in Ukraine – built one of Russia’s largest private business groups.
Both have been linked to Russian President Vladimir Putin and the military-industrial system supporting Moscow’s war against Ukraine.
Currently, the sanctions list covers more than 3,000 individuals and entities connected to Russia’s regime, and is expected to grow, particularly due to renewed frustrations over Russia’s escalating hybrid threats, including drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport and repeated drone incursions in NATO airspace.
The restrictions are renewed every six months, although EU members have discussed moving to a 12-month cycle after extending sectoral sanctions for a year in July.
“Continuing sanctions lists is vital in order to undermine the capabilities of Russia’s military vehicle and put pressure on those who support, ensure or benefit from this aggression,” the Irish Presidency said according to Ukrinform.
“This remains an absolute priority for our presidency,” it concluded.

articles.title: Leaders urge EU to expand Arctic presence amid Russia 'threat'
articles.body:
Leaders urge EU to expand Arctic presence amid Russia 'threat'
Twelve European countries on Monday called for the European Union to step up its presence in the Arctic, as melting ice opens new maritime routes while growing tensions with Russia and the United States increasingly put the region in the geopolitical spotlight.
Twelve European countries meeting in Finland on Monday urged the European Union (EU) to beef up its presence in the Arctic – a contentious geopolitical battleground caught between Russia and US President Donald Trump.
"We call for the European Union to take on a more strategic and proactive role in the European Arctic," the countries' leaders wrote in a joint statement following a European Arctic Summit in the town of Rovaniemi in Finnish Lapland, attended by Denmark, France, Germany, Greece and Sweden, among others.
The EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, said the bloc was in need of icebreakers, but it was not immediately clear if she was proposing joint acquisition or urging member states to bolster their own capacities.
Given "the situation that we are in, and considering climate change and the opening of maritime routes, we need icebreakers or ships that are able to navigate in these very difficult" conditions, Kallas told reporters.

In January, EU chief Ursula von der Leyen suggested the EU could direct part of its ongoing surge in defence spending on a "European icebreaker capability," which is traditionally considered a civilian capability, among other equipment vital to Arctic security.
Interest in the Arctic has grown substantially since the adoption in 2021 of the EU's latest policy strategy for the region.
Read moreEU to boost Greenland investment amid Trump annexation claims
Trump's repeated threats to bring Greenland – a vast, autonomous Danish territory – under US control have since then triggered a diplomatic crisis among Washington's allies.
While his tone has cooled since the beginning of the year, EU countries are determined to increase their presence in the region – well aware of a hostile neighbour on the other side of Finland's long eastern border.
Mounting tensions
Pointing to "the significant and long-term threat Russia poses", countries said Moscow's ambitions to increase its influence in the Arctic and its "hostility towards Europe, including the increase in hybrid activities, highlight the need to strengthen the EU's Arctic policy".
Officials present included Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, EU foreign policy chief Kallas and EU Council President Antonio Costa, as well as leaders from countries such as Romania and Greece.
"What happens here is not a regional story. It is a European one," Costa said.
No formal decisions were taken at the summit.
But the European Commission is expected to present a new Arctic strategy in a matter of weeks, which will steer the union's approach to the Arctic over the coming years.
Read moreTensions in the Arctic: Greenland issues sharp rebuke to Trump-linked oil compan
Countries and leaders can still have a say on the final document, "so in that sense this is quite a timely meeting," Tuomas Tikkanen, senior adviser on European Affairs to Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, who initiated the summit, told AFP.
"The idea is essentially to strengthen the EU's common strategic approach to the Arctic in this situation, where the geopolitical and economic significance of the region is growing considerably," he said.
Melting ice
Interest in the region has increased significantly since the EU's last Arctic policy was adopted in 2021, reflected in the number of high-level guests from non-Arctic countries in attendance.
"The security environment has changed a great deal, and there has been a lot of interest in the region recently," Tikkanen said.
Leaders discussed topics ranging from economic interests to security.
The Arctic region is warming nearly four times faster than the global average as a result of climate change, according to experts, leading to severe consequences for both the environment and local livelihoods.

As sea ice melts, countries such as Russia, China and the United States have been ramping up activity in the region, racing to claim natural resources and new maritime routes.
China and South Korea sent container ships to attempt to transit the Northern Sea Route in Russian waters in August, testing its viability as the passage remains free of ice longer each year.
Trump insisted earlier this year that Washington needed to control Greenland for national security reasons, though he ultimately ruled out annexing it by force.
Soon after, in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.
During a visit to the vast island on September 7, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced a 200-million-euro ($232-million) package for Greenland, vowing to "be more present and to be more engaged in Greenland and in the Arctic".

articles.title: Italy could resume Russian gas imports after Ukraine conflict ends — Deputy PM
articles.body:
MILAN, September 14. /TASS/. Italian Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Transport and Infrastructure Matteo Salvini believes that returning to Russian gas purchases will be possible once the conflict in Ukraine is over.
"It will be possible to resume purchasing Russian gas after the conflict ends. We need to find a diplomatic solution – not by sending weapons, but by supporting the negotiation process," Salvini said in an interview with TASS and Vesti.
The politician, who leads the League party within the ruling coalition, noted that geopolitical crises in Ukraine and the Middle East, along with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, have pushed European fuel prices excessively high. He stated that the Italian government has already spent €3 billion to mitigate the price surge by cutting excise taxes. Salvini also pointed out that Italy currently lacks nuclear power, while the government is attempting to reverse the country's nuclear phase-out, the process will take time.

articles.title: Ukraine wants specifics from partners on halting strikes, Zelenskiy says
articles.body:
Ukraine will support energy ceasefire if US ensures Moscow's intent, Zelenskiy says
KYIV, Sept 14 - President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said on Monday that Kyiv was ready to support a U.S. proposal for a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire on energy sites only if Washington could ensure Moscow was genuinely ready to end its war on Ukraine.
Zelenskiy made his comments in his nightly video address after U.S. President Donald Trump said that Ukraine and Russia had both agreed not to hit each other's energy targets.
"If this can become the first de-escalatory step, a step towards ending Russian strikes against our critical infrastructure and our strikes in response, Ukraine is ready to support de-escalation," Zelenskiy said.
"So far, no one has seen any genuine willingness on Russia's part to bring the war to an end. But if our American partners can secure Russia's genuine readiness to end the war aimed at destroying lives, and to do so honestly and on a long-term basis, Ukraine will take its own de-escalatory steps."
In its 4-1/2-year-long war, Russia has often struck Ukrainian energy sites, a campaign that has caused major damage to heating and power networks and severely disrupted both industry and the daily lives of civilians.
Ukraine's military has for months launched its own attacks on Russian industrial sites, particularly Russia's oil industry, a mainstay of the national economy. Those attacks caused serious shortages of petrol in many Russian regions.
Zelenskiy posted comments earlier on social media that amounted to a denial that Ukraine had formally endorsed Trump's statement that both sides had agreed to halt attacks.
The Ukrainian president said Ukraine was not convinced that Russia was willing to abide by any agreement.
Any accord had to be "reliable, long-term, and actually have a real impact on people's lives", he said.
In his statement, Trump said the two sides had agreed not to hit each other's energy targets.
"Ukraine has agreed not to hit Russian Energy targets. Russia has agreed to do, likewise!" he wrote on social media. REUTERS

articles.title: The U.S. sanctioned Russia’s VTB Bank over its work with Iran. A former Treasury official says the move is also meant to pressure Chinese banks.
articles.body:
The U.S. sanctioned Russia’s VTB Bank over its work with Iran. A former Treasury official says the move is also meant to pressure Chinese banks.
The U.S. Treasury Department has sanctioned Russia’s VTB Bank for taking part in efforts to evade sanctions on Iran.
A Treasury Department press release says VTB opened representative offices in Iran, processed transactions with sanctioned Iranian banks, and helped “move billions of frozen Iranian assets.”
Miad Maleki, an analyst and former official in the U.S. Treasury unit that oversees sanctions, said the measures against VTB should be seen as part of U.S. pressure on China, where a significant share of Iran’s oil revenue is held.
According to Maleki, VTB is the only Russian bank with a branch in mainland China and access to the country’s domestic payment system. Chinese banks continued doing business with VTB even though it has long been under U.S. sanctions related to Russia. But being placed on the Iran sanctions list is far more “toxic.” Maleki believes the Treasury Department expects Chinese banks to begin cutting ties with VTB for fear of secondary sanctions under the Iran sanctions program.
VTB, Russia’s second-largest bank, is state-controlled. The United States first imposed restrictions on VTB in 2014 over Russia’s annexation of Crimea. In 2022, after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the United States placed the bank under blocking sanctions.

articles.title: After the SDF: What comes next for Syria's Kurds?
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
After the SDF: What comes next for Syria's Kurds?
Damascus, Syria - The Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) were dissolved by their commander-in-chief, Mazloum Abdi, on 25 August, bringing an end to Rojava, a 14-year-old experiment in autonomous self-administration in northeast Syria.
Abdi is to take up a new role as a special adviser to President Ahmed al-Sharaa, whilst the senior leadership will occupy various positions within the government.
Sipan Hamo, the former head of the YPG - the primary fighting force of the SDF - had already taken up a position as Deputy Defence Minister for the Eastern Region. Ilham Ahmed, the head of the SDF’s civilian administration, is reported to have been offered a position in parliament.
The dissolution comes seven months after a surprise government offensive in January against the SDF, which saw the armed group lose large swathes of its northeastern territory and be forced into an integration agreement.
Since then, the integration has been advancing on the ground, with this latest development being “largely symbolic” according to Alexander McKeever, a researcher and author of the This Week in Northern Syria newsletter.
“Although the SDF is technically dissolved, on the ground its military and civilian structures continue to operate,” he explained to The New Arab.
“They work in parallel to the government structures that are increasingly visible as integration continues.”
The future for female Kurdish fighters
As part of the dissolution, Mazloum Abdi announced that the SDF’s military had been entirely integrated into the Ministry of Defence.
However, there was one major oversight. Seated next to Abdi during his meeting with al-Sharaa was Nowruz Ahmed, the commander of the YPJ - the SDF’s all-female fighting force.
The YPJ were prohibited from joining the Ministry of Defence because the “government simply has a perspective that women don’t belong in the military,” says McKeever.
Following the announcement, the YPJ released a statement about a meeting with the Ministry of Interior saying, “it was emphasised that the YPJ could be integrated, as a distinct organised force, into the Ministry of Interior”.
There had been previous reports that the YPJ had been offered a role as a counter-terror unit within the Ministry of Defence, but this was denied by Ruksan Mohammed, the YPJ spokesperson, a week before the announcement.
She acknowledged that previously they had been offered to integrate into the Interior Ministry as administrative staff, which they rejected outright.
“It should not have reached a point where the dissolution was announced before a solution to the YPJ issue was found,” Muaz Al-Abdullah, a Middle East Research Manager at ACLED, a conflict tracking organisation, told The New Arab.
“It reflects the balance of power between the two sides, where Damascus is largely able to dictate terms in negotiations.”
However, this strategy presents a danger, he adds, “it will ultimately give a group of trained fighters the reasoning to go against the government either as a group or as lone wolves”.
What role for the Kurdish language?
Another bone of contention surrounds the future role of the Kurdish language within the northeast’s education system.
Many Kurds fear a return to the situation under the Assad regime, before the ‘Rojava Revolution’ in 2012, in which “the state did not recognise Kurdish identity as a legitimate part of Syrian identity. Kurdish language instruction and Kurdish cultural expression were banned,” explains McKeever.
As a result, al-Sharaa has sought to assuage Kurdish fears. In January, following the offensive against the SDF, he announced the recognition of Kurdish as a ‘national language’.
However, McKeever notes that this does not make Kurdish an ‘official’ language of Syria. Syria doesn’t currently have a full constitution, with the law either operating on old Assad-era mandates or 2025’s constitutional declaration.
“Full recognition of Kurdish as an official language may come with the drafting of the constitution but, for now, we cannot know,” he says.
As part of the integration agreement between the SDF and the government, Damascus has stipulated a one-year transition period in which Kurdish language classes are offered for three hours per week, alongside one hour for an elective class on a number of topics like women's history, sociology, or philosophy.
The system for the years after has yet to be decided upon. However, for the last 14 years, Kurdish has been the medium of education and so the disagreement between the SDF and Damascus “comes down to whether there will be a fully translated curriculum”.
Effect on the Turkish peace process
The dissolution of the SDF would have been considerably harder to achieve without the parallel peace process between Turkey and the PKK.
In October 2024, Ankara announced that it was commencing negotiations with the PKK, a Kurdish armed group that has fought a decades-long insurgency against the government.
In May 2025, following a call by its leader Abdullah Ocalan, the PKK announced that it would destroy its weapons and dissolve.
Turkey considered the SDF as the Syrian branch of the PKK, and so “Turkey is the biggest winner in this whole situation,” Al-Abdullah tells The New Arab.
“The whole Kurdish situation is shifting regionally with Kurdish non-state actors increasingly having to engage with their relative states,” he adds.
“The dissolution of the SDF will only add onus on the PKK to reach a settlement with the Turks.”
However, it is regarding language rights that Turkey’s Kurds might have the most to gain from the SDF integration agreement.
“Turkey completely banned the Kurdish language, and has struggled with the Kurdish file for decades, partly as a result,” Henri Barkey, an Adjunct Senior Fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, told The New Arab.
“Whilst the deal that was signed in Syria is bad on language rights, it is far better than what Turkish Kurds have, and so they might look to Syria as a model for their own aims in negotiations.”
Managing Kurdish fears
The Syrian government is seeking to simultaneously entrench its control over the northeast whilst allaying Kurdish fears and distrust of the government.
According to analysts, many Kurds are sceptical of the government's Islamist roots, and its history of violence against minority groups, including a series of massacres targeting Alawite and Druze minorities.
For Barkey, “Sharaa can’t afford to alienate the Kurds as they have over a decade of experience organising and fighting”.
Equally, many in the local Arab communities distrust the SDF and its leadership, due to the perception that, despite the SDF’s official support for ethnic pluralism, it developed a system that centralised power in the hands of Kurdish communities at the expense of local Arabs.
The “greatest challenge” lies in knitting together a social fabric between “communities that have often lived separately for the last decade, with displaced Kurds now returning to areas with large Arab populations and displaced Arabs doing the same in reverse,” says Mckeever.
In August, a convoy of displaced Kurds, who were returning to Ras Al-Ain, were attacked by local Arabs, which triggered a day of riots by Kurds against the government in Hasakah and Qamishli.
A day later, an attack by unknown elements on a security point manned by former SDF fighters who had been recently integrated into the Ministry of Defence killed three and injured several.
“This is the same pattern that you see across Syria along these social fault lines, where you have old grievances and a lack of security,” Mckeever adds.
Whereas for ACLED’s Al-Abdullah, the primary risk is that integration “will remain political, and that Kurds won't actually be brought into the national community and so will continue to identify as Kurdish more so than Syrian”.
The government has offered senior SDF leadership positions, likely so they can play the role of “intermediary between the state and the Kurdish communities within which they still have a lot of support”.
What next?
Whilst integration is far from finished, the dissolution of the SDF has “expedited certain things on the ground,” explains Mckeever.
The government’s internal security forces, previously only deployed within the grounds of a few government compounds, have reportedly deployed to a number of Arab neighbourhoods in Hasakah city.
Equally, certain SDF internal security units have begun the integration process and will likely begin patrols under the Syrian flag.
For al-Sharaa, with integration and the Kurdish file moving from a major political issue to one more technical and bureaucratic, he can likely turn his attention to the last holdout beyond the control of the state - Suweida.
The dissolution of the SDF represents the death knell for a vision for Syria, advocated by Israel and the Druze militias in Suweida, of fragmentation.
“With the government empowered domestically and backed internationally by the US and Turkey, it will be looking towards resolving the Suweida situation,” Al-Abdullah says.
“Israel is using Suweida as a card, and will likely abandon it when its interests require,” says Al-Abdullah.
“The Syrian government now needs to be working on winning back the people of Suweida, who felt so betrayed by the government's actions against them.”
Cian Ward is a journalist based in Damascus, covering conflict, migration, and humanitarian issues
Follow him on X: @CP__Ward
Edited by Charlie Hoyle

articles.title: Occupied Donetsk Miners Threaten Strike Action Ahead of Russian Elections
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Occupied Donetsk Miners Threaten Strike Action Ahead of Russian Elections
Coal miners in temporarily occupied regions of Donetsk and Luhansk are organizing a coordinated work stoppage to coincide with Russia’s State Duma elections, protesting salary delays ranging between four and seven months, according to ASTRA on September 14.
The action, planned by the Independent Union of Miners starting September 18, involves workers submitting simultaneous formal notices of work refusal across multiple facilities.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over ten mines in the region remain operational primarily to pump underground water, a critical function required to prevent catastrophic environmental damage and flooding.
Local authorities repeatedly failed to meet promised payout deadlines. Initial promises to clear backlogs prior to Miner’s Day and later by September 10 passed without payment, pushing expected disbursements to early next year.
Thousands of families have been forced into debt to survive. Labor representatives noted that one mine’s workforce has formally committed to stopping work, with organizing efforts active at two additional sites. Specific facility names are being withheld to prevent preemptive suppression and intimidation by local officials.
Testimonies from inside the temporarily occupied territories detail widespread financial distress. At the Chaikyno mine, operated by Uglekom LLC, management has continuously delayed payments since March and refused to provide workers with official debt certificates needed for legal appeals.
Similar wage disruptions and mass layoffs hit Luhansk region mines in April following owner bankruptcies. Wage defaults have also surfaced within Russia itself, where over 1,700 employees at the Severny Kuzbass company in the Kemerovo region have gone unpaid since October 2025.
Russian authorities were preparing to conduct geological exploration and begin extracting raw materials from at least 18 deposits in temporarily occupied areas of Ukraine.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed this on May 6, referencing a report delivered by the head of Ukraine’s military intelligence, Oleh Ivashchenko.
Zelenskyy stated that Russian forces planned to carry out geological surveys before extracting and removing valuable resources—including titanium, lithium, tantalum, niobium, zirconium, molybdenum, and graphite—from multiple sites across southern Ukrainian lands.

articles.title: World Bank to Send Ukraine $841 Million Under Canadian Guarantee
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Finance Ministry and Prime Minister Serhii Koretskiy said the country will soon receive $841 million in financing from the World Bank, guaranteed by the Canadian government, with the funds earmarked to reimburse the state budget for pension payments.
The financing follows a meeting between Finance Minister Serhiy Marchenko and World Bank Vice President for Europe and Central Asia Antonella Bassani, also attended by Deputy Finance Minister Olha Zykova, who manages international aid projects.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The two sides discussed mobilizing financing for Ukraine through the end of 2026, the continued rollout of the PEACE in Ukraine project, financing under the World Bank’s SPUR 2.0 instrument, and preparations for new joint projects, the ministry wrote in its press release.
Marchenko and Robert Saum, the World Bank’s regional director for Eastern Europe, signed a loan agreement under the Tenth Additional Financing of the “Public Expenditures for Administrative Capacity Endurance in Ukraine” project, known as PEACE in Ukraine. Once the agreement is signed, the project’s total volume will reach $54.3 billion, making it the largest investment project in the World Bank’s history, according to the ministry.
The press release quoted Serhiy Marchenko, Ukraine’s finance minister, as saying: “PEACE remains one of the most effective instruments for supporting Ukraine’s state budget. Thanks to the new financing under Canada’s guarantee, we will be aGle to ensure funding for critically important social expenditure. I am grateful to the government of Canada and the World Bank for their consistent and timely support of Ukraine.”
Ukraine Must Attack Russia’s Missile Plants to Win War, MITS Capital CEO Says
Marchenko also welcomed the approval of the World Bank’s new SPUR 2.0 instrument and called on the institution to help attract more active contributions from international partners. SPUR 2.0 – the Special Program for Ukraine Recovery – is a World Bank initiative aimed at mobilizing resources for Ukraine’s priority recovery needs. The program operates on a multiplier basis: every $1 in grant funding attracted is converted into $3 in loans, a mechanism that could ultimately accumulate up to $6 billion in financial support, according to the ministry.
Ukraine has already appealed to 27 partner countries to join SPUR 2.0, and four have confirmed they will contribute, the ministry wrote.
Ukraine and the World Bank are also preparing six new joint projects – in energy efficiency, housing policy, waste management, agricultural sector support, statistics and digitalization. Marchenko said he hopes preparatory procedures will be completed quickly enough to launch the projects before the end of 2026, the ministry wrote.

articles.title: Air Force Plans Hundreds of Autonomous Fighter and ISR Drones by 2032
articles.body:
NATIONAL HARBOR, Md.—The Air Force plans to field at least 500 semi-autonomous fighter drones known as Collaborative Combat Aircraft by 2032, and another 500 cheap reconnaissance and strike drones known as Massed Modular Aircraft that same year, Air Force Secretary Troy Meink said Sept. 14.
In his keynote address to open AFA’s Air, Space & Cyber conference, Meink said the service would bolster its combat capability—which for decades has mostly come from crewed aircraft such as fighters and bombers—with lower-cost drones that operate with minimal direction from Airmen.
And that future is coming fast, Meink said.
“Because of the steps we are taking today, we will have a significantly different force by 2032,” Meink said. “By then, our special operators will have the ability to employ thousands of autonomous one-way attack systems, and we will have autonomous fighters like Collaborative Combat Aircraft, or CCAs.”
The first iteration of CCAs—General Atomics Aeronautical Systems’ FQ-42A and Anduril Industries’ FQ-44A—are now rolling off the assembly line and will specialize in air-to-air missions. Future “increments” of CCA could focus on other missions, such as air-to-ground strikes, reconnaissance, or electronic warfare operations.
“We intend to have at least 500 of these in service by 2032,” Meink said, and by that time the drones will be performing many of the same missions crewed fighters perform today, he added.
Meink’s projection is the most ambitious target the Air Force has yet to announce for the CCA program. In 2024, his predecessor as Secretary, Frank Kendall, said the service would have 100 CCAs by 2029. Earlier this year, Meink said he expected to have 150 by the end of the decade.
The Air Force is also accelerating a program called Massed Modular Aircraft, which will field drones to take on some of the missions the MQ-9A Reaper performs today. The service in recent months has grown concerned over the pace of Reaper losses in operations against Iran—roughly 45 have been lost so far, or about a quarter of the Air Force’s fleet—and moved to speed up its plans to field MMAs.
Like CCAs, MMA drones will have autonomous capabilities, but they will be cheaper and less complex than CCAs. Air Force officials told reporters Sept. 3 that the air vehicle of an MMAs will cost roughly $10 million, without sensors or other systems included, while CCAs will cost twice as much, at $20 million per air vehicle.
Meink said the Air Force plans to field 100 MMA drones by 2029 and 500 by 2032—higher than previous estimates from Air Force officials.
In a roundtable with reporters later, Meink also said the the Air Force plans to have multiple types of MMA drones from different contractors in its fleet, similar to how its CCA program is working with multiple vendors.
Asked about the expanded plans for the MMA program, Meink pointed to the program’s relatively low cost and the importance of the MQ-9’s combined strike and recon mission.
“That [ISR and strike] mission is a very important mission,” Meink said. “We’re looking at how we do that with a mix of different platforms. … The ability to bring low-cost mass is a driver here, and we expect these to be significantly cheaper than even the MQ-9s or the CCA.”
When asked if the Air Force could buy more than 500 MMA drones, Meink said that will depend on how much money Congress provides in the budget, but added “I think it should probably be much higher than that.”
When the two autonomous drones—MMA and CCA—are in the field, Meink said, they will transform the way the Air Force fights wars.
The sixth-generation F-47 fighter and B-21 Raider stealth bomber are “phenomenal aircraft” that “will be able to do things no other aircraft has ever done before,” Meink said. But they won’t be able to deliver the “massive scale of combat power we need” on their own, he warned. That’s where lower-cost, uncrewed autonomous platforms like CCA and MMA come in.
“When we pair manned aircraft with lower-cost autonomous systems, we will be able to unlock combat power at scale,” Meink said.
Both CCAs and MMAs are being built around an open systems architecture approach that will make it easier to swap different sensors or other capabilities into the drones, using standardized interfaces. Emphasizing the modularity that comes with open systems architecture will accelerate procurement of the systems, Meink said, and increase competition from industry, which will ultimately lower prices, give the Air Force more choices, and improve the drones’ combat power.
Meink told reporters in the roundtable that CCAs will continually evolve, even within the same increment, but that it was too soon to predict what the fleet of 500 will look like by 2032.
“It depends on how the current ones perform, and what additional capabilities the users are saying they need,” Meink said. “Can we evolve that into the current iteration? Do we need a different iteration? We’re working our way through that right now.”
Meink also said the Air Force plans to have “tens of thousands” of the new low-cost Family of Affordable Mass Munition, or FAMM, weapons in its inventory by 2030, and that they are already being used today.
Meink also revealed a name change for General Atomics’ CCA, which the company had been calling Dark Merlin. The FQ-42 will now be called Vengeance, he said. Anduril’s FQ-44 will continue with the name Fury.
General Atomics spokesman C. Mark Brinkley said in a text to Air & Space Forces Magazine that the company will cease using the Dark Merlin name now that the Air Force has chosen its own moniker.
“We love when our customers name their aircraft,” Brinkley said. “Vengeance pretty much sums up what the FQ-42 brings to the fight.”

articles.title: Under Cloud of Scandal, Outgoing Ukrainian Prosecutor General Targets Anti-Corruption Chief
articles.body:
Reported by
Ukraine’s outgoing prosecutor general signed a notice of suspicion Monday targeting the chief of the national anti-corruption agency, accusing him of forging documents for massive financial gain and orchestrating a sham adoption to evade prosecution.
The Prosecutor General, Ruslan Kravchenko, announced in a video statement posted on Telegram that he had formally signed charges against Semen Kryvonos, director of the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU). The move ignited a high-stakes feud among top law enforcement bodies just as Kravchenko left office under a cloud of scandal. Local meda reported that he has left Ukraine.
Kravchenko also broadened his offensive to target a close associate of Oleksandr Klymenko, head of the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO). Without naming the individual, Kravchenko alleged they had attempted to bribe and influence the chief judge of the High Anti-Corruption Court while assisting someone in evading military mobilization.
The accusations triggered an immediate and scathing rebuke from both NABU and SAPO, which dismissed Kravchenko’s claims as a "systematic attack" designed to undermine independent watchdogs. In a joint response, the agencies stated that Kryvonos had not been formally served with any legal documents as of Monday morning, characterizing Kravchenko's video post as public posturing rather than legitimate procedural action.
The public clash comes at a precarious moment for Kravchenko. He submitted his resignation last week after investigators searched his office as part of "Operation Carthage," a wide-ranging probe into a criminal syndicate accused of laundering illicit funds and running fraudulent call centers.
While Kravchenko has not been formally charged or named as a suspect in that inquiry, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has already requested that parliament vote to approve his dismissal. Kravchenko formally retains his post as prosecutor general pending the legislative vote.
